On this page

    Start here: the map, two reading paths and one running campaign

    In this chapter

    • Name the five layers of an ad system and what each one decides.
    • Choose a reading path: the four-hour gist path (three hours of reading, then a one-hour self-test) or the full day.
    • Follow one ad click to a purchase and see what the bill and the report each tell you.

    The gist. An ad system turns a stream of one-off chances to show an ad into money, under contracts that say who pays whom for which event. Five pieces interact: a model guesses what each impression will lead to, a contract says what is billed, an auction and a budget decide what is bought, real-time systems carry out and record each decision, and experiments check whether the ads caused any sales.

    Five layers decide what happens to every impression

    An ad system prices, allocates and settles one-off impression opportunities while its feedback is delayed and incomplete. An impression opportunity is one chance to show one ad to one user in one slot at one moment. Five layers interact, and each has a chapter:

    • A model estimates a conditional expectation, such as the probability that this impression leads to a purchase (Prediction and data).
    • The product contract decides who pays whom for which event, and so who bears which risk (Products and cash flow).
    • Auctions and budgets decide which opportunities are bought, and at what price (Auctions and bidding).
    • Systems execute each decision before its deadline and record it exactly once (Real-time systems).
    • Experiments can test whether the advertising caused sales that would not otherwise have happened (Measurement).

    Profit depends on all five; a gain in one layer can be undone by another. The landscape places them in the industry: ad formats, who sells to whom, and where the money is. The case study, AppLovin and Axon, uses three product names: Axon is AppLovin's prediction and bidding engine; MAX is its mediation product, which runs an auction among ad networks for each ad slot in a publisher's app; Adjust is a mobile measurement partner (MMP) that AppLovin owns; MMPs are normally independent third parties that record app installs and in-app events and credit them to ads.

    Two reading paths

    Read the gist path first: it covers the whole system in about three hours of reading, then a one-hour self-test. It reads chapters 1–3 and the case study, then does the gist set of exercises. Collapsed calculations are available when you want to work through the numbers. For chapters 4–6 it reads only the gist level: the “In this chapter” box, the gist paragraph, and the first sentence of each section, which states that section's claim. The full day reads everything; chapter 7 is optional unless you build serving systems. Chapter 10 is for lookup: reading list, glossary and errata. Terms in the table: CPM, CPC and CPA are prices per 1,000 impressions, per click and per action (such as a purchase); oCPM bills per 1,000 impressions while the platform bids toward the advertiser's target price per action (chapter 3). ROAS (return on ad spend) is revenue credited to ads divided by ad spend. In a first-price auction the winner pays its own bid; in a second-price auction, the highest competing bid.

    The gist path is 20 + 45 + 40 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 40 + 60 = 235 minutes. The full day is 20 + 45 + 40 + 80 + 50 + 40 + 40 + 40 + 60 + 90 = 505 minutes of study plus 15 + 60 + 10 + 10 = 95 minutes of breaks. Ten hours is long for one sitting: the depth set works as well the next morning.

    After the full day you should be able to answer six questions:

    1. How much is a given impression worth, and to whom? (This chapter.)
    2. Which pricing product makes the platform bear conversion risk, and which makes the advertiser bear it? (Billing and bidding.)
    3. How should an advertiser bid under a budget? (Chapter 4.)
    4. Why does a model that scores better on held-out logs not necessarily make more money online? (Chapter 5 and chapter 6.)
    5. How do you keep auction wins, billing and attribution from being conflated in the books? (Chapter 7.)
    6. What evidence would show that a model creates a durable commercial advantage? (Chapter 8.)

    A fictional campaign used throughout

    A shopper taps a shoe store’s ad in an app and buys a pair of shoes. The store is the advertiser, the app owner is the publisher, and the ad network connects them.

    • Attributed conversion. The report counts the purchase for the campaign because it follows an ad click within the campaign’s attribution window, the time allowed between the click and the purchase.
    • Billable conversion. The contract charges $30 for an attributed purchase that meets the billing rules. That $30 is the advertiser’s ad spend for this event.
    • Incremental conversions. These are the additional purchases the campaign generates. A randomized holdout experiment estimates how many extra purchases the campaign produces across a group. If this shopper would have bought the shoes anyway, their purchase adds zero incremental conversions.

    Billing follows the contract. To decide whether to keep spending, the store compares its ad spend with the contribution from incremental purchases after product and fulfillment costs. Google Ads on attributed and incremental conversions · Google Ads on paying for conversions

    Optional worked example for 1,000 impressions

    One campaign, with one set of numbers, runs through the whole reader. Its numbers are teaching assumptions, not AppLovin's rates or industry benchmarks.

    Roles. The advertiser is a merchant that pays for advertising. The publisher owns the app or website with the ad slots. The ad network (later also called the platform) sits between them: it buys impressions from publishers and bills advertisers.

    Events, in order. A bid request is the publisher's invitation to bid on one opportunity. A win means the network won that auction. An impression means the ad was displayed. A click means the user tapped it. A conversion is the agreed target action, here a purchase. Attribution credits an order to an ad by fixed rules; here only orders that follow a click on the ad, within the contract's attribution window, are credited. A billable attributed conversion is a credited order that also passes the contract's checks (deduplication, refunds, chargebacks) and is billed exactly once. Attribution is a crediting rule, not a measurement of cause: a credited order may have happened without the ad.

    The contract. The network charges the advertiser a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable attributed conversion. This is a CPA (cost per action) contract. The network buys the impressions from publishers in auctions and pays the auction price, written PPP per 1,000 impressions, whatever the advertiser is billed. Each order is worth g=$40g=\$40g=$40 of pre-advertising contribution to the advertiser: sales revenue minus the cost of goods, fulfillment and other variable costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. There are N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 similar bid opportunities per day and a daily budget B=$2,000B=\$2{,}000B=$2,000 for buying impressions. Whose budget that is depends on the contract. In chapter 4's main line the advertiser buys directly, so BBB caps its spend. Under the CPA contract it caps the network's payments to publishers (chapter 4's optional network appendix), not the advertiser's bill, which is $30 per conversion however much the network paid.

    The advertising landscape

    In this chapter

    • Trace who pays whom in the three ways ads are bought: guaranteed deals, auctions inside a walled garden, and open programmatic auctions through DSPs, exchanges and SSPs (in apps, through mediation).
    • Say why search, social feeds, display, in-app, video and connected TV, and retail media price differently, and how brand buying differs from performance buying.
    • Place CPM, CPC, CPA and optimized bidding (oCPM, target CPA, Advantage+, Performance Max) on one ladder, and rank two ads by eCPM=1000×pCTR×pCVR×CPA bid\text{eCPM}=1000\times\text{pCTR}\times\text{pCVR}\times\text{CPA bid}eCPM=1000×pCTR×pCVR×CPA bid.
    • Say who converts a click or conversion bid into a price per impression: the platform inside a walled garden, the DSP or ad network on the open web, while the exchange only ranks CPM bids.
    • State what third-party cookies, Apple's ATT and Chrome's 2024–25 decision to keep third-party cookies and retire Privacy Sandbox changed about measurement.
    • Read the 2025 advertising revenue of Alphabet, Meta and Amazon and the US market by format, and know which parts of the field this reader does not cover.

    The gist. Advertising sells users' attention. Advertisers pay; publishers own the screens; platforms in between choose which ad each user sees, mostly by running an auction for every ad slot. Most of the money goes to a few companies that own both the users and the auction, such as Google, Meta and Amazon. Formats differ in how much they reveal about what the user wants right now, and that sets their prices. Pricing has moved from paying per view toward bidding on results such as purchases, which forces the platform to predict those results for every impression. Privacy rules now limit how results can be observed. The rest of this reader goes deep on one slice: performance ads bought in auctions.

    Advertisers pay for attention through three kinds of market

    Money flows from advertisers to whoever controls users' screens, and the route it takes falls into one of three markets: a negotiated deal, an auction inside one company, or an auction across many companies. Five parties appear in every route:

    • The advertiser pays to reach users, from a global brand to a mobile game studio.
    • An agency plans and buys media for large advertisers for a fee; small advertisers buy directly in self-serve tools.
    • The publisher owns the content and the ad slots (its inventory): a news site, a mobile game, a streaming service.
    • A platform is the software, and usually the company, that decides which ad fills a slot and handles the money. Some platforms are their own publisher.
    • The user pays in attention, not cash; spend too much of it and users leave.
    1. Guaranteed (direct) deals. The advertiser or its agency agrees a fixed price and volume with a publisher in advance, for example one million impressions on a sports site's home page next month at a fixed CPM (price per 1,000 impressions). The publisher bears the risk of not delivering the volume. Software may execute the deal (programmatic guaranteed), but the price is negotiated, not auctioned.
    2. Auctions inside a walled garden. A walled garden is a company that owns the users, the ad slots, the auction and the measurement: Google (Search, YouTube), Meta (Facebook, Instagram), Amazon, and ByteDance (TikTok, and Douyin in China, where its ad platform is called Ocean Engine). The company auctions every impression, and outsiders cannot see user-level data. Most of the money is here (below).
    3. Open programmatic. For the rest of the internet, independent websites and apps, no single company owns both sides. Each impression passes through a chain of specialised intermediaries and is usually sold by real-time bidding (RTB): a separate auction for each impression, run within a fraction of a second while the page or app loads. Programmatic means any automated buying; RTB is its auction form.

    The open-programmatic chain has its own vocabulary. A DSP (demand-side platform) is the buyer's software: it receives bid requests, predicts what each impression is worth to its advertisers, and bids within their budgets. An SSP (supply-side platform) is the seller's software: it offers each impression to many buyers, applies the publisher's floor prices and rules, and collects payment. An ad exchange is the marketplace that runs the auction between them; today SSP and exchange are usually one product. Between open auctions and guaranteed deals sit private marketplaces (PMPs): auctions open only to invited buyers, often with a floor price. On the web, publishers moved from calling buyers one at a time to header bidding (from about 2015): the page asks several SSPs to bid at once, and the publisher's ad server then picks the winner among those bids and its direct deals. Each hop takes a fee, so the publisher receives less than the advertiser spends.

    Mobile apps add one more layer. An app usually embeds the software development kits (SDKs) of several ad networks, and mediation software in the app decides which network fills each ad slot. Under a waterfall, mediation calls networks one at a time in a fixed priority order set from their past average prices, and the first one that accepts fills the slot. Under in-app bidding, all networks bid on the same impression at once and the highest bid wins, so a network that values this particular user highly can win even if its average price is low; the industry has moved toward bidding. AppLovin's MAX, Unity's LevelPlay and Google's AdMob are the main mediation products; chapter 8 walks through one MAX auction.

    The running campaign of chapter 1 sits in lane 3a: an ad network buys app impressions in auctions and bills the advertiser per purchase. Walled gardens run the same machinery internally, so most of what later chapters derive applies to them too.

    Formats price differently because they reveal different amounts of intent

    A format is worth more per impression when the context tells the platform what the user wants right now, and when the platform can see whether the ad led to a sale. A search query states a need; a feed only hints at one; a banner on a news article says little.

    FormatWhat the user is doingHow it is usually sold and billedWhat drives its price
    SearchTyping a query that states a current needAuction per query, inside Google or Microsoft; billed per clickExplicit intent; competition on commercial keywords
    Social and feedScrolling content from friends and creatorsAuction inside Meta, TikTok, Snap and others; mostly billed per impression with optimized biddingRich behavioural data and huge scale; intent must be predicted
    Display (open web)Reading a page with banner or native ad slotsOpen programmatic or PMP; billed per impressionWeak intent, fragmented supply, intermediary fees, fraud risk
    In-appPlaying a game or using an app between tasksMediation plus ad networks; publishers paid per impression, advertisers often buy installs or in-app revenueInstall and in-app purchase data; rewarded formats hold full attention
    Video and CTVWatching online video or streaming TVGuaranteed deals and programmatic; billed per impression or per completed viewFull-screen, sound-on attention; mostly brand budgets; harder to link to sales
    Retail mediaShopping on a retailer's site or appAuction inside the retailer (Amazon, Walmart and others); sponsored listings billed per clickPurchase intent plus a closed loop: the seller sees the sale itself

    Search is an early example of an auction market for digital ads. Advertisers bid on keywords; each query triggers an auction among the ads whose keywords match it. In the late 1990s GoTo.com (later Overture) ranked ads by bid and charged each winner its own bid per click. Google’s AdWords Select auction, introduced in 2002, changed two things: it ranked ads by bid times predicted click-through rate, so an ad that users click more often can outrank a higher bid, and each winner paid only what it needed to keep its position. That payment rule is the generalized second-price (GSP) auction. Edelman, Ostrovsky and Schwarz (2007) showed that, unlike a true second-price auction, it does not make bidding one's true value optimal. Google's ranking score today, Ad Rank, combines the bid with a quality estimate built from expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; the advertiser-facing summary of that estimate is the Quality Score. Search remains Google's revenue base: in 2025 “Search & other” brought in $224.5 billion of Google's $294.7 billion advertising revenue, 76%.

    Retail media sells ads on a store's own shelves, and its edge is the closed loop. On Amazon, a Sponsored Products ad is a product listing promoted in search results or on product pages, bought by keyword auction and billed per click. Because the ad, the click and the purchase all happen inside the retailer, it observes the sale directly, without cookies or a third-party measurement company. The retailer can link purchases it observes to ad interactions. Sales outside its measurement coverage may be missing, and the reported conversions use attribution rules. The IAB's broader term is commerce media.

    Connected TV (CTV) is streaming video watched on a television set (smart TV, streaming stick or console). It carries traditional TV budgets and commands high CPMs because the ad fills a large screen with sound on, but viewers rarely click, so tying a CTV ad to a later purchase needs statistical matching rather than a click trail. In mobile apps the comparable high-attention unit is rewarded video: the user opts in to watch a full ad for an in-game reward, and app-install campaigns buy it heavily.

    Brand and performance buy different things

    Brand advertising buys exposure to the right people; performance advertising buys measurable actions. A brand campaign is planned in reach (the number of distinct people who see the ad at least once) and frequency (the average number of times each of them sees it), often with a frequency cap such as three per week. It is bought per impression, often through guaranteed deals, and judged by awareness surveys or later sales studies. A performance campaign is judged by actions it can count, such as installs or purchases, and buys whatever impressions produce them at an acceptable cost, almost always by auction. This reader is about performance buying; brand planning and guaranteed-delivery allocation are among the gaps listed at the end of this chapter.

    Pricing moved the bid toward results, while the auction still sells impressions

    Over three decades the event advertisers bid on moved down the funnel (the sequence impression, click, conversion), but a slot is still sold one impression at a time, so the platform must convert every bid into a price per impression using predicted rates. The main pricing products, in roughly historical order:

    • CPM (cost per mille): pay per 1,000 impressions. The original banner price, still standard for brand, video and most open-web supply.
    • CPC (cost per click): pay per click. It made search advertising work, because a click on a search ad signals interest directly.
    • CPA (cost per action): pay per agreed action, such as an install (then often called CPI) or a purchase. Common with affiliate and mobile ad networks, and the contract of the running campaign; it needs conversions the platform can verify (chapter 3).
    • Optimized bidding: the advertiser states a target per action and the platform bids per impression on its behalf with its own models, while billing stays per impression or per click. TikTok and the Chinese platforms call these products oCPM and oCPC (optimized CPM or CPC, together oCPX). Google's Smart Bidding pursues a target CPA (average cost per conversion) or a target ROAS (return on ad spend: attributed revenue divided by spend). The newest step automates more than the bid. Google's Performance Max (2021) is one goal-based campaign that buys across all Google inventory: Search, YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail and Maps. Meta's Advantage+ campaigns likewise let Meta's models choose audience, placement and creative. Several Chinese oCPX platforms also offer cost guarantees: if realized cost per conversion overshoots the target by more than a stated tolerance, the platform refunds part of the excess.

    Check the billable event, bidding strategy, and campaign KPI separately. Chapter 3 compares pricing and bidding models.

    To rank bids made on different events, the platform restates each as an eCPM (effective CPM): the expected payment per 1,000 impressions. With pCTR the platform's predicted click-through rate (clicks per impression) and pCVR its predicted conversion rate (conversions per click),

    eCPMCPC=1000×pCTR×CPC bid,eCPMCPA=1000×pCTR×pCVR×CPA bid.\begin{aligned}\text{eCPM}_{\text{CPC}}&=1000\times\text{pCTR}\times\text{CPC bid},\\ \text{eCPM}_{\text{CPA}}&=1000\times\text{pCTR}\times\text{pCVR}\times\text{CPA bid}.\end{aligned}eCPMCPC​eCPMCPA​​=1000×pCTR×CPC bid,=1000×pCTR×pCVR×CPA bid.​

    The running campaign's $30 CPA price, used as the bid when the network ranks its own advertisers, with pCTR = 0.01 and pCVR = 0.05, ranks at 1000×0.01×0.05×$30=$151000\times0.01\times0.05\times\$30=\$151000×0.01×0.05×$30=$15, the eCPM of chapter 1. Google's Ad Rank and Meta's “total value” add quality terms to this score, but the core is the same product of bid and predicted rates.

    Worked example

    The higher bid can lose

    Given: one ad slot and two CPC advertisers. A bids $0.30 per click with pCTR = 3%; B bids $0.40 per click with pCTR = 2%. The slot goes to the higher eCPM; there is no floor price.

    1. A's eCPM: 1000×0.03×$0.30=$9.1000\times0.03\times\$0.30=\$9.1000×0.03×$0.30=$9.
    2. B's eCPM: 1000×0.02×$0.40=$8.1000\times0.02\times\$0.40=\$8.1000×0.02×$0.40=$8.
    3. A wins with the lower bid. Under GSP pricing A pays the lowest CPC that still matches B's eCPM: $81000×0.03=$0.26‾≈$0.27 per click.\frac{\$8}{1000\times0.03}=\$0.2\overline{6}\approx\$0.27\text{ per click}.1000×0.03$8​=$0.26≈$0.27 per click.

    Result: A wins at an eCPM of $9 against $8, and pays about $0.27 per click, less than its $0.30 bid.

    Check: at that price the platform expects 1000×0.03×$0.26‾=$81000\times0.03\times\$0.2\overline{6}=\$81000×0.03×$0.26=$8 per 1,000 impressions, exactly B's eCPM, as a second-price rule should give. Ranking by bid alone would hand the slot to B, whose clicks are worth $8 per 1,000 impressions to the platform against A's $9 at the same bids.

    The formula makes the platform's prediction a price-setting variable. If A's pCTR were overestimated, A would win impressions it should not and the platform would collect less than it expected; which party absorbs that error depends on the product (chapter 3). Getting these rates right, and calibrated on the impressions actually won, is the subject of chapter 5.

    Whoever accepts a click or conversion price must predict; an exchange that is paid per impression only ranks prices

    The conversion from a bid to a price per impression is done by whichever party agrees to be paid per click or per conversion while buying impressions. Inside a walled garden that is the platform; on the open web it is the DSP or ad network, never the exchange. The exchange charges every buyer per impression, so its revenue does not depend on whether anyone clicks. It has no use for pCTR or pCVR, and it ranks the bids by price alone.

    Inside a walled garden the platform runs the whole conversion. Suppose the running campaign's advertiser bought with oCPM and a $30 target cost per conversion instead of the $30 CPA price. The platform computes the $15 eCPM above, ranks it against other ads, and in this simplified second-price example charges the runner-up’s eCPM. If the runner-up's eCPM is $12, the advertiser pays $12 per 1,000 impressions, and its expected cost per conversion is ($12/1000)/(0.01×0.05)=$24(\$12/1000)/(0.01\times0.05)=\$24($12/1000)/(0.01×0.05)=$24, below the $30 target. If the goal is to increase conversions at an average cost of at most $30 and budget remains available, a controller may raise bids after enough conversions have been measured. The target is an average over many auctions, not the price of any one impression, and a controller adjusts the bid multiplier using observed costs, the same kind of control as the budget pacing of chapter 4.

    On the open web each layer prices in its own unit:

    LayerPrice it acceptsHow it ranksWho predicts
    Advertiser to DSP or ad networkCPM, CPC, CPA or a ROAS target, as the contract allowseCPM across its own advertisersThe DSP, with its own models
    DSP to exchangeCPM onlyHighest bid above the publisher's floor priceNobody; the bid is already a price per impression
    Exchange to publisherThe exchange's price minus its feeThe publisher's ad server compares it with direct dealsNobody

    The OpenRTB standard, which most exchanges use for bid requests, defines the bid price field as a CPM “although the actual transaction is for a unit impression only” (IAB Tech Lab, OpenRTB 2.6, Bid object).

    Worked example

    The exchange never sees the prediction

    Given: the running campaign's advertiser buys through a DSP that values the impression at the same $15 eCPM, reduces its estimated bid value by 20% for this example, and bids into a first-price exchange. A brand advertiser's DSP bids a flat $7 CPM with no prediction at all.

    1. The performance DSP’s value after the 20% reduction: $15×(1−0.20)=$12 CPM.\$15\times(1-0.20)=\$12\text{ CPM}.$15×(1−0.20)=$12 CPM.
    2. In a first-price auction the winner pays its own bid, so the DSP bids below its value. Suppose it applies the half-value shading rule from Chapter 4’s uniform-threshold model. Here we use the rule to choose an illustrative bid, then show one auction with a $7 competing bid. Its bid is $12/2=$6 CPM.\$12/2=\$6\text{ CPM}.$12/2=$6 CPM.
    3. The exchange compares $6 with $7. It does not know that one bid came from a conversion model and the other from a flat price.

    Result: the brand bid wins at $7 CPM; the exchange ranked two prices per impression and predicted nothing.

    Check: every number the exchange used, $6 and $7, is a price per 1,000 impressions, the same unit it bills in. The pCTR and pCVR behind the $15 stayed inside the DSP.

    Moving the prediction to the bidder has costs. The DSP sees only what the bid request carries (app or site, placement, device, location, and an identifier when consent allows), not the user's history inside the publisher's app. It learns outcomes only for impressions it won, and it wins most where it overpredicted (chapter 5). The exchange cannot down-rank an ad users dislike, so publishers rely on floor prices, blocklists and creative review. An ad network such as AppLovin or Pangle sits in between: it sells to advertisers per install or against a ROAS target, predicts the install rate itself from its SDK data, and bids a CPM into the app's mediation auction (above, and chapter 8).

    Measurement decides what can be optimized, and privacy rules now limit it

    A platform can only optimize toward events it can observe and link to an ad, and since 2020 browsers and Apple's iOS have removed much of the cross-company tracking that made that linking easy. Start with two kinds of measurement. Attribution credits a conversion to an earlier ad by a rule, such as “the last ad clicked within seven days”; it is bookkeeping and can credit sales that would have happened anyway. Incrementality asks how many conversions the ad caused, which needs a randomized experiment with a control group. Optimization and billing run on attribution; whether the advertiser should keep paying depends on incrementality. Chapter 6 develops this difference.

    Linking an ad on one company's property to a purchase on another's relied on shared identifiers. A third-party cookie is a small identifier stored in the browser by a domain other than the site being visited, typically an ad-tech company embedded on many sites, so the same browser can be recognized across all of them. On phones the equivalent is the mobile advertising ID: Apple's IDFA and Google's advertising ID on Android, a per-device identifier that any app could read. Four steps reshaped this:

    1. 2020
      Safari blocks all third-party cookies by default (March 2020); Firefox already blocked known trackers' cookies by default. On those browsers, cross-site conversion measurement through third-party cookies stopped working.
    2. 2021
      Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT), from iOS 14.5, requires an app to ask the user's permission before tracking them across other companies' apps and websites or reading the IDFA; without permission the IDFA reads as all zeros. Install attribution on iOS moved to Apple's own privacy-preserving reports, SKAdNetwork and its successor AdAttributionKit, which send a signed, delayed postback for each attributed install, with no user identifier and with fields coarsened for small campaigns (chapter 6 has the timing).
    3. 2024–25
      Chrome plans, then abandons, removing third-party cookies. Google announced in 2020 that Chrome would phase them out and built replacement “Privacy Sandbox” interfaces for targeting and measurement. After several delays it dropped the removal in 2024, said in April 2025 that Chrome would keep its current approach of letting users choose, and on 17 October 2025 announced it would retire most Privacy Sandbox technologies, including Topics, Protected Audience and Attribution Reporting, on Chrome and Android, citing low adoption.
    4. 2026
      Status at the time of writing (November 2026): Chrome still allows third-party cookies unless the user blocks them, and the retired Privacy Sandbox interfaces are being removed. Safari blocks them; Firefox blocks known trackers' cookies and confines the rest to the site that set them. Consent laws such as the EU's GDPR apply regardless of browser defaults.

    Platforms filled the gap with modelled conversions: where a conversion cannot be linked to an ad, the platform estimates the link from similar users it can observe and reports observed and modelled conversions together. Google, for example, reports both in its standard Conversions column. Two consequences follow. Training labels are partly the output of other models, and are missing more often for users who declined tracking, so they are not a random sample (chapter 5). And walled gardens, which see clicks and often purchases on their own properties, lost less signal than the open web, one reason money keeps concentrating in them.

    The auction-and-prediction machinery in this reader is therefore not a niche: search, social feeds and retail media, where intent is visible or predictable from a company's own data, take most of the money. The open web and the app ecosystem compete for the rest against companies that see the whole loop from impression to purchase; that is where AppLovin (chapter 8) competes.

    Products and cash flow

    In this chapter

    • Describe any ad product by five separate choices: context, creative, how it is sold, what is billed and what is optimized.
    • Distinguish the billable event, bidding strategy, and campaign KPI. Compare how conversion forecasts affect each party under CPM, CPC, CPA, oCPC and oCPM.
    • Explain why CPA billing needs conversions the platform can verify, why oCPC and oCPM exist and differ only in who bears click-rate error, and why platforms selling them offer cost guarantees.
    • Trace $100 of advertiser spend through net and gross revenue recognition: the same $20 gross profit shows as an 80% or a 20% gross margin.
    • Decide whether to scale a budget by comparing the return on the additional spend with the break-even return, one over the contribution margin.

    The gist. An ad product is a contract. It names the event the advertiser pays for and the result the advertiser wants, and these are usually different events. Between the impression the auction sells and the purchase the advertiser wants lie conversion rates that nobody knows exactly. Whoever has to pay when a rate turns out lower than expected carries that risk, and choosing a pricing product (per impression, per click, per purchase, or an “optimized” variant) is choosing who that is. The second half follows the money into the books: a platform's margin, an advertiser's average return and the return on its next dollar are three different numbers, and only the last one says whether to spend more.

    An ad product is five separate choices

    Search, feed, real-time bidding, CPC and performance advertising are not categories of one kind; each answers a different question. Search and feed are user contexts. Real-time bidding (RTB: a separate auction for each impression while the page or app loads) is a way of selling. CPC (cost per click) is a billing event. Performance advertising is an objective: the advertiser pays for, and judges results by, measurable actions such as installs or purchases, unlike brand advertising, which buys reach. Forcing these into one taxonomy produces the wrong objective function downstream. The landscape surveys the values each dimension takes; this chapter needs only the dimensions.

    Dimension Example values What it decides
    User context Search, content feed, in-game interstitial (a full-screen ad between levels) How the user reveals intent, and how much the ad disrupts the product
    Creative Text, video, playable ad (a short interactive demo of a game) How ads are produced, reviewed and measured
    Transaction type Guaranteed deal (fixed price and volume), private auction, open auction via RTB Who commits to volume and who bears the risk of under-delivery
    Billing event Impression, click, install, purchase When money is owed, and who bears the risk that a paid-for impression yields no click or conversion (billing and bidding)
    Optimization objective Clicks, installs, revenue, incremental profit Model labels, observation windows and constraints

    One product takes one value from each row. A rewarded video, an ad the user opts into inside a game for an in-game reward, can be sold in a first-price auction (the winner pays its own bid; chapter 4), billed per impression and optimized toward a target D7 ROAS (defined below). These choices do not conflict, because each belongs to a different dimension. The reward also means that finishing the video does not signal intent to buy. Google AdMob rewarded ads documentation

    The contract must define every event it pays for or optimizes

    “Optimize for purchases” is not yet a contract: each event and value needs an operational definition before a model can target it or an invoice can count it. Does a purchase mean an order placed, a payment completed, or an order still valid after the refund period? Is its value merchandise revenue, a commission or contribution profit? Changing one definition changes training labels, delivery and reports with no change to the model. A campaign setup is therefore an executable contract: conversion events, budget and flight dates (start and end of delivery), audiences, creatives, attribution rules, value postbacks (server-to-server messages that report each conversion and its value to the platform) and billing terms.

    Definitions used later. ROAS (return on ad spend) is revenue credited to ads by the attribution rules divided by ad spend, often quoted as a percentage (300% means 3.0); iROAS (incremental ROAS) uses instead the revenue that would not have occurred without the ads. D7 ROAS counts a cohort's attributed revenue in the window [t0, t0+168 h)[t_0,\ t_0+168\text{ h})[t0​, t0​+168 h), where t0t_0t0​ is acquisition (for apps, the install), and is valid only once the window has closed for every user. LTV (lifetime value) must state its horizon, revenue or contribution, refunds, discounting, and whether acquisition cost is already subtracted; treating revenue LTV as profit overstates what you can afford to bid.

    Billable events, bidding strategies, and campaign KPIs

    The billable event determines what triggers a charge. A bidding strategy determines how bids are set. A key performance indicator (KPI), such as day 7 ROAS, measures the campaign against the advertiser’s goal.

    Units: CPM (cost per mille) is a price per 1,000 impressions, CPC per click, CPI per install, CPA (cost per action) per contractually defined action such as a purchase. CTR is clicks per impression and CVR is conversions per click in these examples; the platform's predictions of them are pCTR and pCVR. eCPM restates any per-event price per 1,000 impressions, eCPM=1000×amount/impressions\text{eCPM}=1000\times\text{amount}/\text{impressions}eCPM=1000×amount/impressions. In oCPM and oCPC the advertiser states a target price per conversion, the platform turns it into a bid with its model, and billing stays per impression or per click.

    In this model the auction sells one impression opportunity and ranks bids in eCPM. When the platform pays for impressions and charges for clicks or conversions, its receipts per impression depend on how often the billable event occurs.

    Pricing modelBillable eventEffect of fewer conversions
    CPMImpressionA lower purchase rate raises the advertiser’s cost per purchase.
    CPCClickA lower purchase rate per click raises the advertiser’s cost per purchase.
    CPA pricingQualifying conversionWith a fixed charge per conversion, the platform collects less per impression when conversions fall.
    oCPCClickThe platform uses predicted conversion rates to bid toward the target. The advertiser’s actual cost per purchase can differ.
    oCPMImpressionThe platform uses predicted conversion rates to bid toward the target. The advertiser’s actual cost per purchase can differ.

    Google Ads calls its automated bidding strategy Target CPA and separately specifies the payment mode. Depending on campaign eligibility, a campaign can bid toward Target CPA and pay for clicks, conversions, or viewable impressions. Google Ads on Display bidding strategies and payment modes

    One campaign under five products

    Given: the running example's forecast pclick=0.01p_{\text{click}}=0.01pclick​=0.01, pconv=0.05p_{\text{conv}}=0.05pconv​=0.05, so q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005; the advertiser's price per purchase a=$30a=\$30a=$30. The forecast sets fixed charges of $15 per 1,000 impressions, $1.50 per click, and $30 per conversion in this example. The same impressions are delivered in both scenarios. The platform’s media cost stays fixed.

    1. Bids, each ranked at an eCPM of $15. CPM: 1000×0.0005×$30=$151000\times0.0005\times\$30=\$151000×0.0005×$30=$15 CPM. CPC and oCPC: 0.05×$30=$1.500.05\times\$30=\$1.500.05×$30=$1.50 per click, ranked at 1000×0.01×$1.50=$151000\times0.01\times\$1.50=\$151000×0.01×$1.50=$15. CPA: $30 per purchase, ranked at 1000×0.0005×$30=$151000\times0.0005\times\$30=\$151000×0.0005×$30=$15. oCPM: 1000×0.01×0.05×$30=$151000\times0.01\times0.05\times\$30=\$151000×0.01×0.05×$30=$15 CPM. Under CPC the advertiser chose the 0.05; under oCPC and oCPM the platform's pCTR and pCVR supplied the rates.
    2. Scenario A, true CTR 0.005, CVR as forecast: per 1,000 impressions, 5 clicks and 5×0.05=0.255\times0.05=0.255×0.05=0.25 purchases. Bills: CPM and oCPM $15; CPC and oCPC 5×$1.50=$7.505\times\$1.50=\$7.505×$1.50=$7.50; CPA 0.25×$30=$7.500.25\times\$30=\$7.500.25×$30=$7.50.
    3. Scenario B, true CVR 0.025, CTR as forecast: 10 clicks and 10×0.025=0.2510\times0.025=0.2510×0.025=0.25 purchases. Bills: CPM, oCPM, CPC and oCPC $15 (10×$1.5010\times\$1.5010×$1.50 for the click products); CPA $7.50.

    Result: cost per purchase doubles to $60 exactly where the advertiser bears the mis-estimated rate: CPM and oCPM in both scenarios, CPC and oCPC in scenario B. Under CPA it stays $30; the platform absorbs the shortfall.

    With impression billing, fewer clicks or fewer purchases per click raise the advertiser’s cost per purchase. With click billing, fewer purchases per click raise it. With fixed per-conversion pricing, either change reduces the platform’s receipts per impression.

    Equal expected bills are a modelling convenience. Prediction errors can average out across the traffic actually bought if they have mean zero on that traffic. Selection can change that average. In addition, both sides need to account for systematic error and manipulable reports (the platform discounts pCTR on traffic it distrusts, the advertiser shades its CPM bid), so in practice expected bills differ across products.

    CPA needs a billing event the platform can verify

    Under CPA the conversion count sets the bill, so the platform must verify conversions itself or through a trusted third party. For apps that party is usually a mobile measurement partner (MMP, such as Adjust or AppsFlyer), which records installs and reported in-app events and attributes them to ads. An event reported by the advertiser still depends on the advertiser’s instrumentation. To see why, suppose the advertiser reports only a fraction kkk of its conversions, 0<k<10<k<10<k<1.

    • Under CPA, under-reporting pays. The bill per impression becomes a k qa\,k\,qakq, smaller by the factor kkk at once. Allocation follows the platform's eCPM=1000 a pCTR pCVR\text{eCPM}=1000\,a\,\text{pCTR}\,\text{pCVR}eCPM=1000apCTRpCVR; if pCVR is pooled across advertisers or updates with a lag, it does not fall, and the advertiser keeps the same impressions for less. With k=1/2k=1/2k=1/2 it pays $7.50 instead of $15 per 1,000 impressions while still ranked at $15.
    • Under oCPM, reports only affect allocation. The bill is the auction price per impression. Under-reporting scales pCVR by kkk, so the eCPM falls by kkk unless the target rises from aaa to a/ka/ka/k: 1000 a pCTR (k pCVR)=k⋅eCPM,1000 ak pCTR (k pCVR)=eCPM.\begin{aligned}1000\,a\,\text{pCTR}\,(k\,\text{pCVR})&=k\cdot\text{eCPM},\\ 1000\,\tfrac{a}{k}\,\text{pCTR}\,(k\,\text{pCVR})&=\text{eCPM}.\end{aligned}1000apCTR(kpCVR)1000ka​pCTR(kpCVR)​=k⋅eCPM,=eCPM.​ The restored eCPM wins the same impressions at the same price under either auction rule, so under-reporting leaves the invoice unchanged in this model. A feedback controller or guarantee based on reported conversions can change that incentive.

    The CPA gain lasts only while allocation ignores the reports. With an instant, advertiser-specific model, restoring allocation needs the price a/ka/ka/k, and the bill is back to (a/k) k q=a q(a/k)\,k\,q=a\,q(a/k)kq=aq.

    How click and impression billing allocate forecast risk

    Optimized bidding can target conversions while charging for clicks or impressions. Conversion billing is also possible when the contract defines which conversions qualify and how they are verified. Moving only the bid still helps the advertiser: under plain CPC it had to convert its $30 purchase value into a click bid with one fixed guess of the purchase rate per click, while under oCPC or oCPM the platform estimates a post-click conversion probability for each impression opportunity from user features and the advertiser's conversion reports.

    QuestionoCPCoCPM
    What the advertiser statesTarget cost per conversion, e.g. $30Same
    Auction scoreeCPM = 1000 × pCTR × pCVR × target, times any bid adjustment for pacing or cost controlSame
    Billable eventClickImpression
    Charge in an ideal second-price example with a $12 clearing eCPM and predicted CTR of 1%$12 ÷ (1000 × 0.01) = $1.20 per click$12 per 1,000 impressions
    Who pays when pCTR is too highThe platform: fewer clicks, so fewer charges (scenario A: $7.50 per 1,000 impressions instead of $15)The advertiser, until cost control lowers the bids or a cost guarantee pays (scenario A: $60 per purchase)
    Who pays when pCVR is too highThe advertiser (scenario B: $60 per purchase)The advertiser
    Charge for an impression without a clickNo click chargeThe impression is billable under the example contract

    Here both products use the same auction score and face the same competition. The billing event determines how a shortfall in clicks affects the invoice. Actual delivery also depends on pricing, pacing, and how the platform learns from campaign outcomes.

    • Platform freedom. Under oCPM the platform is paid for every impression it serves, so it can buy impressions that lead to conversions without a click, and it knows its revenue at serving time. Under oCPC an impression without a click pays nothing.
    • Incentives on click rate. At a fixed price per click and a fixed purchase rate per click, a higher click rate raises volume while leaving cost per purchase unchanged. At a fixed price per impression, it lowers cost per purchase. Changes in click forecasts can also change auction bids and prices.
    • Formats. Feeds, video and rewarded ads often have no click that signals interest; billing every format per impression puts them under one rule.
    • Trust. “Pay only when someone clicks” is easier to sell to an advertiser that distrusts the platform's models. In search the click is itself the signal of intent, and Google Ads documents Target CPA as a bidding strategy and click billing as a payment mode.
    • Fraud on ad networks. When publishers are separate companies, oCPM lets a publisher pad its impressions until the platform briefly overestimates conversions on its traffic, and the cost guarantee, which is computed per campaign, cannot be charged back to that publisher. Click billing requires a billable click. A publisher’s incentive also depends on how the platform pays the publisher.

    In both models, a lower purchase rate per click raises the advertiser’s cost per purchase at the fixed charges in the example.

    Cost guarantees for optimized bidding

    With optimized bidding, a contract may include a cost guarantee that compensates the advertiser when its cost per conversion exceeds the target by a specified amount. In scenario B an oCPC advertiser with a $30 target paid $60 per purchase because pCVR was biased. Overruns arise even with no bias, from selection: the auction buys the impressions where the estimate is highest, so even an unbiased model overpredicts on the impressions it wins (the winner's curse, chapter 5). A cost overrun can trigger compensation when the contract specifies a guarantee.

    Dual bids limit variance while the model learns

    A new campaign's conversion model has little data, so its bids are noisy. A dual bid states two prices: one for a frequent shallow event, such as an install, whose rate the platform already estimates well, and one for the rare deep event, such as a purchase. One possible rule converts each target into an impression value by multiplying it by its predicted event probability per impression. The bidder uses the lower of those two values as the maximum bid. This rule lets the frequent event cap a bid based on a noisy estimate of the rarer event. Taking the lower value can lose auctions that the deep-event bid alone would win.

    Platform margin, advertiser return and scaling are different questions

    A platform can hold an 80% gross margin while its advertiser loses money on every additional dollar. Below, one $100 budget is entered in two income statements, and then we ask what scaling does to each side. Amounts are for one period, “spend” is what the advertiser is billed, and refunds, credits and taxes are ignored.

    1. What is the denominator of an 80% gross margin?

    Four accounting terms first.

    • Take rate: the amount the platform keeps after paying the publisher, divided by total advertiser spend.
    • Gross vs net revenue recognition: a platform that recognizes revenue gross books the full advertiser spend as revenue and the publisher payout as a cost; one that recognizes revenue net books only the amount it keeps.
    • Cost of revenue: costs directly incurred to deliver the service, such as serving, data and payment processing. Under gross recognition it also includes the publisher payout, called TAC (traffic acquisition cost).
    • Gross profit = recognized revenue − cost of revenue. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ recognized revenue.
    Worked example

    $100 of spend under net and gross recognition

    Given, for one period: advertiser spend S=$100S=\$100S=$100; publisher payout P=$75P=\$75P=$75 (a period total here, not chapter 1's price per 1,000 impressions); the platform's direct service costs D=$5D=\$5D=$5, all classified as cost of revenue. Compare two platforms with identical cash flows, one that qualifies for net recognition and one that qualifies for gross recognition.

    1. Take rate, a cash-flow ratio identical for both: (S−P)/S=($100−$75)/$100=25%(S-P)/S=(\$100-\$75)/\$100=25\%(S−P)/S=($100−$75)/$100=25%.
    2. Net recognition: revenue =S−P=$25=S-P=\$25=S−P=$25; cost of revenue =D=$5=D=\$5=D=$5; gross profit =$25−$5=$20=\$25-\$5=\$20=$25−$5=$20; gross margin =$20/$25=80%=\$20/\$25=80\%=$20/$25=80%. The $75 payout appears in neither line.
    3. Gross recognition: revenue =S=$100=S=\$100=S=$100; cost of revenue =P+D=$75+$5=$80=P+D=\$75+\$5=\$80=P+D=$75+$5=$80 (the $75 is TAC); gross profit =$100−$80=$20=\$100-\$80=\$20=$100−$80=$20; gross margin =$20/$100=20%=\$20/\$100=20\%=$20/$100=20%.
    4. Gross profit per dollar of advertiser spend, under both: $20/$100=20%\$20/\$100=20\%$20/$100=20%.

    Result: same cash, same $20 gross profit; reported gross margin is 80% under net recognition and 20% under gross.

    Check: the two margins share the numerator and their denominators are S−PS-PS−P and SSS, so gross margin (gross) = take rate × gross margin (net) =0.25×0.80=0.20=0.25\times0.80=0.20=0.25×0.80=0.20.

    The 80% does not mean the platform keeps 80% of the ad budget, nor that 80% is profit; R&D, sales, taxes and the cost of capital still come out. Before comparing two ad companies' gross margins, align their revenue recognition. Here 80% versus 20% reflects no difference in efficiency at all.

    Which treatment applies is set by accounting standards, not chosen by the platform.

    Optional: who may recognize revenue gross

    Calling oneself an “agent” in a contract does not decide it. Under IFRS 15 and its US counterpart ASC 606, a platform that controls the ad placement before it passes to the advertiser is a principal and recognizes the gross amount; otherwise it is an agent and recognizes only its net fee. Indicators of control are primary responsibility for delivery, inventory risk (for example, buying impressions before any advertiser order) and discretion over price. Summary of IFRS 15 principal-versus-agent requirements

    2. Why does the advertiser's profit fall while its sales rise?

    Switch to the advertiser's ledger. Its revenue is what consumers pay it for goods; it has nothing to do with the $25 the platform recognizes. Let mmm be the advertiser's contribution margin: the fraction of each incremental sales dollar left after goods, fulfillment and other variable costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. Take m=40%m=40\%m=40%, constant across volume. “Profit” below means incremental contribution profit after ad spend, incremental sales × mmm − ad spend, and each column's revenue is assumed to be truly incremental.

    Advertiser's ledgerFirst $100Additional $50Cumulative $150
    Incremental sales revenue$300$75$375
    Variable non-advertising costs (60% of sales)$180$45$225
    Contribution before ad spend (40% of sales)$120$30$150
    Ad spend$100$50$150
    Contribution profit after ad spend$20−$20$0
    iROAS (incremental sales ÷ ad spend in that column)3.01.52.5

    The first $100 generates $120 of contribution and earns $20 after paying for itself. The additional $50 generates only $30 of contribution and loses $20 on its own. Sales rise from $300 to $375 while profit falls from $20 to zero.

    3. Average iROAS hides the loss on the additional budget

    Let CCC be ad spend and RRR the incremental revenue it generates. Contribution profit is mR−CmR-CmR−C, which for C>0C>0C>0 and m>0m>0m>0 is non-negative exactly when R/C≥1/mR/C\ge 1/mR/C≥1/m. So the break-even iROAS is 1/m1/m1/m: 2.5 at m=40%m=40\%m=40%. The decision to add spend ΔC\Delta CΔC, which brings additional incremental revenue ΔR\Delta RΔR, applies the same test to the increment: ΔR/ΔC\Delta R/\Delta CΔR/ΔC, the marginal iROAS, must reach 1/m1/m1/m.

    Worked example

    Should the advertiser add the extra $50?

    Given: m=0.4m=0.4m=0.4; incremental revenue R=$300R=\$300R=$300 at C=$100C=\$100C=$100 and R=$375R=\$375R=$375 at C=$150C=\$150C=$150, same window and revenue definition.

    1. Break-even iROAS: 1/m=1/0.4=2.51/m=1/0.4=2.51/m=1/0.4=2.5.
    2. Marginal iROAS of the increment: ΔR/ΔC=($375−$300)/($150−$100)=$75/$50=1.5\Delta R/\Delta C=(\$375-\$300)/(\$150-\$100)=\$75/\$50=1.5ΔR/ΔC=($375−$300)/($150−$100)=$75/$50=1.5.
    3. Profit change from the increment: ΔΠ=m ΔR−ΔC=0.4×$75−$50=−$20\Delta\Pi=m\,\Delta R-\Delta C=0.4\times\$75-\$50=-\$20ΔΠ=mΔR−ΔC=0.4×$75−$50=−$20.
    4. Average iROAS of the whole budget: $375/$150=2.5=1/m\$375/\$150=2.5=1/m$375/$150=2.5=1/m, so contribution profit at $150 is 0.4×$375−$150=$00.4\times\$375-\$150=\$00.4×$375−$150=$0.

    Result: do not add the $50. It lowers contribution profit by $20, although the cumulative iROAS of 2.5 still meets the break-even threshold.

    Check: profit at $100 is 0.4×$300−$100=$200.4\times\$300-\$100=\$200.4×$300−$100=$20 and at $150 is $0, a change of −$20. Equivalently, the increment needed ΔR≥2.5×$50=$125\Delta R\ge2.5\times\$50=\$125ΔR≥2.5×$50=$125 and delivered $75.

    The cumulative 2.5 sits at break-even only because the early high-return spend subsidizes the late low-return spend. The trading analogue: a scaled-up strategy's marginal capacity may not cover its costs while the book's average return hides the loss.

    Why does each additional dollar return less? Incremental revenue grows less than linearly in spend because a bidder buys its best opportunities first, so every extra dollar buys the best one still left, which is worse than everything already bought. Total return from spending down a list sorted best to worst is concave by construction. Linear growth would need the millionth impression to be as likely to cause a sale, and as cheap, as the first. Four forces make the list slope down:

    • Price rises with volume. In a first-price model with a fixed set of eligible opportunities and a single bid, raising that bid wins more impressions in expectation and raises the payment on impressions the lower bid would have won. In chapter 4's auction model, where every user is identical, spending $500 a day buys 158,114 impressions and spending $2,000 would buy 316,228: four times the budget, twice the impressions. This is market impact: the other bidders for the same users are the order book you walk up.
    • Worse users. A higher bid clears the bar for users with lower predicted conversion rates, so each additional conversion comes from a less likely buyer.
    • Saturation. The audience that wants the product is finite. More spend shows the ad again to the same people, and a fifth exposure adds far less than the first.
    • Lower incrementality. As spend grows, more of the people reached would have bought anyway, so caused revenue rises more slowly than attributed revenue (the ratio κ in section 5 falls with scale).

    Returns are roughly linear only while the advertiser is small relative to the market, far from moving prices or saturating its audience: a strategy well below its capacity. Very small budgets can even return less per dollar than slightly larger ones, because the platform's model cannot learn from a handful of conversions and brand recall needs repeated exposure, so the full curve is often S-shaped. Scaling decisions are usually made past that bend, in the concave region analysed here.

    4. Platform gross profit can grow while customer profit falls

    Now combine the two ledgers. Assume the platform always keeps 25% of the budget, its direct service costs are always 5% of the budget, and it recognizes revenue net.

    MetricAd budget $100Ad budget $150
    Platform net revenue$25$37.50
    Platform direct service costs$5$7.50
    Platform gross profit$20$30
    Platform gross margin80%80%
    Advertiser contribution profit$20$0

    Scaling up raises platform gross profit by $10 and cuts the advertiser's profit by $20. Customer retention and competition constrain a platform from exploiting this, but platform revenue growth, a high gross margin and customer profit growth do not automatically move together. An objective such as “maximize sales subject to cumulative iROAS ≥ 2.5” picks the $150 plan, which meets the constraint exactly and has higher sales; of these two plans, maximizing advertiser profit picks the $100 plan (the fitted curve in the optional box above puts the optimum at $75). An algorithm can execute its objective flawlessly and still produce a commercially bad outcome.

    5. The strongest assumption: revenue must be truly incremental

    “The platform attributes the order to the ad” and “the order would not have happened without the ad” are different claims. Suppose attributed revenue is A=$300A=\$300A=$300 but the revenue the ads caused is only R=$200R=\$200R=$200. Then the first $100 of spend already loses money: 0.4×$200−$100=−$200.4\times\$200-\$100=-\$200.4×$200−$100=−$20. In general, write κ=R/A\kappa=R/Aκ=R/A for caused ÷ attributed revenue. Profit is mR−C=mκA−CmR-C=m\kappa A-CmR−C=mκA−C, so for m,κ>0m,\kappa>0m,κ>0 attributed ROAS must reach

    AC≥1mκ=10.4×2/3=3.75,\frac{A}{C}\ge\frac{1}{m\kappa}=\frac{1}{0.4\times2/3}=3.75,CA​≥mκ1​=0.4×2/31​=3.75,

    above the reported 3.0. The ratio κ\kappaκ comes from a randomized experiment (chapter 6), not from the attribution report, and it can exceed 1 when attribution misses caused sales. To judge a platform such as Axon (chapter 8), ask: under the same measurement definition, margin and budget, how much does it raise the customer's incremental contribution profit, and how much of that survives as the budget grows? The platform's gross margin cannot answer it.

    Auctions and bidding: from advertiser value to a bid

    In this chapter

    • Name the decision-maker, contract and objective first: under the running $30 CPA contract the advertiser should buy nothing.
    • Derive the win probability from the distribution of the highest competing bid: a $6 CPM bid wins 30% of auctions.
    • Derive the advertiser's best bid when it pays the auction price: $4 CPM in first price, $8 CPM in second price.
    • Treat a budget as a cap, not a target: $2,000 leaves money unspent, while $500 lowers the bids to $3.16 and $4.47 CPM.
    • Read the general rules: bid shading, the budget multiplier and pacing as a feedback loop.

    The gist. An auction decides whose ad is shown and what the winner pays. A buyer must first know what an impression is worth to it under its contract; for an advertiser, that is the extra profit the ad causes. Then comes one trade-off: a higher bid wins more often, but in a first-price auction it also raises the price of every win, so the best bid sits below value. In a second-price auction the winner pays the runner-up's price, so bidding your value is best. A budget is a limit, not a goal; a sensible campaign can leave money unspent. Pacing is the feedback loop that keeps spending on track through the day.

    Start with whose money and whose objective

    The decision-maker here is the advertiser (or an agent buying for it), and its objective is incremental contribution after advertising costs. Contribution is revenue minus goods, fulfillment and other variable costs; “incremental” counts only sales the ads caused.

    Advertiser objective=incremental sales contribution−total advertising bill.\text{Advertiser objective}=\text{incremental sales contribution}-\text{total advertising bill}.Advertiser objective=incremental sales contribution−total advertising bill.

    Take the contract from Chapter 1: the advertiser pays a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable attributed order. Per successful impression, a billable order occurs with probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005; the ad causes an extra order with probability Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002; each extra order is worth g=$40g=\$40g=$40 of contribution. These are teaching inputs, fixed as the bid changes.

    Incremental contribution per impression=Δq g=0.0002×40=$0.008,Expected bill per impression=q a=0.0005×30=$0.015,Advertiser gain per impression=0.008−0.015=−$0.007.\begin{aligned} \text{Incremental contribution per impression}&=\Delta q\,g=0.0002\times40=\$0.008,\\ \text{Expected bill per impression}&=q\,a=0.0005\times30=\$0.015,\\ \text{Advertiser gain per impression}&=0.008-0.015=-\$0.007. \end{aligned}Incremental contribution per impressionExpected bill per impressionAdvertiser gain per impression​=Δqg=0.0002×40=$0.008,=qa=0.0005×30=$0.015,=0.008−0.015=−$0.007.​

    With DDD expected impressions the advertiser gains D(Δq g−q a)=−0.007DD(\Delta q\,g-q\,a)=-0.007DD(Δqg−qa)=−0.007D, so its best choice is zero impressions. No bid fixes a contract that loses on every impression; renegotiating, raising causal lift or stopping come first. A reselling network keeps a different ledger, its spread (collections minus publisher payments), and can profit while the advertiser loses. The optional network-spread appendix works that case, including its $7.50 and $6.3246 CPM bids.

    A separate worked contract: the advertiser pays the auction cost

    To study a bid worth making, change the contract: the advertiser buys impressions directly and pays exactly the auction price, with no fee or markup. It no longer pays the $30 CPA; causal lift and contribution per order are unchanged. This is an analytical baseline, not AppLovin's contract.

    Why does a $6 CPM bid win 30% of opportunities?

    We win when our bid beats the highest competing bid, so the win probability is the chance that this competing bid falls below ours. If competitors bid $3, $5 and $9 CPM, the price to beat is ZZZ = $9 CPM: a $6 CPM bid loses and a $10 CPM bid wins. ZZZ is called the competitive threshold. With no floor price (a seller's minimum price) and at least one competitor,

    Z=max⁡{competing bids},win  ⟺  b≥Z.Z=\max\{\text{competing bids}\},\qquad \text{win}\iff b\ge Z.Z=max{competing bids},win⟺b≥Z.

    Ties (probability zero below) go to us. The threshold decides whether we win; the auction rule decides what we pay.

    ZZZ varies across auctions and is unknown in advance, so model it as random: Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L), meaning equal-length price intervals in $0–20 CPM are equally likely, on every opportunity, whatever we bid. We win exactly when ZZZ lands in [0,b][0,b][0,b], an interval of length bbb out of LLL. So the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of ZZZ is the win probability:

    F(b)=P(Z≤b)=bL,0≤b≤L.F(b)=P(Z\le b)=\frac{b}{L},\qquad 0\le b\le L.F(b)=P(Z≤b)=Lb​,0≤b≤L.

    A $6 CPM bid wins against thresholds in $0–6 and loses against $6–20: 6/20 = 30% and 14/20 = 70%. For b≥Lb\ge Lb≥L, F=1F=1F=1, so bidding above LLL buys nothing.

    $0$5$10$15$20 CPM

    Win: thresholds $0–6.0 CPM → 6.0 / 20 = 30%. Lose: thresholds above $6.0 CPM → 70%.

    This explorer only shows the win probability of a bid. The advertiser calculator below chooses the bid.

    Across NNN opportunities, linearity of expectation (no independence needed) gives expected wins WWW:

    E[W]=N F(b)=1,000,000×0.30=300,000 wins.\mathbb E[W]=N\,F(b)=1{,}000{,}000\times0.30=300{,}000\ \text{wins}.E[W]=NF(b)=1,000,000×0.30=300,000 wins.

    The uniform threshold has density f(z)=1/Lf(z)=1/Lf(z)=1/L on [0,L][0,L][0,L], so F(b)=∫0bf(z) dz=b/LF(b)=\int_0^b f(z)\,dz=b/LF(b)=∫0b​f(z)dz=b/L. In other markets the win probability is still F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b), just not b/Lb/Lb/L: if 80% of thresholds lie below $6 CPM, a $6 CPM bid wins 80%. Uniform individual bids do not give a uniform threshold: the maximum of nnn independent Uniform(0,L)\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Uniform(0,L) bids has CDF (b/L)n(b/L)^n(b/L)n. Floor prices, discrete bid steps, varied opportunity types and competitors who react to us each need their own model. Correlation across opportunities leaves E[W]\mathbb E[W]E[W] unchanged and changes only the spread of the realized count: positive correlation widens it, negative correlation narrows it.

    First-price bidding: maximize the advertiser's contribution after cost

    In a first-price auction the winner pays its own bid, so a higher bid buys more wins but pays more on each; here the best bid is $4 CPM, half the $8 CPM value. A loss yields neither contribution nor cost. Let C1(b)C_1(b)C1​(b) be expected ad spend and J1(b)J_1(b)J1​(b) expected incremental contribution after spend:

    C1(b)=NF(b) b,J1(b)=NF(b) (w−b).C_1(b)=NF(b)\,b,\qquad J_1(b)=NF(b)\,(w-b).C1​(b)=NF(b)b,J1​(b)=NF(b)(w−b).

    w−bw-bw−b is the gain per won impression; NF(b)NF(b)NF(b) is the expected number won.

    Worked example

    The budget restricts the choice; it does not require full spend

    A budget removes bids that cost too much; if the best bid survives, the budget changes nothing and money stays unspent.

    Second price: pay the competing bid, so bid your value

    Beyond uniform prices: advertiser bidding and pacing

    In the one-slot model, a first-price bidder trades off a lower payment against fewer wins. A second-price bidder can bid its value. When a budget multiplier exists, it scales the value used to set both bids. Keep the direct-buying assumptions, but let F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b) be any continuous win probability with density f=F′f=F'f=F′. Objectives are per opportunity.

    Bid shading in first price

    j1(b)=(w−b)F(b),j1′(b)=(w−b)f(b)−F(b)=f(b)[w−b−F(b)f(b)].j_1(b)=(w-b)F(b),\qquad j_1'(b)=(w-b)f(b)-F(b)=f(b)\Bigl[w-b-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)}\Bigr].j1​(b)=(w−b)F(b),j1′​(b)=(w−b)f(b)−F(b)=f(b)[w−b−f(b)F(b)​].

    Where f(b)>0f(b)>0f(b)>0, an interior optimum solves

    b=w−F(b)f(b).b=w-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)}.b=w−f(b)F(b)​.

    The gap F/fF/fF/f is bid shading: fewer wins, each cheaper. If FFF is log-concave (log⁡F\log FlogF is concave, as for the uniform and for the maximum of independent uniforms), this equation has at most one root, and that root is the best bid. With no root the best bid is a corner: zero if w−b−F/f≤0w-b-F/f\le0w−b−F/f≤0 throughout, and the top of the support if it is positive throughout (for the uniform, w≥2Lw\ge2Lw≥2L gives b=Lb=Lb=L, the LLL in the min above). For the uniform, F/f=bF/f=bF/f=b gives w/2w/2w/2. If the threshold is the higher of two independent Uniform(0,L)\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Uniform(0,L) bids, F=(b/L)2F=(b/L)^2F=(b/L)2, f=2b/L2f=2b/L^2f=2b/L2, F/f=b/2F/f=b/2F/f=b/2, so b=w−b/2b=w-b/2b=w−b/2 and b=2w/3=$0.0053333b=2w/3=\$0.0053333b=2w/3=$0.0053333 ($5.3333 CPM). Per million requests it earns 106(w/3)(2w/(3L))2=$189.6310^6(w/3)(2w/(3L))^2=\$189.63106(w/3)(2w/(3L))2=$189.63; applying the uniform rule w/2w/2w/2 instead earns 106(w/2)(w/(2L))2=$160.0010^6(w/2)(w/(2L))^2=\$160.00106(w/2)(w/(2L))2=$160.00, 15.6% less.

Then (log⁡F)′=f/F(\log F)'=f/F(logF)′=f/F is nonincreasing, so F/fF/fF/f is nondecreasing, and h(b)=w−b−F(b)/f(b)h(b)=w-b-F(b)/f(b)h(b)=w−b−F(b)/f(b) is strictly decreasing. Since j1′=f hj_1'=f\,hj1′​=fh with f>0f>0f>0, j1′j_1'j1′​ changes sign at most once, and only from positive to negative. So j1j_1j1​ rises up to the root of hhh and falls after it, making the root the global maximum on [0,U][0,U][0,U]. If h≤0h\le0h≤0 everywhere, j1j_1j1​ never rises and b=0b=0b=0 is best.     Truthful bidding in second price

    j2(b)=∫0b(w−z)f(z) dz,j2′(b)=(w−b)f(b).j_2(b)=\int_0^b(w-z)f(z)\,dz,\qquad j_2'(b)=(w-b)f(b).j2​(b)=∫0b​(w−z)f(z)dz,j2′​(b)=(w−b)f(b).

    The derivative is nonnegative below www and nonpositive above it, so bidding www is optimal for every FFF. This covers one slot. Multi-slot auctions (GSP, generalized second price), quality-weighted bids, floors and fees need their own models. Some major exchanges use first price; Google Ad Exchange announced its move in 2019.

    The advertiser's budget multiplier

    A binding budget makes the advertiser bid as if each impression were worth w/(1+μA)w/(1+\mu_A)w/(1+μA​) instead of www. The budget multiplier μA≥0\mu_A\ge0μA​≥0 is zero when the budget is slack, otherwise just large enough that expected spend equals BBB. Uniform thresholds give b=w/[2(1+μA)]b=w/[2(1+\mu_A)]b=w/[2(1+μA​)] in first price and b=w/(1+μA)b=w/(1+\mu_A)b=w/(1+μA​) in second price.

    It is also the budget's price: contribution after cost gained per extra budget dollar. At our $500 cap, first price gives μA=w/(2bB)−1=0.008/(2×0.0031623)−1≈0.2649\mu_A=w/(2b_B)-1=0.008/(2\times0.0031623)-1\approx0.2649μA​=w/(2bB​)−1=0.008/(2×0.0031623)−1≈0.2649, and indeed w/[2(1+μA)]=bBw/[2(1+\mu_A)]=b_Bw/[2(1+μA​)]=bB​ reproduces the $3.1623 CPM bid; a $501 cap adds about $0.26. Second price gives μA=w/bB−1≈0.7889\mu_A=w/b_B-1\approx0.7889μA​=w/bB​−1≈0.7889 with bB=2BL/Nb_B=\sqrt{2BL/N}bB​=2BL/N​. At $2,000 both caps are slack and μA=0\mu_A=0μA​=0.

A finite check: J∗(B)=wNB/L−BJ^*(B)=w\sqrt{NB/L}-BJ∗(B)=wNB/L​−B gives J∗(501)−J∗(500)=$0.2643J^*(501)-J^*(500)=\$0.2643J∗(501)−J∗(500)=$0.2643.

    When opportunities differ, with values wiw_iwi​, one multiplier serves them all: bid as if each value were wi/(1+μA)w_i/(1+\mu_A)wi​/(1+μA​). Intuition: the last budget dollar must earn the same everywhere, or money should move to where it earns more. That the rule is optimal whenever such a μA\mu_AμA​ exists is proved below (the sufficiency theorem of Everett, 1963). One exists here by the intermediate value theorem: under the continuity, compactness, and uniqueness assumptions in the proof below, total expected spend S(μ)S(\mu)S(μ) is continuous, nonincreasing and tends to 0; if S(0)>B>0S(0)>B>0S(0)>B>0, some μA\mu_AμA​ gives S(μA)=BS(\mu_A)=BS(μA​)=B. Without that continuity a multiplier can fail to exist, which Everett also shows. In practice wiw_iwi​ is an estimate, and bidding on noisy estimates wins most often where the estimate is too high (the winner's curse). Fees belong in the bill, and objectives such as volume under a ROAS target are different problems.

    Pacing keeps the objective while controlling spend over time

    Pacing is online control of how fast money is spent: the bidder adjusts μA\mu_AμA​ from observed spend. The first-price bidder still needs a shading rule. The uniform rule used here depends on the shape of FFF but does not require knowing LLL to compute the shaded bid. Let ttt index control periods, ctc_tct​ be spend in period ttt, sts_tst​ the target spend and η>0\eta>0η>0 a step size in 1/dollar:

    μA,t+1=max⁡{0, μA,t+η (ct−st)}.\mu_{A,t+1}=\max\{0,\ \mu_{A,t}+\eta\,(c_t-s_t)\}.μA,t+1​=max{0, μA,t​+η(ct​−st​)}.

    Three things follow directly: overspending raises the multiplier and lowers bids; the floor at zero means bids never rise past the profit optimum just to spend money; and any resting point with μA>0\mu_A>0μA​>0 has ct=stc_t=s_tct​=st​. Split the day into ten periods of 100,000 opportunities. At the $2,000 cap the flat target is $200 per period; the $4 CPM optimum spends 105(0.004)2/0.02=$8010^5(0.004)^2/0.02=\$80105(0.004)2/0.02=$80; starting at zero, μA\mu_AμA​ stays zero and the day spends $800. At the $500 cap the target is $50, and spend equals $50 when 105b2/0.02=5010^5b^2/0.02=50105b2/0.02=50, i.e. b=$0.0031623b=\$0.0031623b=$0.0031623, which is the static budget-binding bid with μA≈0.2649\mu_A\approx0.2649μA​≈0.2649. With η=0.0085\eta=0.0085η=0.0085 per dollar and the first-price bid w/[2(1+μA)]w/[2(1+\mu_A)]w/[2(1+μA​)], the controller gets there in a few periods:

    Periodμ_A at startBid ($ CPM)Spend

    20.25503.1873$50.79

    40.26393.1649$50.08

    Period 1 overspends by $30, so μA\mu_AμA​ jumps to 0.0085×30=0.25500.0085\times30=0.25500.0085×30=0.2550; afterwards each error is about a third of the previous one, because near the resting point one unit of μA\mu_AμA​ moves period spend by about $79.06, and 1−0.0085×79.06≈0.331-0.0085\times79.06\approx0.331−0.0085×79.06≈0.33.

    Not proved: convergence, which depends on the step size, delayed bills and traffic swings. If η×79.06\eta\times79.06η×79.06 exceeded 2, the linearized update would reverse the error and amplify it near the fixed point. Away from it, the nonlinear update and the zero floor can produce bounded oscillations; the appendix's pacing simulation shows three step sizes, including one that oscillates. The rule also controls only expected spend; hard caps need the reservation and settlement mechanisms in Chapter 7.

    Different decision-maker and contract

    Here an intermediary maximizes advertiser payments minus media cost. It charges the advertiser $30 per billable attributed conversion and buys publisher impressions in auctions. Its value per impression is v=qa=$0.015v=qa=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015, not the advertiser's w=Δqg=$0.008w=\Delta qg=\$0.008w=Δqg=$0.008, and its $2,000 budget limits publisher payments, not the advertiser's bill. Its optimal bids of $7.50 and $6.3246 CPM can coexist with advertiser losses. None of this describes Axon.

    Advertiser spend, publisher payment, and network receipts

    A network that buys per impression and sells per conversion keeps a ledger that can be positive while the advertiser's is negative. Two published examples fix the prices. In Epom's ad-arbitrage example a network buys publisher impressions at $2 CPM and resells them at $5 CPM. In Kevel's CPA example 9,000 impressions yield 18 billable conversions at $5 each, $90 in total, or $90 ÷ 9,000 × 1,000 = $10 eCPM (revenue restated per 1,000 impressions). Our own combination, which neither source describes: buy Kevel's 9,000 impressions at Epom's $2 CPM.

    ParticipantCalculationAmount
    Advertiser's ad bill18 conversions × $5 CPAPays $90
    Publisher's ad revenue9,000 impressions ÷ 1,000 × $2 CPMReceives $18
    Advertiser payments minus media cost$90 collected − $18 paid to the publisherKeeps $72

    The network pays for every impression but is paid only per conversion: if the same $18 of impressions yields 2 conversions, it collects $10 and loses $8. The advertiser's ledger depends on how many conversions the ad caused. If each caused order leaves $8 of contribution, all 18 caused gives 18 × $8 − $90 = +$54, but only 9 caused gives 9 × $8 − $90 = −$18. The network keeps $72 either way. Attributed conversions decide the bill; incremental ones decide the advertiser's gain (Chapter 6). Chapter 1 uses the same calculations for the running campaign.

    Budget pacing is online control, not even spending

    The pacing rule from the main line finds the network's budget multiplier from spend alone, but whether it settles depends on the step size. The bid follows from the multiplier: b=v/(1+μt)b=v/(1+\mu_t)b=v/(1+μt​) in second price, or v/(2(1+μt))v/\bigl(2(1+\mu_t)\bigr)v/(2(1+μt​)) in uniform first price. This is an illustration, not a stability proof (feedback control in RTB advertising studies real controllers).
