    Prediction and the data it learns from

    In this chapter

    • State exactly what the conversion model predicts, and why a bid needs that probability to be right in absolute terms: a strictly increasing score transformation preserves AUC, while doubling valid probabilities doubles an unadjusted value-based bid.
    • See why the ad that wins an auction is overpredicted even by an unbiased model: with ten equal ads and 20% prediction noise, the winner's prediction averages 31% too high.
    • Recognize three ways the training logs mislead: the delivery policy chooses which outcomes you see, negative downsampling inflates probabilities (a 4.76% output is really 0.05%, a 95× overvaluation), and late conversions make young data look worse (a 10.2% gap from label age alone).
    • Learn the competing-price distribution from auction feedback in which a loss reveals only that the price was above the bid.

    The gist. A bid is a predicted probability times a price, so the prediction must be right in absolute terms, not merely in the right order. Two forces push it wrong. The auction picks the ad with the highest prediction, and the highest of several noisy guesses is usually too high. And the model learns from logs the system produced itself: it sees outcomes only for ads it chose to show, engineers discard most non-converting examples to save compute, and conversions arrive days late. Each distortion has a known correction, and each fails silently if skipped. The bidder also needs the distribution of competing prices, which auction logs reveal only partly: a loss says the price was higher than the bid, not by how much.

    The model predicts the billable event per displayed impression

    The conversion model's target is the probability that one successfully displayed impression produces the event the contract pays for. Let xxx be the information available when the bid is placed (user, context, ad slot and ad). Define three indicators, each 1 if the event happens and 0 otherwise: SSS, the impression is displayed successfully; KKK, the user clicks; YYY, a conversion that the attribution rules credit to this impression's click occurs within the observation window (the period after the ad in which a conversion counts, for example 7 days). The running campaign's CPA contract (Chapter 1) bills post-click attributed purchases, so a billable event needs K=1K=1K=1 and Y=1Y=1Y=1:

    q(x)=P(K=1,Y=1∣x,S=1)=P(K=1∣x,S=1)⋅P(Y=1∣K=1,x,S=1).q(x)=P(K=1,Y=1\mid x,S=1)=P(K=1\mid x,S=1)\cdot P(Y=1\mid K=1,x,S=1).q(x)=P(K=1,Y=1∣x,S=1)=P(K=1∣x,S=1)⋅P(Y=1∣K=1,x,S=1).

    This is the chain rule; it does not assume clicks and conversions are independent. CTR (click-through rate) is clicks per impression and CVR (conversion rate) is conversions per click; pCTR and pCVR are a model's predictions of them (Chapter 2). Always state the denominator: the second factor is per click, q(x)q(x)q(x) is per displayed impression. If a model already predicts conversions per impression, do not multiply by CTR again. If the contract also pays for view-through conversions (a conversion after an impression with no click), add the qualifying K=0K=0K=0 branch.

    Before the auction we do not yet know whether we will win or whether the ad will render. With win probability F(b)F(b)F(b) at bid bbb (Chapter 4) and display success rate ρ=P(S=1∣win)\rho=P(S=1\mid\text{win})ρ=P(S=1∣win), one bid request yields F(b) ρ q(x)F(b)\,\rho\,q(x)F(b)ρq(x) expected billable conversions, assuming the response does not depend on the bid itself and failed displays never convert. A network paid aaa per billable conversion values a displayed impression at v(x)=q(x) av(x)=q(x)\,av(x)=q(x)a; with the running values q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 and a=$30a=\$30a=$30, v=$0.015v=\$0.015v=$0.015, i.e. $15 CPM. If media is billed per win and failed displays have no value, use expected receipts ρq(x)a\rho q(x)aρq(x)a per win. If media is billed only on display, both expected receipts and media cost per win carry the display probability. The advertiser’s value is different: w(x)=Δq(x) gw(x)=\Delta q(x)\,gw(x)=Δq(x)g, the causal lift in purchase probability times contribution per order. A model of qqq predicts attributed response; it says nothing about Δq\Delta qΔq, which needs experiments (Chapter 6).

    Bidding needs calibrated probabilities, not just good ranking

    A model that ranks impressions correctly can still bid wrongly, because the bid uses the probability's value, not its rank. Take the running example. A model that outputs 0.00100.00100.0010 wherever the truth is 0.00050.00050.0005, doubling every prediction, orders impressions exactly as the true model does. A value bidder using it bids 0.0010×$30=$0.0300.0010\times\$30=\$0.0300.0010×$30=$0.030, $30 CPM instead of $15: twice what the impression is worth.

    Two standard metrics separate these properties. Call a sample a positive if the event occurred and a negative otherwise. AUC (area under the ROC curve) is the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative, ties counting one half. It depends only on the order of the scores, so the doubled model has the same AUC. A model is calibrated if, among samples predicted at probability ppp, the event frequency is ppp once labels have matured (the observation window has closed and late conversions are in). Log loss is the average of −[yln⁡p+(1−y)ln⁡(1−p)]-\bigl[y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)\bigr]−[ylnp+(1−y)ln(1−p)] over a fixed evaluation set. Here yyy is the observed binary label, ppp is the predicted probability, and ln⁡\lnln is the natural logarithm. For true event probability qqq, the expected loss is −qln⁡p−(1−q)ln⁡(1−p)-q\ln p-(1-q)\ln(1-p)−qlnp−(1−q)ln(1−p). Its derivative in ppp is (p−q)/(p(1−p))(p-q)/(p(1-p))(p−q)/(p(1−p)), negative below qqq and positive above. This makes the doubled forecast worse in expected log loss here. Check calibration on slices too (expensive publishers, new users, one country): good average calibration can hide large errors that cancel. Accept a model only when ranking, calibration, stability across slices and business outcomes all hold up. Google's click-prediction paper treats calibration as a system problem in this sense. McMahan et al. 2013

    Retrieval, ranking and the auction each filter the candidates

    Prediction runs as a funnel, and an ad dropped early can never win later. Candidate retrieval cheaply narrows the eligible ads to the few worth scoring; ranking estimates response and value for that small set; value estimates, budgets, eligibility rules and the auction then pick the winner. Improving ranking AUC does nothing for a high-value ad that retrieval never passed on. Meta's Andromeda is one published example of staged retrieval followed by ranking. Meta 2024 Andromeda

    Features describe the advertiser and campaign (an advertiser's unit of budget, targeting and goal), the creative (the image, video or text shown), the slot, the user or context, and past interactions. Each feature must be available at decision time, permitted, and identical in meaning in training and serving. A new creative has no feedback history, so the model must lean on content and context features, and an exploration budget must buy it impressions; otherwise past winners keep collecting labels and new candidates never get the chance to prove themselves.

    Optional: training a conversion model when only clicks reveal conversions (ESMM)

    A pCVR model trained only on clicked impressions is applied to all impressions; the clicked ones are a selected subset. This is called sample selection bias. ESMM (Entire Space Multi-Task Model) trains on all impressions using the chain impression → click → conversion: it is supervised on click labels (pCTR) and on click-and-convert labels (pCTCVR = pCTR × pCVR, the chain rule above), so pCVR is learned indirectly through the product of the two model outputs. This provides supervision on the full impression sample through the click and joint-event objectives. It does not guarantee unbiased pCVR estimates. It does not fix selection created by the serving policy, delayed labels or causal identification, which are the subjects of the rest of this chapter. Ma et al. 2018, ESMM

    Auction winners are overpredicted even by an unbiased model

    When several ads have equal true value and the auction picks the highest noisy estimate, the winner’s estimate can be too high on average even if each ad’s estimate is unbiased. This is a form of the winner’s curse.

    Worked example

    Two ads with $8 or $12 CPM estimates

    Both ads are worth $10 per 1,000 impressions. Each independently receives a predicted value of $8 or $12 CPM with equal probability. Before selection, either ad’s prediction averages ($8+$12)/2=$10(\$8+\$12)/2=\$10($8+$12)/2=$10. The higher prediction wins. Either ad may win a tie because both have the same true value.

    Predictions for A and BProbabilityWinning prediction
    $8 and $825%$8 CPM
    $8 and $12, in either order50%$12 CPM
    $12 and $1225%$12 CPM

    At least one ad scores $12 in 75% of auctions, so the winning prediction averages 0.25×$8+0.75×$12=$110.25\times\$8+0.75\times\$12=\$110.25×$8+0.75×$12=$11 CPM. The winner’s true value stays at $10 CPM. Selecting the larger estimate raises the average selected estimate by $1 CPM.

    Take 10 ads with the same true value VVV. Each prediction is V(1+0.2 εi)V(1+0.2\,\varepsilon_i)V(1+0.2εi​) with independent standard normal εi\varepsilon_iεi​: unbiased, with 20% noise. The winner's prediction is V(1+0.2 M)V(1+0.2\,M)V(1+0.2M), where M=max⁡iεiM=\max_i\varepsilon_iM=maxi​εi​. Since P(M≤m)=Φ(m)10P(M\le m)=\Phi(m)^{10}P(M≤m)=Φ(m)10, with Φ\PhiΦ the standard normal CDF and φ\varphiφ its density, MMM has density 10 φ(m) Φ(m)910\,\varphi(m)\,\Phi(m)^910φ(m)Φ(m)9, and

    E[M]=∫−∞∞m⋅10 φ(m) Φ(m)9 dm≈1.5388.\mathbb{E}[M]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} m\cdot 10\,\varphi(m)\,\Phi(m)^{9}\,dm\approx1.5388 .E[M]=∫−∞∞​m⋅10φ(m)Φ(m)9dm≈1.5388.
    How to calculate 1.5388 with numerical integration

    Start with the probability that the maximum is below a cutoff. For one standard normal draw, Φ(m)\Phi(m)Φ(m) is the probability of drawing a value at or below mmm. All ten independent draws must meet the cutoff for their maximum to meet it. For example, Φ(0)=1/2\Phi(0)=1/2Φ(0)=1/2, so the probability that all ten draws are at or below zero is (1/2)10=1/1024(1/2)^{10}=1/1024(1/2)10=1/1024.

    Turn that cumulative probability into a weighted average. Differentiating Φ(m)10\Phi(m)^{10}Φ(m)10 gives the density 10Φ(m)9φ(m)10\Phi(m)^9\varphi(m)10Φ(m)9φ(m). A narrow interval of width Δm\Delta mΔm near mmm contains approximately this density times Δm\Delta mΔm in probability. Multiply by mmm to get that interval’s contribution to the mean. The integrand is therefore g(m)=10mφ(m)Φ(m)9g(m)=10m\varphi(m)\Phi(m)^9g(m)=10mφ(m)Φ(m)9. Negative values contribute negatively.

    Evaluate the integral on a grid. Use the range −8 to +8 and split it into 1,600 equal intervals, so the spacing h=16/1600=0.01h=16/1600=0.01h=16/1600=0.01. At each grid point mj=−8+jhm_j=-8+jhmj​=−8+jh, evaluate g(mj)g(m_j)g(mj​). Composite Simpson’s rule fits a quadratic over each pair of intervals and integrates it. In the combined sum, the endpoint weights are 1 and the interior weights alternate 4 and 2. Multiply the weighted sum by h/3h/3h/3.

    The omitted tails contribute at most 20φ(8)≈1.01×10−1320\varphi(8)\approx1.01\times10^{-13}20φ(8)≈1.01×10−13 in absolute value. This follows from ∣g(m)∣≤10∣m∣φ(m)|g(m)|\le10|m|\varphi(m)∣g(m)∣≤10∣m∣φ(m) and ∫8∞mφ(m) dm=φ(8)\int_8^\infty m\varphi(m)\,dm=\varphi(8)∫8∞​mφ(m)dm=φ(8). Halving the grid spacing to 0.005 gives the same result to ten decimal places.

    This Python code reproduces the calculation using the standard library. erfc is the complementary error function. Here it evaluates the normal cumulative probability as Φ(m)=12erfc⁡(−m/2)\Phi(m)=\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(-m/\sqrt2)Φ(m)=21​erfc(−m/2​).

    from math import erfc, exp, fsum, pi, sqrt

def integrand(m):
    phi = exp(-m * m / 2) / sqrt(2 * pi)
    Phi = erfc(-m / sqrt(2)) / 2
    return 10 * m * phi * Phi**9

def expected_maximum(intervals):
    h = 16 / intervals
    odd = fsum(integrand(-8 + j * h) for j in range(1, intervals, 2))
    even = fsum(integrand(-8 + j * h) for j in range(2, intervals, 2))
    return h / 3 * (integrand(-8) + 4 * odd + 2 * even + integrand(8))

print(f"{expected_maximum(1600):.10f}")  # 1.5387527308
print(f"{expected_maximum(3200):.10f}")  # 1.5387527308

    Rounding the expected maximum 1.5387527308 to four decimal places gives 1.5388. This maximum is measured in standard deviations of the prediction error. Since one standard deviation is 20% of the true value in this example, the average winning estimate is about 30.775% above true value.

    Numerical integration gives 1.5388. The winning prediction therefore averages V(1+0.2×1.5388)≈1.308 VV(1+0.2\times1.5388)\approx1.308\,VV(1+0.2×1.5388)≈1.308V, about 31% above true value in this example. If the winner pays its own bid and that bid equals the target cost per conversion times the predicted conversion probability, a $30 target implies about $30×1.30775=$39.23\$30\times1.30775=\$39.23$30×1.30775=$39.23 in total spend per conversion over many auctions. This calculation assumes the same true conversion probability for every ad and bids that use the prediction directly.

    What offline calibration can detect. A check that compares only the overall average prediction with the overall average outcome can miss the error. In the two-ad example, predictions average $10 CPM before selection, while the $8 and $12 score groups each have a true value of $10 CPM. A calibration check by score would reveal both errors if the offline data had representative outcomes for both groups. Logs collected under an earlier bidding policy may cover a different set of impressions. To measure calibration on the traffic the current policy buys, compare its predictions with observed conversion rates after the conversion window closes, grouped by score and relevant traffic segments. In the toy model every true value is $10, so the conditional mean at either score is $10. Using that conditional mean removes the error here. In a real auction, a score can carry useful information. Calibration by score before selection also need not survive selection if other bids or context carry extra information about the winner’s value. Shrink noisy predictions toward an estimated baseline and evaluate the resulting bids on the traffic they buy.

    With equal true values, the scores differ only because of noise. When true values differ, the size of the gaps relative to the noise helps determine how much selection affects the winning prediction.

    The delivery policy decides which outcomes you see

    Ad logs are not a passive sample of the world: every outcome in them was selected by the system's own past decisions. Eligibility rules (targeting, budget, frequency caps, content policy) decide which ads may compete; retrieval decides which get scored; bidding decides which opportunities are bought; rendering and privacy rules decide which outcomes are observed. A CVR model fitted on won impressions estimates P(Y=1∣x,shown by the old policy)P(Y=1 \mid x, \text{shown by the old policy})P(Y=1∣x,shown by the old policy), not the rate on traffic the old policy never bought. No model can recover labels for actions that were never taken.

    Inverse propensity scoring can evaluate a new policy from old logs when the logging policy gave each action used by the new policy a positive probability and recorded that probability. Then each logged outcome is weighted by the ratio of the two policies' probabilities for the action taken, a method called inverse propensity scoring (IPS). For example, if the new policy always shows ad B, the old policy showed B on one comparable request in ten, and B's purchase rate there is 2%, then per logged request the weighted B outcome averages 0.1×10×0.02=0.020.1\times10\times0.02=0.020.1×10×0.02=0.02, exactly B's purchase rate: the weight of 10 undoes the 1-in-10 selection. The price is variance. A choice logged with probability 0.05 gets weight 20, so a handful of rare outcomes can dominate the estimate. This is why the exploration that creates the randomness costs real money, and why it must be logged exactly.

    Negative downsampling inflates predicted probabilities

    Training pipelines usually keep every positive but only a fraction of negatives, and a model trained on that sample predicts the sampled rate, which is far above the true rate until corrected. Let ppp be the true event probability for a fixed feature value, sss (0<s≤10<s\le 10<s≤1) the probability that a negative is kept, independently of everything else, and psp_sps​ the event rate among kept samples, which is what an unweighted model learns.

    Worked example

If training instead weighted each kept negative by 1/s1/s1/s, the model already targets the original population and needs no correction; check calibration on representative held-out data to know which case you are in.     Delayed labels make young data look worse

    A conversion can arrive days after the impression, so an impression that has not converted yet is not a negative, and data read too early understates conversion rates. Waiting for every label to mature costs the model freshness, so a pipeline must choose an observation window, a maturity rule (train or compare only on cohorts whose labels are, say, 95% final), a model of the delay, and a backfill policy for labels that arrive late. Delayed feedback and elapsed-time sampling

    Assume, for illustration, that the delay from impression to conversion is exponential with mean 3 days, and that the observation window is long enough (say 30 days) for truncation to be ignored; with a finite attribution window WWW, use H(min⁡(t,W))/H(W)H(\min(t,W))/H(W)H(min(t,W))/H(W) for the fraction of in-window conversions visible by age ttt. The share of eventual conversions visible at label age ttt days is then H(t)=1−e−t/3H(t)=1-e^{-t/3}H(t)=1−e−t/3 (HHH is the delay CDF, not the competing-bid CDF FFF). Labels are 95% final only when e−t/3=0.05e^{-t/3}=0.05e−t/3=0.05, at t=3ln⁡20≈9.0t=3\ln 20\approx 9.0t=3ln20≈9.0 days. Two single-age cohorts with the same eventual conversion probability of 1.0%, read at ages 7 and 5 days, show 0.903% and 0.811%: the younger cohort looks 10.2% worse with no real difference. Compare outcomes at matched label ages or adjust for the delay distribution.

    Nor is a young unconverted impression a negative. If its eventual conversion probability is ppp, then "converts eventually and not yet by age ttt" has probability p (1−H(t))p\,(1-H(t))p(1−H(t)), and "not yet converted" has probability 1−p H(t)1-p\,H(t)1−pH(t). Dividing (Bayes' rule),

    P(converts eventually∣not yet at age t)=p (1−H(t))1−p H(t).P(\text{converts eventually}\mid\text{not yet at age }t)=\frac{p\,(1-H(t))}{1-p\,H(t)} .P(converts eventually∣not yet at age t)=1−pH(t)p(1−H(t))​.

    For p=1%p=1\%p=1% at t=1t=1t=1 day, H(1)=0.283H(1)=0.283H(1)=0.283 and the probability is 0.72%, still 72% of the base rate.

    Pitfall: time leakage

    Each training example may contain only information available at decision time. Account state after the purchase, counters already incremented by this purchase and attribution outcomes decided later must not leak into features. A point-in-time join needs event time, processing time and feature-pipeline version tracked separately. A model that wins offline through leakage does not degrade slightly online; it loses the very inputs its predictions depended on.

    Learning competing prices from censored auction feedback

    The bidder in Chapter 4 assumed the distribution of the competitive threshold ZZZ (the highest competing bid) was known; in practice it must be learned from our own auction records, and those records show prices only partly. A price is censored when a record reveals only an interval for it. In an ideal second-price auction (no reserve price) a win reveals ZZZ exactly, because we pay it; a loss reveals only Z>bZ>bZ>b. Treating the win prices as an ordinary regression sample therefore learns a selected distribution: at a fixed bid, every threshold above the bid is missing.

    The running example shows how badly. With ZZZ uniform between 0 and L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02 per impression ($20 CPM) and a constant bid of $6 CPM, we win 30% of requests (Chapter 4). The win prices are uniform on $0 to $6, averaging $3 CPM, while the true average threshold is $10 CPM. The losses, which a price regression throws away, carry the missing information.

    The fix is a likelihood (the probability or density the model assigns to the observed records) in which each record contributes the probability of exactly what it reveals. Let F(z∣x)F(z\mid x)F(z∣x) and f(z∣x)f(z\mid x)f(z∣x) be the conditional CDF and density of ZZZ. A second-price win reveals the value ZZZ, so it contributes the density f(Z∣x)f(Z\mid x)f(Z∣x); a loss reveals Z>bZ>bZ>b, so it contributes P(Z>b∣x)=1−F(b∣x)P(Z>b\mid x)=1-F(b\mid x)P(Z>b∣x)=1−F(b∣x). For independent requests the probabilities multiply, so the log-likelihood ℓ\ellℓ is a sum over won and lost requests, where xxx denotes the logged features, bbb is the submitted bid, and ZZZ is observed on wins:

    ℓsecond price=∑winln⁡f(Z∣x)+∑lossln⁡(1−F(b∣x)).\ell_{\text{second price}}= \sum_{\mathrm{win}}\ln f(Z\mid x) +\sum_{\mathrm{loss}}\ln\bigl(1-F(b\mid x)\bigr).ℓsecond price​=win∑​lnf(Z∣x)+loss∑​ln(1−F(b∣x)).

    In a first-price auction our payment is our own bid, so a win reveals only Z≤bZ\le bZ≤b. Every record is then censored, and

    ℓfirst price=∑winln⁡F(b∣x)+∑lossln⁡(1−F(b∣x)).\ell_{\text{first price}}= \sum_{\mathrm{win}}\ln F(b\mid x) +\sum_{\mathrm{loss}}\ln\bigl(1-F(b\mid x)\bigr).ℓfirst price​=win∑​lnF(b∣x)+loss∑​ln(1−F(b∣x)).

    This is the likelihood of a binary win/loss outcome. Without a parametric form for FFF it pins down FFF only at the bids actually placed, so learning the whole curve needs variation in bids. Never label your own winning first-price bid as the competitors' price. Some exchanges return extra signals, such as the minimum bid that would have won; check the actual interface.

Wins and losses must be decided purely by the price comparison, and, once the logged xxx includes everything the bidder used, the bid must carry no further information about the threshold: P(Z≤z∣x,b)=F(z∣x)P(Z\le z\mid x,b)=F(z\mid x)P(Z≤z∣x,b)=F(z∣x) (non-informative censoring). Timeouts, creative rejections, budget filtering and users leaving the page are not "the price exceeded the bid" and must not be coded as such losses. RTB monograph, Chapter 3

    Attribution, experiments and observability

    In this chapter

    • Tell attribution, a credit rule that drives billing, from incrementality, the causal effect that decides whether spend is profitable.
    • Read a holdout experiment end to end: attributed ROAS 5, incremental ROAS 2, and a −$1,000 profit estimate whose 95% interval, [−$2,830, +$830], spans zero.
    • Convert an effect per assigned user into an effect per exposed user, and see why comparing exposed users with the control group doubles the effect in the example.
    • Match the experiment to the question: a model A/B test ranks two policies; only a channel test says whether advertising pays at all.
    • Know what privacy rules (ATT, SKAdNetwork, AdAttributionKit) and fraud do to the labels and bills you observe.

    The gist. Attribution rules assign conversion credit for reporting and optimization. Billing follows the contract, which may use qualifying attributed conversions. A randomized holdout experiment estimates incremental conversions by comparing outcomes between groups with and without the campaign. Privacy restrictions, reporting delays, and invalid traffic affect what can be measured.

    Attribution assigns credit; experiments measure causation

    Attribution is a bookkeeping rule that assigns each conversion to one ad touchpoint (a click or an impression), because billing and optimization need an owner for every conversion. The common rule is last touch: the last qualifying click within a lookback window wins, and an unclicked impression can claim the conversion within a shorter view-through window if no click qualifies. Windows vary by contract; the timeline uses typical app-install defaults. For mobile apps an MMP (mobile measurement partner; Chapter 3) does the matching: its SDK inside the advertiser's app reports installs and in-app events, networks send it their click and impression claims, and it sends the winner a postback (a server-to-server notice of the attributed event).

    1. t = 0
      Impression. The ad renders; the network sends the MMP an impression claim.
    2. click
      Click. The user taps; the network sends a click claim and opens the app store.
    3. ≤ 7 d
      Install = first open. The SDK reports the first launch, not the download. The MMP credits the last click in the past 7 days; with no click, an impression in the past 24 hours.
    4. minutes
      Install postback to the winning network; losing networks typically hear nothing.
    5. later
      In-app events. Purchases inherit the install's attribution and trigger further postbacks.

    Incrementality asks how many conversions exist because the ad ran. The two disagree in both directions: a real conversion can be credited to the wrong touchpoint, and a correctly credited one may have happened anyway. Last-touch and view-through rules systematically reward ads placed next to purchases users were already going to make, such as retargeting existing customers or spraying cheap impressions to collect view-through credit.

    Attribution answers

    Which touchpoint gets credit for this conversion? Attribution rules assign credit for reporting and optimization. A contract can use qualifying attributed conversions or installs as billable events.

    Incrementality answers

    How many conversions exist because the ad ran? Defined for a population relative to what would have happened without the campaign. A randomized holdout can estimate the effect and its uncertainty. The estimated effect can be negative.

    Rich observational data does not substitute for randomization: in large Facebook experiments, observational methods did not reliably recover the experimental effects, because targeting uses signals the analyst cannot see that also predict purchases. Gordon et al., observational methods versus large Facebook experiments

    A holdout experiment measures what the ads caused

    A holdout experiment randomly splits one eligible population into a treatment group, where the campaign may deliver, and a control group (the holdout), where it may not; the difference in outcomes is what the campaign caused. The example is a self-contained advertiser campaign, not the running network campaign. The contribution rate is the share of net revenue (after refunds) left after non-advertising variable costs. ROAS and iROAS are as defined in Chapter 3: revenue credited to the campaign, and revenue it caused, each divided by ad spend. Assume correct randomization, a matured window, and no interference between the groups.

    What a 95% confidence interval tells you

    Suppose a holdout test records 1,200 purchases in treatment and 1,000 in control, with 100,000 users in each group. The observed difference is 200 purchases. Ad spend is $5,000. Each purchase brings $50 of net revenue and leaves 40% of it, or $20, after non-advertising variable costs. If you ran the same test again with fresh users from the same population, both groups’ counts could change even if the campaign’s true effect stayed fixed. The standard error estimates the standard deviation of the observed difference across repetitions.

    A 95% confidence interval is built by a procedure that would cover the fixed true effect in about 95 out of 100 repetitions, under the assumptions of the calculation. Each repetition produces its own estimate and interval. In this test, the interval runs from about 109 to 291 additional purchases per 100,000 assigned users. That describes uncertainty about the campaign’s average effect. A prediction for the observed purchase difference in a future test would require a separate calculation.

    1. Compute the estimate. Equal group sizes let us subtract the purchase counts directly. The estimated lift is 1,200 − 1,000 = 200 purchases.
    2. Estimate how much each count can fluctuate. One user contributes either zero or one purchase. At purchase probability ppp, the variance of that outcome is p(1−p)p(1-p)p(1−p). Each group’s count adds 100,000 independent user outcomes, so its variance is 100,000 times the variance for one user. Use the observed purchase rate to estimate ppp in each group: Treatment:100,000(0.012)(1−0.012)=1,185.6,Control:100,000(0.010)(1−0.010)=990.\begin{aligned} \text{Treatment:}\quad 100{,}000(0.012)(1-0.012)&=1{,}185.6,\\ \text{Control:}\quad 100{,}000(0.010)(1-0.010)&=990. \end{aligned}Treatment:100,000(0.012)(1−0.012)Control:100,000(0.010)(1−0.010)​=1,185.6,=990.​
    3. Add the variances of the two counts. If the treatment count comes in 30 higher, estimated lift goes up by 30. If the control count comes in 30 higher, estimated lift goes down by 30. Both fluctuations contribute uncertainty. Let XTX_TXT​ and XCX_CXC​ be the treatment and control counts. Variance squares the size of a fluctuation, so the control count’s coefficient contributes (−1)2=1(-1)^2=1(−1)2=1. The covariance term is zero because the counts are independent in this model: Var⁡(XT−XC)=Var⁡(XT)+Var⁡(XC).\operatorname{Var}(X_T-X_C)=\operatorname{Var}(X_T)+\operatorname{Var}(X_C).Var(XT​−XC​)=Var(XT​)+Var(XC​). The estimated variance is 1,185.6+990=2,175.61{,}185.6+990=2{,}175.61,185.6+990=2,175.6 purchases squared. Taking the square root puts the standard error back in purchases: 2,175.6≈46.64\sqrt{2{,}175.6}\approx46.642,175.6​≈46.64.
    4. Compute the margin of error. With large independent groups, the sampling error is approximately normal. The middle 95% of a standard normal lies between −1.96 and +1.96. Multiply 1.96×46.64≈91.41.96\times46.64\approx91.41.96×46.64≈91.4 purchases, then subtract and add that margin to 200 to get approximately [108.6, 291.4].

    Use the interval to compare the estimate with a decision threshold. The margin of error gives the distance from the point estimate to either endpoint in this calculation. The endpoints let you compare the same experiment with two different business thresholds:

    Business questionThresholdWhat the interval supports
    Did the ads generate additional purchases?0 purchasesThe whole interval is above zero. The test supports a positive sales effect.
    Did the ads pay for themselves?$5,000 ÷ $20 = 250 purchasesThe interval spans 250. Both a loss and a profit are compatible with the test at this confidence level.

    At the point estimate, 200 additional purchases contribute $4,000 before ads, so the campaign loses $1,000 after ad spend. Applying the same calculation to the unrounded interval endpoints gives a profit interval of about −$2,828 to +$828.

    Worked example

    Holdout experiment: from attributed ROAS to a decision

    Given: 100,000 users per group. Over the same matured window, treatment makes 1,200 purchases and control 1,000. Ad spend is $5,000, all in treatment. Attribution credits 500 purchases to the campaign. Net revenue is $50 per purchase and the contribution rate 40%, so each purchase contributes $50×0.40=$20\$50\times0.40=\$20$50×0.40=$20 before ad spend. Each user buys at most once, independently of other users.

    1. Attributed ROAS: 500×$50÷$5,000=5500\times\$50\div\$5{,}000=5500×$50÷$5,000=5.
    2. Lift (equal group sizes, so counts compare directly): 1,200−1,000=2001{,}200-1{,}000=2001,200−1,000=200 incremental purchases per 100,000 users assigned to treatment.
    3. iROAS: 200×$50÷$5,000=2200\times\$50\div\$5{,}000=2200×$50÷$5,000=2. Each incremental revenue dollar yields $0.40 of contribution, so break-even iROAS is 1÷0.40=2.51\div0.40=2.51÷0.40=2.5.
    4. Incremental contribution after ad spend: 200×$20−$5,000=−$1,000200\times\$20-\$5{,}000=-\$1{,}000200×$20−$5,000=−$1,000. Break-even lift: $5,000÷$20=250\$5{,}000\div\$20=250$5,000÷$20=250 purchases.
    5. Non-incremental credit: at the point estimate, at least 500−200=300500-200=300500−200=300 credited purchases would have happened anyway (if the ad never suppresses a purchase).
    6. Standard error of the lift. Each group's purchase count is binomial with variance np(1−p)n p(1-p)np(1−p), and the variances of independent groups add (derivation below). With the observed rates: 100,000×0.012×0.988=1,185.6100{,}000\times0.012\times0.988=1{,}185.6100,000×0.012×0.988=1,185.6 and 100,000×0.010×0.990=990100{,}000\times0.010\times0.990=990100,000×0.010×0.990=990, so SE=1,185.6+990=2,175.6=46.6\text{SE}=\sqrt{1{,}185.6+990}=\sqrt{2{,}175.6}=46.6SE=1,185.6+990​=2,175.6​=46.6. The lift is 200/46.6=4.3200/46.6=4.3200/46.6=4.3 standard errors from zero.
    7. 95% interval: 200±1.96×46.64=200±91.4200\pm1.96\times46.64=200\pm91.4200±1.96×46.64=200±91.4 (unrounded SE), i.e. [108.6, 291.4]≈[109, 291][108.6,\ 291.4]\approx[109,\ 291][108.6, 291.4]≈[109, 291] purchases.
    8. Map through the linear formulas: iROAS =lift×$50/$5,000=\text{lift}\times\$50/\$5{,}000=lift×$50/$5,000 gives [1.09, 2.91][1.09,\ 2.91][1.09, 2.91]; contribution =$20×lift−$5,000=\$20\times\text{lift}-\$5{,}000=$20×lift−$5,000 gives [−$2,828, +$828]≈[−$2,830, +$830][-\$2{,}828,\ +\$828]\approx[-\$2{,}830,\ +\$830][−$2,828, +$828]≈[−$2,830, +$830].
    9. Decision. Break-even (250) lies inside the interval, so the sign of profit is unresolved.

    Result: the campaign causes purchases (lift 200, 95% CI [109, 291]); its profit is −$1,000 at the point estimate with 95% CI ≈ [−$2,830, +$830], while attributed ROAS says 5.

    Check: both ROAS figures equal purchases × $50/$5,000 = purchases/100, so their ratio is 500/200 = 2.5. Contribution also equals $5,000×(0.40×iROAS−1)\$5{,}000\times(0.40\times\text{iROAS}-1)$5,000×(0.40×iROAS−1): at iROAS 1.086 that is −$2,828, matching step 8.

    Optional: the standard error of a difference in purchase rates

    Assumptions. Each of the n1n_1n1​ treatment users buys (at most once) with probability p1p_1p1​, each of the n0n_0n0​ control users with probability p0p_0p0​, all users independently.

The ppp's are unknown, so the observed rates 0.012 and 0.010 are plugged in. Per assigned user the standard error is 46.6/100,000=0.00046646.6/100{,}000=0.00046646.6/100,000=0.000466.

    Interval. Δ^\hat\DeltaΔ^ is a difference of two averages of many independent indicators, so by the central limit theorem it is approximately normal; with about 1,000 purchases per group the approximation is good, and ±1.96\pm1.96±1.96 standard errors covers the true lift with probability about 95%. With repeat purchases, use the variance of purchases per user. With variable order values, estimate uncertainty in contribution directly. If you randomize clusters, such as regions, account for dependence within each cluster.

    Assignment is not exposure

    Many users assigned to treatment never see the ad (no slot won, app never opened, ad scrolled past). Under the assumptions below, dividing the effect per assigned user by the treatment exposure rate gives the average effect among users who would be exposed if assigned to treatment. Write TTT for random assignment (1 = treatment), DDD for actual exposure (1 = exposed, 0 = unexposed), YYY for each user’s purchase outcome, and c=P(D=1∣T=1)c=P(D=1\mid T=1)c=P(D=1∣T=1) for the exposure rate in treatment. The intent-to-treat effect (ITT) is the difference in mean outcome by assignment, YˉT=1−YˉT=0\bar Y_{T=1}-\bar Y_{T=0}YˉT=1​−YˉT=0​. With random assignment, no interference, and comparable outcome measurement, it estimates the effect of assignment. The effect of treatment on the treated (TOT, per exposed user) is estimated by the Wald ratio, an instrumental-variables estimator that uses random assignment as the instrument

    τTOT=YˉT=1−YˉT=0c,\tau_{\text{TOT}}=\frac{\bar Y_{T=1}-\bar Y_{T=0}}{c},τTOT​=cYˉT=1​−YˉT=0​​,

    valid if, in addition, control users cannot be exposed, assignment changes purchases only through exposure (the exclusion restriction), and c>0c>0c>0. Reason: treatment users who would not be exposed contribute zero to the ITT, so the ITT is ccc times the average effect among those who would be (derivation below).

    Worked example

    ITT, TOT and the naive comparison with exposure logs

    Given: the holdout experiment above, plus hypothetical exposure data. In treatment, 40,000 users were exposed and bought 800 times; the other 60,000 bought 400 times. Ghost-ad logs (described below) flag the 40,000 control users who would have been exposed; they bought 600 times, and the other 60,000 control users bought 400 times.

    1. ITT per assigned user: (1,200−1,000)/100,000=0.002(1{,}200-1{,}000)/100{,}000=0.002(1,200−1,000)/100,000=0.002 purchases, SE 46.64/100,000=0.000466446.64/100{,}000=0.000466446.64/100,000=0.0004664.
    2. Exposure rate c^=40,000/100,000=0.40\hat c=40{,}000/100{,}000=0.40c^=40,000/100,000=0.40. TOT: 0.002/0.40=0.0050.002/0.40=0.0050.002/0.40=0.005 purchases per exposed user, SE 0.0004664/0.40=0.0011660.0004664/0.40=0.0011660.0004664/0.40=0.001166 (treating c^\hat cc^ as known; it is estimated from 100,000 users). z=0.005/0.001166=4.3z=0.005/0.001166=4.3z=0.005/0.001166=4.3, the same as ITT: this equality holds in the fixed-exposure-rate approximation. If the rate is estimated, account for its sampling variation and its covariance with the estimated purchase lift.
    3. Totals agree: 100,000×0.002=40,000×0.005=200100{,}000\times0.002=40{,}000\times0.005=200100,000×0.002=40,000×0.005=200 purchases, so iROAS is still 2.
    4. Naive comparison: 800/40,000−1,000/100,000=0.020−0.010=0.010800/40{,}000-1{,}000/100{,}000=0.020-0.010=0.010800/40,000−1,000/100,000=0.020−0.010=0.010 per exposed user, i.e. 400 "incremental" purchases, twice the truth. The ghost logs show why: would-be-exposed control users buy at 600/40,000=0.015600/40{,}000=0.015600/40,000=0.015 against 0.010 overall. Delivery reaches people who were more likely to buy anyway, and that gap of 0.005 is exactly the bias.

    Result: TOT = 0.005 purchases per exposed user; the naive estimate (0.010) is 2× too high.

    Check: c^×τTOT=0.40×0.005=0.002=ITT\hat c\times\tau_{\text{TOT}}=0.40\times0.005=0.002=\text{ITT}c^×τTOT​=0.40×0.005=0.002=ITT, and naive − TOT = 0.010 − 0.005 = 0.005, the gap in step 4.

    In an auction, withholding the campaign from a control user does not leave the slot empty: the next-best ad wins, so every effect here is relative to the ads the user would otherwise see, not to no ad. Ghost ads (Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer, 2017) log exposure in control too: the ad server runs the auction with the campaign included, records a "ghost impression" whenever the campaign would have won and rendered, then serves the runner-up. Comparing exposed with ghost-exposed users estimates TOT directly and more precisely, if the ghost logic replicates real delivery exactly.

Here it is close to the fixed-rate approximation in the example.

    Naive bias. Exposed treatment users are those with Di(1)=1D_i(1)=1Di​(1)=1, so

    E[Y∣D=1,T=1]−E[Y∣T=0]=τTOT+(E[Yi(0)∣Di(1)=1]−E[Yi(0)]).\mathbb{E}[Y\mid D=1,T=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0] =\tau_{\text{TOT}}+\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y_i(0)\mid D_i(1)=1\bigr]-\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y_i(0)\bigr]\Bigr).E[Y∣D=1,T=1]−E[Y∣T=0]=τTOT​+(E[Yi​(0)∣Di​(1)=1]−E[Yi​(0)]).

    The bracket is how much more likely the would-be-exposed are to buy without the ad; it is positive when delivery targets likely buyers. In the example it is 0.015−0.010=0.0050.015-0.010=0.0050.015−0.010=0.005.

    What ghost ads add. Ghost logs observe Di(1)D_i(1)Di​(1) in control too, so TOT can be estimated as exposed treatment minus ghost-exposed control: 0.020−0.015=0.0050.020-0.015=0.0050.020−0.015=0.005. Its standard error, from the two binomial counts on 40,000 users each, is 800(0.98)+600(0.985)/40,000=1,375/40,000=0.000927\sqrt{800(0.98)+600(0.985)}/40{,}000=\sqrt{1{,}375}/40{,}000=0.000927800(0.98)+600(0.985)​/40,000=1,375​/40,000=0.000927, so z=0.005/0.000927=5.4z=0.005/0.000927=5.4z=0.005/0.000927=5.4. That standard error is 20.5% below the Wald ratio's 0.001166; the variance ratio (0.001166/0.000927)2=1.58(0.001166/0.000927)^2=1.58(0.001166/0.000927)2=1.58 is worth 58% more users, because the never-exposed strata contribute sampling variation to the assignment comparison while their expected causal effect is zero under exclusion. The logs give a diagnostic for exclusion: never-exposed users buy at 400/60,000 in both groups, consistent with assignment acting only through exposure. The older placebo design, which shows control users a public-service ad (PSA), fails under optimized delivery: the optimizer delivers the PSA to different users than it would deliver the real ad, so the two exposed groups are not comparable.

    Model tests and channel tests answer different questions

    A model A/B test, which randomizes traffic between two delivery policies, can show that policy B beats policy A; only a channel incrementality test, which compares advertising with not advertising or with a different budget, can show that advertising pays at all. Geo experiments randomize regions instead of users and come in several designs (go dark, heavy-up, budget levels); choose the question first and the design second. Google GeoX experiment types

    Ad experiments leak between arms: a shared budget makes the arms compete for one quota, one arm's bids move the other arm's prices, and users cross devices and regions. Document how each leak is handled, and read results only at equal, mature label age (Chapter 5).

    Report both parties' metrics. A network paid per attributed conversion earns on easy-to-attribute conversions, incremental or not; the advertiser gains only from incremental ones (Chapter 4's network appendix). A policy judged on network revenue alone drifts toward the former.

    Privacy and fraud limit what can be observed

    Privacy rules and fraud decide which outcomes can be observed at all, and the gaps are not random. On iOS two distinct Apple mechanisms matter. ATT (App Tracking Transparency, iOS 14.5, 2021) requires user permission, through a system prompt, before an app tracks the user across other companies' apps and websites or reads the IDFA (Identifier for Advertisers, the per-device ad identifier that made user-level attribution possible). SKAdNetwork (SKAN) and its successor AdAttributionKit (iOS 17.4) are Apple's privacy-preserving attribution APIs, which per Apple need no ATT prompt: the device itself decides which ad gets credit for an install and sends the network a signed, delayed postback with no user identifier. For small campaigns, crowd-anonymity thresholds blank or coarsen fields such as the conversion value (an app-set integer from 0 to 63 encoding post-install activity). Postbacks arrive after each conversion window closes (or the app locks it early), plus a random delay. The windows start at the app's first launch, which may itself come up to 60 days after install, so the last postback can come 41 days after first launch. Apple ad attribution

    Optional: the SKAdNetwork 4 postback schedule

    AdAttributionKit keeps the same three windows. Postbacks are signed and carry a unique identifier (SKAdNetwork transaction-id, AdAttributionKit postback-identifier), so receivers can reject forgeries and replays.

    1. before day 0
      Engagement and install. The install must follow a StoreKit-rendered ad tap within 30 days or a view-through impression within 24 hours, and the user must first launch the app within 60 days of installing it.
    2. day 0
      First launch. The conversion windows below are counted from here.
    3. days 0–2
      Window 1. The app may raise its conversion value; the postback carries the fine value (0–63) if the crowd is large enough, otherwise a coarse value (low, medium, high), or none at the lowest crowd tier. Sent 24–48 hours after the window closes.
    4. days 3–7
      Window 2. Coarse value only; not sent at the lowest crowd tier. Sent 24–144 hours after close.
    5. days 8–35
      Window 3. Coarse value only; not sent at the lowest crowd tier. The last postback can arrive as late as day 41 after first launch (35 days + 144 hours).

    For training, a missing postback cannot be labeled "not converted"; postbacks without user identifiers cannot be joined back to users without extra assumptions; a signed event proves authenticity, not incrementality; and missingness depends on consent rates and campaign size. A new platform that subsidizes impression purchases has bought delivery, not training labels it can join across customers under long-term consent.

    Check fraud layer by layer, because each layer is a separate attack surface: is the supply real, was the impression rendered, was the click human, is the conversion valid, was attribution hijacked, was the purchase refunded? In click injection, for example, Android malware detects an install in progress and fires a fake click just before first open, taking last-touch credit for an install that was happening anyway. Supply-chain standards cover only the first layer: ads.txt (app-ads.txt for apps) lists, on the publisher's own domain, which ad systems may sell its inventory; sellers.json lists the sellers each SSP (supply-side platform; Chapter 2) or exchange pays; the OpenRTB SupplyChain object lists every hop a bid request passed through. None guarantees traffic quality. IAB ads.txt, IAB sellers.json and SupplyChain FAQ

    As in trading, positive expected value per trade does not guarantee survival: correlated fake events, retroactive window changes, chargebacks and paying publishers before advertisers pay all concentrate risk. A fraud model is one layer; per-source exposure limits, settlement reconciliation, clawback rights and gradual ramp-up of new sources are the others.

    Real-time advertising systems

    In this chapter

    • Turn a 120 ms tmax, measured at the exchange, into an 80 ms compute deadline at the bidder.
    • Follow one bid through the win, display and billing notices, and say which of them creates a payment obligation.
    • Prove that the hard-budget invariant C+R≤BC+R\le BC+R≤B survives every event, and see why a timeout may never release a reservation.
    • Estimate with Little's law how much budget open reservations lock (about $1.49 at a 60 s billing delay), and what reserving expected cost instead risks ($0.48 at P99 if wins are independent, $21.62 if they move together).

    The gist. This is an optional deep dive for engineers. Latency tails, retries and idempotency work here as anywhere else; this chapter covers only what advertising adds. A bid is worth nothing if it reaches the exchange after the auction deadline, and that deadline includes the network trip. Winning an auction is not the same as showing the ad, and showing it is not always the same as owing money: the exchange sends separate notices, late and sometimes twice. A hard budget must therefore hold back each bid's maximum cost until a notice proves what is owed. A local timeout alone does not settle a payment obligation. Finally, a release that changes labels, windows or traffic mix changes what the system optimizes, not just how fast it runs.

    The accounting examples use the optional CPA-network case from Chapter 4: a network buys publisher impressions and bills advertisers per attributed conversion. The ledger and reservation rules apply to any contract once its payment obligations are written down.

    Three pipelines, tied together by one chain of events

    An ad network runs three pipelines that must agree on what happened. The control pipeline manages campaigns (an advertiser's unit of budget, targeting and goals), creatives (the ad assets), budgets and configuration releases. The online pipeline answers each bid request before its deadline: eligibility applies hard filters (targeting, budget, approved creative, block lists, consent), retrieval narrows the eligible campaigns to a few hundred, then prediction, ranking and bidding run on a versioned, read-only online snapshot of configuration and features. The event pipeline records delivery, billing, attribution, training data and reconciliation. The diagram is a teaching architecture, not Axon's or any other company's implementation.

    One impression spans milliseconds to months, and each event proves something different (time scales illustrative):

    1. 0 ms
      Bid request. The exchange sends the request; the tmax window is measured at the exchange.
    2. ≤ 120 ms
      Bid response. Must reach the exchange inside tmax. The budget reservation is made before the response leaves.
    3. + ms to s
      Auction result. Win notice (nurl) or loss notice (lurl), if the exchange sends them. A win is not a delivered or billable impression.
    4. + seconds
      Render. The creative loads on the device and fires the impression pixel, or fails.
    5. + s to hours
      Billing notice. burl fires when the impression becomes billable under the exchange's policy; retries and late arrivals are normal. The reservation becomes confirmed spend.
    6. + days
      Clicks and conversions. Attributed inside the attribution window; they create the CPA receivable. Refunds and chargebacks arrive later still.
    7. monthly
      Settlement. The exchange's statement, your log and the advertiser bill are reconciled; corrections are posted as compensating entries.

    The bid deadline is measured at the exchange

    A bid that arrives after tmax is discarded, and the window includes the network trip both ways. OpenRTB, the IAB Tech Lab's real-time bidding protocol, defines the fields this chapter uses (OpenRTB 2.6):

    • tmax (request): the maximum time, in milliseconds, the exchange allows for bids to be received, including internet latency.
    • price (bid): the bid, quoted as CPM (dollars per thousand impressions) even though it buys one impression.
    • nurl, lurl, burl (bid): the win, loss and billing notice URLs. The spec says a win does not necessarily mean a delivered, viewed or billable ad; burl is called when the impression becomes billable under the exchange's own policy. All three are optional.
    • ${AUCTION_PRICE}: a macro the exchange substitutes into notice URLs, giving the clearing price in the bid's units (CPM). The bidder writes its own notice URLs, so it embeds its own bid id in them.
    Worked example

    A 120 ms deadline, split into stage budgets

    Given (all values illustrative, not an industry standard): tmax = 120 ms; network round-trip P99 of 30 ms for this exchange and region, measured as a round trip in the bidder's own logs; safety margin δ\deltaδ = 10 ms. The bidder cannot see when the exchange sent the request, so it budgets from its own receipt time.

    1. Network allowance: tnet=30 mst_{\text{net}} = 30\ \text{ms}tnet​=30 ms
    2. Compute deadline after receipt: tc=tmax⁡−tnet−δ=120−30−10=80 ms\begin{aligned}t_c &= t_{\max} - t_{\text{net}} - \delta\\ &= 120 - 30 - 10 = 80\ \text{ms}\end{aligned}tc​​=tmax​−tnet​−δ=120−30−10=80 ms​
    3. Stage budgets (ms): decode and eligibility 10, feature reads 15, retrieval 10, inference 30, budget admission 5, pricing and encoding 5, slack 5. 10+15+10+30+5+5+5=8010+15+10+30+5+5+5 = 8010+15+10+30+5+5+5=80

    Result: 80 ms of compute after receipt, passed to each stage as an absolute deadline. A stage that misses it takes its declared fallback, or the request gets no bid.

    Check: 30 + 10 + 80 = 120 ms. The usual tail caveats apply: stage P99s do not add up to an end-to-end P99, and fan-out to many feature shards needs hedged reads or default features.

    What advertising adds is that every fallback has a price. Default features, a smaller model and no bid each bias value differently. Bidding with stale configuration, an exhausted quota or a creative of unknown review status can create real spend and breach contracts. Give each fallback preconditions, a maximum dollar exposure and a logged reason code; otherwise "higher availability" may just move losses into the ledger.

    Win, display and billing are different events

    Only the event the contract names creates a payment obligation, and the system must record each such event exactly once. Continue the network example from the Chapter 4 appendix: a first-price auction (the winner pays its own bid) and the budget-constrained network bid of 6.324555 CPM, that is at most $0.006324555 for one impression, with no fees.

    Before the response leaves, the system fixes the bid's business identity, (exchange, BidRequest.id, Imp.id, Bid.id), and records the campaign, model, feature, configuration and experiment versions. The exchange belongs in the key because request ids are unique only within one exchange, and Imp.id only within one request (it is often just 1). The budget service then reserves the bid's maximum cost.

    Notices arrive at least once, so the deduplication key for a posting is that business identity plus the event type, never a transport message id. A transport id posts every exchange retry: a double payment and a settlement dispute. A key without the exchange merges two exchanges' notices that share an auction id: a real payable is dropped and its reservation never clears. A notice that repeats a key with a different ${AUCTION_PRICE} is not a duplicate. Send it to exception handling.

    A nurl call means the bid won. It is not evidence of delivery or billing. A burl call means the impression became billable, typically on render or on view. At that point the network books the billed amount (${AUCTION_PRICE}/1000 for one impression) as spend and releases the rest of the reservation. If the billed amount ever exceeds the reserved cap, the hard-budget premise is broken: route the case to exception handling. A missing impression pixel does not prove that nothing is owed, so a local timeout cannot release the reservation.

    Clicks and conversions arrive days later through a separate pipeline and create receivables, which can still be reversed by refunds. Keep three records apart: media payables owed to exchanges and publishers, advertiser receivables, and training and attribution events. A single "conversion success" field cannot serve all three. At settlement, your event log, the exchange's statement and the advertiser's bill are compared; discrepancies are fixed with compensating entries under a named authority, since deduplication covers only the events you received.

    The contract decides which event is billable, and the reservation must cover the worst case under that contract. If 100 bids win and 90 ads display, win-based billing charges for 100 events and display-based billing for 90. Under either contract each open bid can still cost up to its full bid, so a hard-quota reservation cannot be cut by 10% because display succeeds 90% of the time. How display-based billing changes the optimal bid is worked out in the Chapter 4 appendix.

    A hard budget is an invariant over reservations

    The reservation scheme keeps confirmed ledger spend within the hard budget under the assumptions below. The same guarantee covers actual obligations when each cap bounds all payable charges and each release settles or extinguishes the corresponding obligation. A payable charge outside those assumptions can breach the budget even if the ledger invariant held. All quantities are ledger dollars for one accounting period. Let CCC be confirmed media spend, RRR the sum of caps of bids that are open (admitted, not yet billed or released), and BBB the hard media budget. Bid iii has cost cap cic_ici​ (the most it can ever be charged, fees included) and billed amount pip_ipi​. The rules are:

    invariant:C+R≤Badmit i only if C+R+ci≤B:R←R+cifirst billing of open i, pi≤ci:C←C+pi,  R←R−ciauthoritative loss or cancellation of open i:R←R−ciwin notice, duplicate, local timeout:no change\begin{aligned} &\text{invariant:} && C+R\le B\\ &\text{admit } i \text{ only if } C+R+c_i\le B: && R \leftarrow R+c_i\\ &\text{first billing of open } i,\ p_i\le c_i: && C \leftarrow C+p_i,\; R \leftarrow R-c_i\\ &\text{authoritative loss or cancellation of open } i: && R \leftarrow R-c_i\\ &\text{win notice, duplicate, local timeout:} && \text{no change} \end{aligned}​invariant:admit i only if C+R+ci​≤B:first billing of open i, pi​≤ci​:authoritative loss or cancellation of open i:win notice, duplicate, local timeout:​​C+R≤BR←R+ci​C←C+pi​,R←R−ci​R←R−ci​no change​

    Proof. Assume every bid has a reliable cap with pi≤cip_i\le c_ipi​≤ci​, each bid moves from open to billed or released at most once, and each rule applies atomically. The at-most-once property comes from a per-bid state (open → closed) that is tested and changed in the same atomic step as the posting; the deduplication key only suppresses repeats of the same event. A billing notice for an already released bid, or a loss notice for an already billed one, goes to exception handling instead of the ledger. Initially C=R=0≤BC=R=0\le BC=R=0≤B. Suppose the invariant holds before an event; check each event type:

    • Admission: the new total is C+R+ciC+R+c_iC+R+ci​, which the guard requires to be at most BBB.
    • Billing: the total changes by pi−ci≤0p_i-c_i\le 0pi​−ci​≤0.
    • Loss or cancellation: the total changes by −ci≤0-c_i\le 0−ci​≤0.
    • Win notice, duplicate notice, timeout: no change.

    By induction the invariant holds after every event. Because RRR is a sum of nonnegative caps of open bids, R≥0R\ge0R≥0, so C≤BC\le BC≤B. ∎ With many serving nodes, admission must be an atomic check-and-reserve: a serializable counter, or escrow, where node nnn holds quota QnQ_nQn​ with ∑nQn≤B\sum_n Q_n\le B∑n​Qn​≤B and keeps its own Cn+Rn≤QnC_n+R_n\le Q_nCn​+Rn​≤Qn​. Then ∑n(Cn+Rn)≤B\sum_n (C_n+R_n)\le B∑n​(Cn​+Rn​)≤B, by the same proof per node. This requires every notice for bid iii to be applied at the node that reserved it, and quota transfers between nodes to be atomic.

    Worked example

    One bid through the ledger at the last bid's worth of budget

    Given: the Chapter 4 appendix bid of 6.324555 CPM, every win displays, burl is the contractual billing signal and lurl is authoritative for losses. The ledger uses whole micro-dollars (µ$, millionths of a dollar). The cap 6,324.555 µ$ is rounded up to ccc = 6,325 µ$, because rounding down would under-reserve on every bid. A billed 6,324.555 µ$ is also posted as 6,325 µ$, with the residue trued up at reconciliation. BBB = 2,000,000,000 µ$ ($2,000). Start: CCC = 1,999,987,350 µ$ and one earlier bid jjj is open, so RRR = 6,325 µ$ and the headroom B−C−RB-C-RB−C−R is 6,325 µ$: room for exactly one more bid.

    EventLedger actionCRHeadroom
    0. StartBid j open1,999,987,3506,3256,325
    1. Admit bid iC + R + c = 2,000,000,000 ≤ B; R += 6,3251,999,987,35012,6500
    2. nurl for iNone: only burl is billable1,999,987,35012,6500
    3. burl for iC += 6,325; R −= 6,325 (release c − p = 0)1,999,993,6756,3250
    4. burl for i againDedup key exists; transaction rolls back1,999,993,6756,3250
    5. Local timeout for jNone; new bid k rejected (2,000,006,325 > B)1,999,993,6756,3250
    6. lurl for jAuthoritative loss; R −= 6,3251,999,993,67506,325

    Result: C = 1,999,993,675 µ$ ($1,999.993675), R = 0; C+R≤BC+R\le BC+R≤B held after every event, with equality from event 1 through event 5.

    Check: open bids = 1 (j) + 1 admitted (i) − 1 billed (i) − 1 released (j) = 0, matching RRR = 0; CCC rose by exactly one posting, 1,999,987,350 + 6,325 = 1,999,993,675 µ$.

    Pitfall: releasing on a timer

    Suppose event 5 had released jjj on its local timeout. Then RRR = 0, bid kkk is admitted (RRR = 6,325), and jjj's late burl posts 6,325 µ$ with no reservation behind it: CCC = 2,000,000,000 and C+RC+RC+R = 2,000,006,325 µ$ > BBB. If kkk also bills, confirmed spend overshoots by 6,325 µ$. One timeout costs one bid; a regional notice outage releases thousands.

    A reservation may be released only on evidence that the obligation is gone: an authoritative loss notice, a cancellation, a reconciliation result, or a contractual cutoff that extinguishes any remaining payment. An empirical bound on callback delay, a local TTL or an expired lease is not such evidence. Without a discharge mechanism, the choice is between holding the reservation indefinitely and accepting statistical overspend within an explicit limit, which is no longer a hard budget.

    A cap on the advertiser's CPA bill is a separate problem. Conversions from impressions already delivered keep arriving after buying stops, so that cap needs contract terms and explicit tracking of in-flight conversion obligations. The media ledger cannot stand in for it.

    What full-cap reservation costs, and what the shortcut risks

    Prompt loss notices make full-cap reservation cheap; reserving expected cost instead frees budget but gives up the guarantee. To size the first effect, use Little's law. Assume a steady state in which bids are admitted at rate λ\lambdaλ per second (local symbol, not the appendix multiplier) and bid iii stays open for time WiW_iWi​ with mean WWW. Over a long window of length TTT, the area under the open-count curve equals the sum of all holding times, about λT⋅W\lambda T\cdot WλT⋅W. Dividing by TTT gives the average number open:

    nˉopen=λW,W=(1−F) Tloss+F Tbill,\bar n_{\text{open}}=\lambda W,\qquad W=(1-F)\,T_{\text{loss}}+F\,T_{\text{bill}},nˉopen​=λW,W=(1−F)Tloss​+FTbill​,

    where F=b/LF=b/LF=b/L is the win probability, a loser waits TlossT_{\text{loss}}Tloss​ on average for its loss notice and a winner waits TbillT_{\text{bill}}Tbill​ for its billing notice, not its win notice.

    Worked example

    Budget locked by open reservations

    Given: NNN = 1,000,000 bids spread evenly over one day; FFF = 0.316228 at the 6.324555 CPM bid with LLL = $0.02; cap 6,325 µ$; mean loss-notice delay 2 s and mean billing delay 60 s (illustrative).

    1. Arrival rate: λ=1,000,000/86,400≈11.574\lambda = 1{,}000{,}000/86{,}400 \approx 11.574λ=1,000,000/86,400≈11.574 bids per second.
    2. Mean holding time: W=0.683772×2+0.316228×60≈20.341 s\begin{aligned}W &= 0.683772\times 2 + 0.316228\times 60\\ &\approx 20.341\ \text{s}\end{aligned}W​=0.683772×2+0.316228×60≈20.341 s​
    3. Open reservations: λW≈235.43\lambda W \approx 235.43λW≈235.43, locking 235.43×$0.006325≈$1.49235.43\times\$0.006325\approx\$1.49235.43×$0.006325≈$1.49 of the $2,000 budget.
    4. At a 1-hour mean billing delay: W≈1,139.79W \approx 1{,}139.79W≈1,139.79 s, so about 13,192 reservations and $83.44 are locked.

    Result: about 235 open reservations and $1.49 locked on average under the illustrative delays and evenly spread traffic. The average can hide peaks. Missing loss notices can hold substantially more budget, as the example below shows.

    Check: winners contribute 11.574×0.316228×60≈219.611.574\times0.316228\times60\approx219.611.574×0.316228×60≈219.6 of the 235.43 open reservations, losers the remaining 11.574×0.683772×2≈15.811.574\times0.683772\times2\approx15.811.574×0.683772×2≈15.8.

    The shortcut is to reserve expected cost, win probability times bid, instead of the cap. That admits about 1/F1/F1/F times as many concurrent bids near the end of a budget, but overspend is then controlled only statistically. Its tail depends on how correlated the outcomes are, and incidents are exactly what makes outcomes correlated.

    Worked example

    Reserve the cap or reserve the expected cost?

    Given: remaining headroom HHH = $10 near the end of the period; bid bbb = $0.006324555 per impression, win probability F=b/L=0.31622775F = b/L = 0.31622775F=b/L=0.31622775; every admitted bid stays open until the headroom is used up, then all resolve; overshoot means confirmed spend above HHH.

    1. Full-cap reservation, ccc = 6,325 µ$, admits ⌊10,000,000/6,325⌋=1,581\lfloor 10{,}000{,}000 / 6{,}325 \rfloor = 1{,}581⌊10,000,000/6,325⌋=1,581 bids. Even if all win, spend is 1,581×$0.006324555≈$9.999≤H1{,}581 \times \$0.006324555 \approx \$9.999 \le H1,581×$0.006324555≈$9.999≤H.
    2. Expected-cost reservation is F b=b2/L=0.31622775×0.006324555≈$0.002000=2,000 μ$,\begin{aligned}F\,b &= b^2/L\\ &= 0.31622775 \times 0.006324555\\ &\approx \$0.002000 = 2{,}000\ \mu\$,\end{aligned}Fb​=b2/L=0.31622775×0.006324555≈$0.002000=2,000 μ$,​ so k=10,000,000/2,000=5,000k = 10{,}000{,}000 / 2{,}000 = 5{,}000k=10,000,000/2,000=5,000 bids are admitted, with expected spend 5,000×$0.002=$10.00=H5{,}000 \times \$0.002 = \$10.00 = H5,000×$0.002=$10.00=H.
    3. Overshoot is b (W−kF)b\,(W-kF)b(W−kF), where WWW is now the number of wins (local symbol). If outcomes are independent, W∼Binomial(5,000, 0.316228)W\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(5{,}000,\,0.316228)W∼Binomial(5,000,0.316228) with standard deviation 5000×0.316228×0.683772≈32.88\sqrt{5000 \times 0.316228 \times 0.683772} \approx 32.885000×0.316228×0.683772​≈32.88. With the normal approximation (reasonable here since kF(1−F)≈1,081kF(1-F)\approx1{,}081kF(1−F)≈1,081), the P99 lies 2.326 standard deviations above the mean, so the P99 overshoot is 2.326×32.88×$0.006324555≈$0.48.\begin{aligned}&2.326 \times 32.88 \times \$0.006324555\\ &\approx \$0.48.\end{aligned}​2.326×32.88×$0.006324555≈$0.48.​
    4. With perfect positive correlation, all bids share a single win indicator: all 5,000 win with probability FFF, and otherwise none win. In the all-win outcome, spend 5,000×$0.006324555≈$31.625{,}000 \times \$0.006324555 \approx \$31.625,000×$0.006324555≈$31.62, overshoot $31.62−$10=$21.62\$31.62 - \$10 = \$21.62$31.62−$10=$21.62.

    Result: expected-cost reservation admits 5,000 bids instead of 1,581; its overshoot is about $0.48 at P99 under independence and $21.62 (216% of headroom) when outcomes move together.

    Check: the concurrency gain is 6,325/2,000≈3.16≈1/F=3.1626{,}325/2{,}000 \approx 3.16 \approx 1/F = 3.1626,325/2,000≈3.16≈1/F=3.162, and 5,000/1,581≈3.165{,}000/1{,}581 \approx 3.165,000/1,581≈3.16. The worst case also equals k b (1−F)=5,000×0.006324555×0.683772≈$21.62k\,b\,(1-F) = 5{,}000 \times 0.006324555 \times 0.683772 \approx \$21.62kb(1−F)=5,000×0.006324555×0.683772≈$21.62.

    Optional: partial correlation, and how overspend grows with bids in flight
