    Measure the cost of conservative reservation as lost payments minus media cost, not as lock contention or budget-service load.

    Releases can change what the system optimizes

    In an ad system a release can change the objective itself, not just latency or error rates. Three traps are specific to advertising.

    • Labels must be matured. Train only on examples whose attribution window has closed, so that a missing conversion is a real negative (Chapter 5). If one release changes both the model and the attribution window, you cannot tell why online results moved. Version the model, the calibrator (the map from raw score to probability), feature definitions and budget-control parameters together, or a rollback may not restore the old behavior.
    • A shadow model cannot show profit. A shadow deployment scores live traffic without driving decisions. It exposes latency and score-distribution anomalies, but it buys nothing, so it cannot show that the model makes money.
    • A canary buys different traffic. When a new model controls a share of live bids, it changes which opportunities are won and at what prices. That selection is part of its effect. Compare arms under the same budget constraint, on matured labels, and check traffic mix and price distribution before reading the result (Chapter 6).

    Decision logs make this analysis possible only if each bid opportunity links its feature versions, predictions, bid policy, experiment arm, outcome reasons and later billing and attribution events.

    Monitoring should tie each signal to an economic consequence and a first check; thresholds come from contracts and loss tolerance. Duplicate billing, budget violations and changes to value definitions should each trigger a stop-loss on their own, because conversion reports arrive days too late.

    Signal Investigate first Conclusions you cannot draw directly
    Win rate up while profit down Bids, competing prices, traffic mix, fees The model is definitely worse, or definitely better
    Clicks up while conversions down Creatives, landing pages, click authenticity, label maturity CTR (click-through rate) should get more weight
    Sudden drop in spend Eligibility, deadlines, quota, economic constraints All under-delivery is a pacing failure
    Sudden drop in reported CPA Windows, attribution rules, event deduplication, backfill The customer got an equally large incremental lift
    Offline gain, online decline Time leakage, calibration, traffic selection, latency, release versions Just switch to a bigger model
    Wins up, billed impressions flat Render failures, creative load errors, billing-notice integration The extra wins are delivered impressions
    Open-reservation age rising Missing loss or billing notices, an exchange outage, contract cutoffs The reservations are safe to expire

    AppLovin and Axon

    In this chapter

    • Say what Axon, AppLovin Ads and MAX each are, and trace one MAX auction from ad request to billing, including what the publisher, the winning bidder and AppLovin each earn.
    • Separate what every MAX bidder learns from what only the auctioneer sees, and both from what AppLovin says Axon is allowed to train on.
    • Explain how an advertiser's two settings, a ROAS goal and a daily budget, become one bid per impression, and read which of the two is binding.
    • Explain how a prediction advantage turns into retained profit, and why a sharper model can raise profit with no change in win rate.
    • Name the evidence that would distinguish a real moat from metrics that merely look good, and read AppLovin's net revenue for what it can and cannot tell you.

    The gist. AppLovin sits on both sides of one market. MAX runs the auction inside publishers' apps; AppLovin Ads, powered by the Axon model, is one of the bidders in that auction, and it earns nearly all of the company's revenue. Running the auction shows AppLovin every bid, but seeing data is not permission to train on it, and the company says Axon does not use rivals' bids. A better model makes money by moving spend toward impressions that convert, even when the number of wins stays fixed in the uniform-threshold example. So a real moat shows up in advertisers' incremental returns on comparable supply, not in win rates, publisher prices or revenue growth.

    Labels: public fact (an SEC filing or AppLovin's own documentation, which is a company statement, not an audit), inference (our reasoning) and unknown. Hypothetical numbers are teaching assumptions. Pages retrieved November 12, 2026.

    What the products are

    AppLovin sells three things that are easy to blur: a prediction engine, the ad product it powers, and the auction where that product bids. Publishers here are app developers; ad networks reach their inventory through an SDK (a library compiled into the app). Mediation software in the app picks the demand source for each ad request, either by calling networks in a fixed order (a waterfall) or by real-time bids (in-app bidding). A DSP (demand-side platform) bids for advertisers. MAX is AppLovin's mediation product, which the company calls its in-app bidding solution. Axon is AppLovin's prediction and bidding engine (the filings say "recommendation engine"). The advertiser product it powers is Axon Ads Manager in the 2025 Form 10-K and AppLovin Ads in the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q; this chapter says AppLovin Ads.

    Public fact. AppLovin describes Axon as the AI advertising engine that powers AppLovin Ads. AppLovin bids on each impression according to the value Axon assigns to it for a given advertiser, aiming at that advertiser's return-on-ad-spend (ROAS) goal. The 2025 10-K and the Q3 2026 10-Q both say this product generates substantially all of AppLovin's revenue; the 10-K adds that revenue from other services "was not material". Axon official description, AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    Public fact. MAX's partner documentation describes a "unified first-price auction" in which the highest bidder wins, and its OpenRTB specification says bidders are expected "to pay the CPM amount they bid in full". DSPs bid through AppLovin Exchange over OpenRTB 2.5; ad networks bid through tokens from their own SDKs. Non-bidding networks enter at a CPM set by the publisher or by auto-CPM from their recent reported CPMs. The documented sequence for one ad request: MAX auction flow, AppLovin OpenRTB specification, bid responses and notices, auto-CPM

    1. Request
      Ad request. The app asks for an ad. MAX collects bid tokens from the network SDKs it initialized at launch and sends the request to the MAX ad server.
    2. ≤ tmax
      Bids. The auction server sends bid requests to SDK bidders and to DSPs in AppLovin Exchange. Only bids returned within the timeout tmax count.
    3. Resolve
      Unified auction. Bids are merged with the publisher's waterfall networks at their CPM prices; the highest CPM wins. Invalid bids (below the floor, missing or zero) get a loss notice now.
    4. Load
      Win and loss notices. The winner's ad is loaded. If the load fails, the winner gets a loss notice. Other bidders get their loss notice after a winning ad loads.
    5. Render
      Billing. When the ad renders (video starts, or a graphic is displayed), MAX calls the winner's billing URL, the signal on which DSPs should count impressions and spend.

    Public fact. The notices carry prices. ${AUCTION_PRICE}, the final price, is substituted into both the win URL and the loss URL, "so every bidder (win or loss) sees the final paid price". The winner also receives ${AUCTION_MINIMUM_BID_TO_WIN}, defined as the second-highest bid. A loss notice carries an OpenRTB loss-reason code. These are MAX's semantics; other exchanges define their notices differently (Chapter 7). MAX notice macros

    Worked example · hypothetical numbers

    One MAX auction: who earns what

    Given, for one ad request (prices in dollars CPM unless marked per impression): publisher floor $3.00; waterfall network W entered at $5.50. Bids: AppLovin Ads $7.50, SDK bidder X $6.80, DSP Y $6.00, DSP Z $2.00. AppLovin Ads bids for an advertiser who pays a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per conversion, with conversion probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 per impression, so value v=qa=$0.015v=qa=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015 per impression; $7.50 CPM is an illustrative bid, chosen using the half-value rule from the Chapter 4 appendix. Let φ=5%\varphi=5\%φ=5% be the MAX fee on winning auction spend; MAX's real fee rate is not disclosed. For this stylized CPA contract, assume the fee is charged to a third-party bidder on top of the publisher payment.

    1. Filter. Z's $2.00 is below the $3.00 floor, so Z gets a loss notice during the auction.
    2. Rank by CPM: $7.50 (AppLovin Ads) > $6.80 (X) > $6.00 (Y) > $5.50 (W). AppLovin Ads wins and, under first price, pays its bid: b=$7.50 CPM=$7.50/1000=$0.0075 per impression.b=\$7.50\ \text{CPM}=\$7.50/1000=\$0.0075\ \text{per impression}.b=$7.50 CPM=$7.50/1000=$0.0075 per impression.
    3. Notices. The winner learns the second-highest bid, $6.80, so it paid $7.50 − $6.80 = $0.70 CPM more than needed to win. X and Y each receive AUCTION_PRICE = $7.50 in their loss notices: the price they had to beat.
    4. Render and bill. The billing URL fires at render; the publisher is credited $0.0075 for this impression.
    5. AppLovin's revenue when its own bidder wins: the advertiser charge minus the publisher payment, per impression and in expectation over the conversion: v−b=$0.015−$0.0075=$0.0075.v-b=\$0.015-\$0.0075=\$0.0075.v−b=$0.015−$0.0075=$0.0075.
    6. Counterfactual: X wins at the same $7.50. AppLovin earns only the MAX fee: φ b=0.05×$0.0075=$0.000375 per impression.\varphi\,b=0.05\times\$0.0075=\$0.000375\ \text{per impression}.φb=0.05×$0.0075=$0.000375 per impression.

    Result: the publisher earns $7.50 per 1,000 such impressions whoever wins; AppLovin expects $7.50 per 1,000 when its own bidder wins and $0.375 when a third party wins at the same price, a factor of 20 under the assumed prices and fee.

    Check: (v−b)/(φb)=0.0075/0.000375=20(v-b)/(\varphi b)=0.0075/0.000375=20(v−b)/(φb)=0.0075/0.000375=20. The winning price ($7.50) is at least the second bid ($6.80), as a highest-bid-wins auction requires; among comparable eligible real-time bids, a reported winning price below a losing bidder’s own valid bid would warrant reconciliation against publisher settlement records. The notice itself is generated by the auctioneer.

    Under these inputs the auctioneer earns more when its own bidder wins; at a fixed publisher payment bbb that holds only if v−b>φbv-b>\varphi bv−b>φb. The example shows a possible incentive, not auction behavior. Inference. When AppLovin Ads buys through MAX in an action-based arrangement, it pays the publisher per impression but is paid per action, so it bears the conversion-rate risk between the two, the same segment a CPA network bears (risk map, Chapter 3).

    Public fact. The 10-K states that AppLovin is an agent, not a principal, in its advertising arrangements: it does not control the inventory before it passes to the advertiser. Under US GAAP an agent reports revenue net, so reported revenue is advertiser payments minus amounts paid or payable to publishers. Revenue is recognized when an impression is delivered (impression-based arrangements) or when a specified action such as a click or install occurs (action-based arrangements). Reported revenue was $5,480.7 million in 2025 (up 70.0% from $3,224.1 million in 2024) and $2,184.8 million in Q3 2026 (up 55.5% from $1,405.0 million in Q3 2025); both exclude the divested Apps business. Revenue recognition note, AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    Inference. Because revenue is net, reported revenue reveals neither total advertiser spend nor the take rate (the share of advertiser spend the platform keeps; Chapter 3). In the worked example the advertiser pays $15 per 1,000 impressions in expectation and AppLovin books $7.50; a filing shows only the latter. MAX is "free for publishers" per its website, but the same FAQ says bidding networks pay AppLovin a fee on the ad revenue they generate, and the filings describe MAX revenue as a percentage of client or winning auction spend. Since revenue outside AppLovin Ads is immaterial, MAX's value to AppLovin lies mainly in the supply and auction position it provides, not in its fees. MAX website FAQ, AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    A ROAS goal and a budget are constraints; Axon turns them into one bid per impression

    An AppLovin advertiser never types a bid. Its two main settings are the two constraints of its problem: spend at most the budget each day, and earn at least the ROAS goal in revenue per dollar spent. Axon then bids on every impression so as to buy as much predicted revenue as those two constraints allow. The per-impression work sits in Axon's predictions; the two settings only fix how predicted revenue is turned into a price, and how much of it to buy.

    Public fact. AppLovin's campaign API takes the following:

    • A goal type: purchase-revenue ROAS, ad-revenue ROAS or blended ROAS, as well as cost-per-install and cost-per-event goals.
    • A goal value, set once for all countries or per country.
    • A ROAS day target, day 7 or day 28: the revenue window counted from install.
    • A required daily budget, set once for all countries or per country.

    The goal type is fixed when the campaign is created; the goal value and the budget can be changed later. Two bidding strategies are listed:

    • target_goal_with_cpi_billing: AppLovin “aims to control the cost per result around your target goal” and charges per install.
    • auto_bidding_with_cpm_billing: it “aims to fully use your budget while maximizing results at the lowest possible cost per result” and charges per impression.

    AppLovin campaign management API. The documentation does not publish the bidding algorithm. What follows is the standard model of bidding under a value goal and a budget (Aggarwal, Badanidiyuru and Mehta, 2019), not AppLovin's disclosed method.

    Model. For each impression iii, Axon predicts its value, the expected day-7 revenue it will produce:

    vi=P(install∣i)×E[D7 revenue∣install, i].v_i=P(\text{install}\mid i)\times\mathbb E[\text{D7 revenue}\mid\text{install},\,i].vi​=P(install∣i)×E[D7 revenue∣install,i].

    With ROAS goal RRR (0.4 for 40%) and a pacing factor λ\lambdaλ between 0 and 1, it bids

    bi=λ viR.b_i=\lambda\,\frac{v_i}{R}.bi​=λRvi​​.
    • The goal sets the exchange rate. Paying vi/Rv_i/Rvi​/R for viv_ivi​ of expected revenue earns exactly RRR, so vi/Rv_i/Rvi​/R is the most the impression is worth at the goal. MAX's auction is first-price (the winner pays its bid; see above), so bidding vi/Rv_i/Rvi​/R everywhere yields a campaign ROAS of exactly RRR in expectation, provided the predictions are calibrated.
    • The budget sets λ\lambdaλ. If bidding vi/Rv_i/Rvi​/R would spend more than the budget, the pacing controller lowers λ\lambdaλ until expected spend equals the budget, and ROAS comes out above the goal. If it would not, λ=1\lambda=1λ=1: the goal binds and the campaign spends less than its budget.
    • The predictions pick the impressions. One multiplier scales every bid, so a user predicted to bring twice the revenue gets twice the bid. This is why two settings suffice; chapter 4 shows why one multiplier is the right answer for a budget.
    Worked example

    Which constraint binds

    Given, for one country and one day: N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 alike opportunities, each with a 0.5% install probability and $2 expected D7 revenue per install, so v=0.005×$2=$0.01v=0.005\times\$2=\$0.01v=0.005×$2=$0.01 per impression ($10 CPM). The highest competing bid is Z∼Uniform(0,$0.05)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,\$0.05)Z∼Uniform(0,$0.05), as in chapter 4's model with a $50 CPM ceiling. ROAS goal 40%.

    1. Bid at λ=1\lambda=1λ=1: $0.01/0.4=$0.025\$0.01/0.4=\$0.025$0.01/0.4=$0.025 per impression, $25 CPM. It wins with probability 0.025/0.05=0.50.025/0.05=0.50.025/0.05=0.5: 500,000 impressions.
    2. Spend 500,000×$0.025=$12,500500{,}000\times\$0.025=\$12{,}500500,000×$0.025=$12,500; D7 revenue 500,000×$0.01=$5,000500{,}000\times\$0.01=\$5{,}000500,000×$0.01=$5,000; ROAS 5,000/12,500=40%5{,}000/12{,}500=40\%5,000/12,500=40%; 2,500 installs at $5 each.
    3. Budget $20,000: it does not bind. The campaign spends $12,500 and leaves $7,500 unspent.
    4. Budget $5,000: it binds. Expected spend is Nb2/LNb^2/LNb2/L, so the controller lowers the bid to b=5,000×0.05/106=$0.0158 ($15.81 CPM),b=\sqrt{5{,}000\times0.05/10^6}=\$0.0158\ (\$15.81\text{ CPM}),b=5,000×0.05/106​=$0.0158 ($15.81 CPM), which is λ=15.81/25=0.632\lambda=15.81/25=0.632λ=15.81/25=0.632. It wins 316,228 impressions for $5,000 and earns $3,162 of D7 revenue, a ROAS of 63.2%, with 1,581 installs at $3.16.

    Result: with a slack budget the goal binds, ROAS lands on 40% and $7,500 goes unspent; with a $5,000 budget the budget binds, bids fall to 63% of the goal-implied bid, and ROAS rises to 63%.

    Check: when every impression has value vvv and costs its bid bbb, ROAS is v/bv/bv/b: 0.01/0.025=40%0.01/0.025=40\%0.01/0.025=40% and 0.01/0.0158=63.2%0.01/0.0158=63.2\%0.01/0.0158=63.2% ✓. Spend 316,228×$0.0158114=$5,000316{,}228\times\$0.0158114=\$5{,}000316,228×$0.0158114=$5,000 ✓.

    SettingsBinding constraintBidSpendD7 revenueROASInstalls
    Goal 40%, budget $20,000Goal$25.00 CPM$12,500$5,00040.0%2,500
    Goal 40%, budget $5,000Budget$15.81 CPM$5,000$3,16263.2%1,581

    Reading the table as an advertiser:

    • Spend below budget means the goal is the lever. Raising the budget changes nothing. Lowering the goal buys volume at a worse rate.
    • The marginal return is far below the average. Moving from a 40% to a 30% goal adds $7,500 of spend and $1,325 of D7 revenue, a marginal ROAS of 17.7% even though the campaign reports 31.6% (chapter 3 explains why).
    • Spend at budget with ROAS above the goal means the budget is the lever. Raising the budget buys volume until ROAS falls to the goal.
    • Set the goal from lifetime economics. The goal counts only seven (or 28) days of revenue, so derive it from the long-run return you need. If D7 revenue is typically a quarter of first-year revenue and you need a first-year ROAS of 120%, set the D7 goal at 0.25×120%=30%0.25\times120\%=30\%0.25×120%=30%. Revenue is not profit: break-even on contribution needs a return of 1/m1/m1/m, where mmm is the contribution margin (chapter 3).
    • The ROAS is attributed, not caused. It counts revenue the attribution rules credit to AppLovin; only a holdout test shows how much the ads caused (chapter 6).
    • Billing decides who bears which error. With CPI billing the advertiser pays per install, so AppLovin bears errors in the predicted install rate, as the platform bears click-rate errors under CPC (chapter 3). Errors in predicted revenue per install stay with the advertiser and show up as missed ROAS. With CPM billing the advertiser bears both.

    Seeing data is not the same as being allowed to train on it

    Keep three sets apart: what every bidder learns, what only the auctioneer sees, and what its own bidder may train on.

    Public fact (company statement). AppLovin's Axon page lists the inputs it says Axon uses: device and network information; engagement data about apps, ads and other digital properties, collected by AppLovin or shared by partners; advertisers' own user data, if they choose to share it; and win/loss notices from MAX, which the page says all bidders receive. The page says the models do not ingest other bidders' bid information or user data. Separately, the 10-K describes a flywheel: as more advertisers use its solutions, AppLovin gains "access to more data regarding users and user engagement", and as distribution grows it gains "better insights for Axon AI". Axon data description, AppLovin 2025 10-K, Business section

    What every MAX bidder learns (public fact)

    The bid request for each auction it is invited to. For evaluated bids: win or loss, a loss-reason code, and the final price AUCTION_PRICE. If it wins, the second-highest bid. A billing call when its ad renders.

    What only the auctioneer sees

    All bids submitted for an auction, and which invited bidders did not bid; waterfall CPM prices, floors and other publisher settings; load and render outcomes for all networks.

    On a first-price win the final price is the bidder's own bid, so the minimum-to-win field is what reveals the competition; a valid outbid loss notice reveals the price to beat (how bidders learn from such feedback: Chapter 5).

    Public fact. Adjust is an MMP (mobile measurement partner), the kind of normally independent third party advertisers use to attribute installs and in-app events to the ads that drove them. AppLovin owns it: the 10-K says Adjust is operated by a wholly owned subsidiary and that data generated by Adjust's services is not shared with AppLovin or used to optimize its recommendation engine unless a customer directs it. AppLovin also sold its Apps business, its own mobile games, to Tripledot; the sale closed on June 30, 2025, for cash plus about 22% of Tripledot's ordinary shares. AppLovin treats Tripledot as a related party, and Tripledot still buys AppLovin Ads. Securities class actions are pending that allege materially false or misleading statements, including about the advertising solutions; AppLovin says the allegations lack merit, and allegations are not findings. AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q, including legal proceedings

    Inference. The phrase "data flywheel" bundles four propositions with different evidentiary status:

    PropositionStatusWhat public sources say
    MAX receives every bid in order to run the auction.Public factFollows from the documented unified auction: the auction server must see the bids to rank them.
    Axon is permitted to use those bids.Contract terms unknownThe company’s description addresses model inputs. Permission to use rival bids would depend on contracts and applicable rules.
    The training pipeline actually uses them.UnknownNo public audit either way.
    Only AppLovin has the data that matters for training.UnknownNot established. Final prices go to every participating bidder. The full bid vector stays with MAX, and the company says Axon does not use it. The 10-K says engagement data grows with distribution but gives no measure of its value. Adjust data is excluded by default.

    Merging the four into one "flywheel" assumes the advantage the argument is supposed to prove. Unknown. Public materials do not reveal Axon's architecture, features or training, nor how much of a quarter's growth came from the model, creatives, supply, customer mix or attribution rules.

    How a prediction advantage becomes retained profit

    Better information can never hurt a single bidder in a fixed market; it pays by changing which impressions the bidder buys and at what price, and how much of the gain the bidder keeps depends on the market. Let Π(I)\Pi(\mathcal I)Π(I) be the set of feasible policies (same objective, actions and budget constraints) that can be computed from information I\mathcal II. Then

    Iold⊆Inew  ⇒  Π(Iold)⊆Π(Inew)  ⇒  max⁡π∈Π(Inew)E[u(π)] ≥ max⁡π∈Π(Iold)E[u(π)].\mathcal I_{\text{old}}\subseteq\mathcal I_{\text{new}}\;\Rightarrow\;\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{old}})\subseteq\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{new}})\;\Rightarrow\;\max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{new}})}\mathbb E[u(\pi)]\ \ge\ \max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{old}})}\mathbb E[u(\pi)].Iold​⊆Inew​⇒Π(Iold​)⊆Π(Inew​)⇒π∈Π(Inew​)max​E[u(π)] ≥ π∈Π(Iold​)max​E[u(π)].

    The proof: the better-informed bidder can ignore the extra information and replay the old policy. The premises are that competitors and the clearing-price distribution stay fixed, the information is free, available at decision time and refines the old, and the policy optimizes on accurate values. A higher offline AUC (ranking quality on held-out logs) establishes none of these.

    In the uniform-threshold model, let v^old\hat v_{\rm old}v^old​ and v^new\hat v_{\rm new}v^new​ be calibrated estimates of the impression’s dollar value. Assume the same mean prediction and that both models’ bids lie in the linear part of the win curve. The change in expected profit is N[Var⁡(v^new)−Var⁡(v^old)]/(4L)N[\operatorname{Var}(\hat v_{\rm new})-\operatorname{Var}(\hat v_{\rm old})]/(4L)N[Var(v^new​)−Var(v^old​)]/(4L), with the same expected win count. In the example below, profit rises from $2,812.50 to $3,825 at 375,000 expected wins. In a separate example with fixed true value, multiplying the forecast by a factor rrr changes profit by a factor 1−(r−1)21-(r-1)^21−(r−1)2 and spend by a factor r2r^2r2 while bids stay within the threshold range. That example holds the forecast error fixed. Chapter 5 shows how selecting the highest of several noisy scores can also lead to overprediction.

    For the refinement formula, let s=v^s=\hat vs=v^ be a calibrated value estimate, so the conditional expected true value at score sss is sss. The threshold is independent of the value and score. At bid s/2s/2s/2, conditional expected profit is (s−s/2)(s/(2L))=s2/(4L)(s-s/2)(s/(2L))=s^2/(4L)(s−s/2)(s/(2L))=s2/(4L). Across NNN opportunities, expected profit is N[Var⁡(s)+(E[s])2]/(4L)N[\operatorname{Var}(s)+(\mathbb E[s])^2]/(4L)N[Var(s)+(E[s])2]/(4L). The mean term cancels when old and new predictions have the same mean. Expected wins are NE[s]/(2L)N\mathbb E[s]/(2L)NE[s]/(2L), so they stay fixed because the win probability is linear over this range.

    Inference. How much of a model's gain AppLovin keeps is shaped by market structure as well as model performance. Bidding more for better opportunities raises publisher revenue; competitors and publishers' floor prices adjust; advertisers push for better pricing. The split depends on whether the information is exclusive and stable, whether customers have alternatives, and how the platform charges.

    Evidence that separates a moat from good-looking metrics

    A moat exists if, on the same supply surface (the inventory one can bid on), with comparable data permissions and budgets, new advertisers and extra budget keep producing incremental contribution for advertisers. Compare incremental contribution per dollar with competing bidders on matched inventory, and check whether that advantage persists. Correct for survivorship bias: a showcase of surviving high-return customers proves nothing about the rest.

    Three explanations for growth need different evidence. A better model shows up as higher performance on matched supply at the same budget; privileged data, in which signals each bidder was entitled to use; self-preferencing, in loss notices that contradict the documented auction rules (any bidder can check those) and, for an own bidder that might see rivals' bids before bidding, in an audit of bid-time data access, which loss notices cannot reveal. An advertiser holdout measures one campaign's causal return; separating causes needs a comparison that varies the proposed mechanism.

    Three metrics look good without proving any of this. Attributed revenue is what the attribution rule credits to the ad; incremental revenue would not have happened without it (Chapter 6). D7 ROAS is attributed revenue in the seven days after acquisition divided by acquisition spend (defined in Chapter 3).

    1. Higher pCTR with flat ROAS. If predicted click-through rate (pCTR) and the clearing CPM both rise while D7 ROAS stays flat, the model may simply be buying more clickable traffic at a higher price. Decompose the change into price and traffic mix first.
    2. Higher publisher eCPM. Publisher eCPM (revenue per thousand impressions) can rise while advertisers gain nothing: in the miscalibration example under the same market assumptions, aggregate publisher revenue rises about 5.4% while the bidder’s profit falls.
    3. Subsidized growth. Inference (generic, not a claim about AppLovin's practices). Credits or discounts buy room for trial and error, not unbiased labels. Labels from subsidized customers, cheap traffic or retargeting (ads to users who already engaged) may not transfer once full pricing applies. Check retention after subsidies end and calibration by segment.

    Takeaways

    • Axon is the model, AppLovin Ads the product that earns nearly all revenue, MAX the first-price auction where it bids. Every bidder whose bid was evaluated receives the final price in its notice (whether rejected bids, e.g. below the floor, also receive it is not documented). Revenue is reported net, so advertiser spend and take rate are not disclosed.
    • The auctioneer earns far more when its own bidder wins than from its fee on a rival's win. Neutrality is the claim to test. Loss-notice prices can flag inconsistencies among eligible real-time bids for reconciliation, but not an own bidder that sees rivals' bids before bidding and bids just above them; that needs an audit of bid-time data access.
    • With uniform thresholds and interior bids, refinement can raise profit at a constant expected win count; miscalibration moves spend to first order and profit only to second order. Neither win rate nor publisher eCPM identifies a better model.

    Comprehensive exercises and answers

    How to use the two sets

    • Gist set, Questions 1–4, 40 points. Do it right after the gist path. About 60 minutes: 45 closed-book, 15 to mark yourself. Pass: 32 or more, with no conceptual error on Questions 2 or 3.
    • Depth set, Questions 5–10, 60 points. Do it after reading chapters 4–7 in full, after a break or on another day. About 90 minutes: 65 closed-book, 25 to mark. Pass: 48 or more, with no conceptual error on Questions 5 or 6. If you skipped the optional chapter 7, skip Question 10 and pass at 40 out of 50.
    • Scoring. 10 points per question. Questions 1–3 and 5–7 are calculations, marked on the numbers and on naming the right party, unit and assumption; each answer shows a full worked solution. Questions 4 and 8–10 are conceptual, marked against the listed points a full-marks answer must contain. Pass marks are this reader's own, not an industry standard. Timings assume fluency in probability; Questions 3, 5 and 6 take longest.
    • Sources. Q1 chapter 1; Q2 chapter 2 and chapter 3; Q3 chapter 6 and chapter 3; Q4 chapter 8; Q5 chapter 4; Q6 chapter 5; Q7 chapter 5; Q8 chapter 5; Q9 chapters 5–6; Q10 chapter 7.

    The gist. There are two sets. The gist set checks the four ideas the rest of the field rests on: what one impression is worth and to whom; who pays when a predicted rate is wrong, and who turns a bid into a price per impression; credited versus caused sales and whether the next dollar still pays; and what evidence would show a durable data advantage. The depth set checks the machinery behind them: bidding under a budget, why the auction's winners are overpredicted, calibration after sampling, learning prices from censored feedback, diagnosing an offline win that loses online, and recording money exactly once. Each question uses new numbers or a new angle, so it tests whether you can apply a mechanism, not whether you remember a worked example.

    Gist set: four questions, 40 points, about 60 minutes

    These four questions test the mechanisms every later chapter builds on, and need little beyond the gist path. Question 3 also uses two chapter 6 sections beyond their first sentences, the holdout test and exposed versus assigned users; read them first if you took the gist path. The parameters below are the running campaign; Question 1 uses them, and the depth set returns to them.

    Shared parameters for Questions 1, 7 and 9. The running campaign from “A fictional campaign used throughout” (Start here), worked through in chapter 4's optional appendix on network bidding. Question 5 specifies the advertiser's direct-buying contract separately; the other questions state their own numbers.

    • Opportunities. N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 statistically identical bid opportunities (bid requests from publishers). Every auction win yields exactly one successful impression; display failures are ignored here (Real-time advertising systems relaxes this).
    • Contracts. The ad network sells to the advertiser on CPA terms: it charges a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable attributed conversion, a conversion that the agreed attribution rules credit to the ad and that the contract makes payable. It buys impressions from publishers in first-price auctions: the winner pays its own bid, per impression.
    • Conversion probability. Each impression produces a billable attributed conversion with probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005, the same for every opportunity and independent of the bid and of competition. The network's expected collections per impression are v=qa=$0.015v=qa=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015.
    • Advertiser economics. Pre-advertising contribution per order is g=$40g=\$40g=$40: sales revenue minus goods, fulfillment and other per-order variable costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. The true causal lift is Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002: for the same opportunity, showing the ad raises the probability of an order by 0.0002 compared with not showing it. Here Δq<q\Delta q<qΔq<q is a property of the given numbers, not a general law; attribution can both credit orders the ad did not cause and miss orders it did.
    • Competition. The competitive threshold ZZZ is the highest competing bid for an opportunity, in dollars per impression, with Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L), L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02, independently across opportunities. A bid bbb wins when b≥Zb\ge Zb≥Z, so the win rate is F(b)=b/LF(b)=b/LF(b)=b/L for 0≤b≤L0\le b\le L0≤b≤L.
    • Objective. In the network bidding appendix, the network picks one uniform bid bbb to maximize expected advertiser payments less media cost: expected collections from the advertiser minus expected payments to publishers. Its budget caps payments to publishers, not the advertiser's spend.
    • Units. “Spend”, “bill” and “collections” mean expected values. CPM is a price per thousand impressions; eCPM (effective CPM) expresses any expected amount per impression as an amount per thousand impressions. Dollars per impression × 1,000 = CPM.
    Question 1: Ad spend, attribution, and incrementality. Using the shared parameters above, compute three amounts per 1,000 impressions. Find (a) expected ad spend, (b) contribution from attributed conversions, and (c) incremental contribution. Assume every attributed conversion meets the billing rules in this example. Explain why incremental contribution and the network’s expected collections differ.
    Reference answers and scoring points
    Worked solution

    Ad spend and contribution per 1,000 impressions

    Given: q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 billable attributed conversions per impression, a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable conversion, g=$40g=\$40g=$40 contribution per order, Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002 caused orders per impression.

    1. (a) Expected ad spend. An impression generates a charge of aaa with probability qqq. 1000 q a=1000×0.0005×30=1000×$0.015=$15 eCPM\begin{aligned}1000\,q\,a &= 1000\times 0.0005\times 30\\ &= 1000\times\$0.015 = \$15\ \text{eCPM}\end{aligned}1000qa​=1000×0.0005×30=1000×$0.015=$15 eCPM​
    2. (b) Contribution from attributed conversions, valued at ggg. 1000 q g=1000×0.0005×40=1000×$0.020=$20 eCPM\begin{aligned}1000\,q\,g &= 1000\times 0.0005\times 40\\ &= 1000\times\$0.020 = \$20\ \text{eCPM}\end{aligned}1000qg​=1000×0.0005×40=1000×$0.020=$20 eCPM​
    3. (c) Incremental contribution uses the expected additional orders. 1000 Δq g=1000×0.0002×40=1000×$0.008=$8 eCPM\begin{aligned}1000\,\Delta q\,g &= 1000\times 0.0002\times 40\\ &= 1000\times\$0.008 = \$8\ \text{eCPM}\end{aligned}1000Δqg​=1000×0.0002×40=1000×$0.008=$8 eCPM​

    Result: (a) $15 in ad spend, (b) $20 in contribution from attributed conversions, (c) $8 in incremental contribution, per 1,000 impressions.

    Check: (b)/(a) = g/a=40/30g/a = 40/30g/a=40/30 = 4/3 ✓, and (c)/(b) = Δq/q\Delta q/qΔq/q = 0.4 ✓. Using attributed conversions suggests a gain of $20 − $15 = $5 per thousand impressions; it actually loses $15 − $8 = $7. Equivalently its cost per caused order is qa/Δq=0.015/0.0002=$75qa/\Delta q = 0.015/0.0002 = \$75qa/Δq=0.015/0.0002=$75 against g=$40g=\$40g=$40, matching chapter 4's appendix.

    Why incremental contribution differs from collections. A full-marks answer makes these points:

    • Receivables are set by the contract. The network collects $30 for every billable attributed conversion, whether or not the ad caused it. Its expected revenue per impression is qaqaqa; bids priced off Δq g\Delta q\,gΔqg would misprice every auction (here they would value an impression at $8 instead of $15 eCPM).
    • Incremental contribution is an input to the advertiser’s objective. Subtract ad spend to obtain incremental profit.
    • The gap is a separate risk. A $7 loss per thousand impressions is a churn risk. Track it as its own metric or constraint (an incremental-CPA or iROAS guardrail), not by rewriting the receivables forecast.

    Scoring: 2 points for each number; 4 points for distinguishing the two objectives.

    Question 2: Billing, bidding, and conversion risk. A game studio buys rewarded-video impressions (ads a player opts into for an in-game reward) on an oCPM product: it sets a target of $30 per purchase, is billed per 1,000 impressions, and judges the campaign on D7 ROAS (chapter 3). The platform forecasts pCTR = 0.02 clicks per impression and pCVR = 0.04 purchases per click. Assume the platform’s media cost per impression is fixed in parts (a)–(d). Hold the per-event charges fixed after setting them from the forecast. As in chapter 3's worked example, each product's expected bill at the forecast equals its eCPM bid. (a) Identify the auctioned opportunity, billable event, bidding target, and campaign KPI. Can the studio conclude that it pays only when a purchase happens? (b) The true CTR turns out to be 0.01; CVR is as forecast. Compute the cost per purchase under oCPM, and under oCPC, CPC and CPA products bid from the same forecast. Who absorbs the error in each case? (c) Repeat with the true CVR at 0.02 and CTR as forecast. (d) Which risk does no pricing product move off the studio? (e) The studio instead buys through a DSP that bids into an open first-price exchange, using the same forecast. Who converts the $30 target into a price per impression, what does the exchange rank, and who bears the CTR error now (chapter 2)?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    (a) The auction sells an impression opportunity and compares bids on an eCPM basis. The billable event is an impression. The bidding target is $30 per purchase, and the campaign KPI is D7 ROAS. The contract charges for impressions even when they produce zero purchases.

    Worked solution

    Two forecast errors across four pricing models

    Given: pCTR = 0.02, pCVR = 0.04, $30 per purchase; expected bill at the forecast equals the eCPM bid.

    1. Bids. oCPM: 1000×0.02×0.04×$30=$241000\times0.02\times0.04\times\$30=\$241000×0.02×0.04×$30=$24 per 1,000 impressions. oCPC: the same $30 target and the same $24 eCPM, billed per click, so each click is charged $24/(1000×0.02)=$1.20\$24/(1000\times0.02)=\$1.20$24/(1000×0.02)=$1.20. CPC: 0.04×$30=$1.200.04\times\$30=\$1.200.04×$30=$1.20 per click, ranked at 1000×0.02×$1.20=$241000\times0.02\times\$1.20=\$241000×0.02×$1.20=$24. CPA: $30 per purchase, ranked at 1000×0.02×0.04×$30=$241000\times0.02\times0.04\times\$30=\$241000×0.02×0.04×$30=$24.
    2. (b) True CTR 0.01: per 1,000 impressions, 1000×0.01=101000\times0.01=101000×0.01=10 clicks and 10×0.04=0.410\times0.04=0.410×0.04=0.4 purchases. Bills: oCPM $24; oCPC and CPC 10×$1.20=$1210\times\$1.20=\$1210×$1.20=$12; CPA 0.4×$30=$120.4\times\$30=\$120.4×$30=$12. Cost per purchase: oCPM $24/0.4=$60\$24/0.4=\$60$24/0.4=$60; oCPC, CPC and CPA $12/0.4=$30\$12/0.4=\$30$12/0.4=$30.
    3. (c) True CVR 0.02: 1000×0.02=201000\times0.02=201000×0.02=20 clicks and 20×0.02=0.420\times0.02=0.420×0.02=0.4 purchases. Bills: oCPM $24; oCPC and CPC 20×$1.20=$2420\times\$1.20=\$2420×$1.20=$24; CPA 0.4×$30=$120.4\times\$30=\$120.4×$30=$12. Cost per purchase: oCPM, oCPC and CPC $60; CPA $30.

    Result: A lower CTR raises the studio’s cost per purchase to $60 under oCPM. Under oCPC, CPC and CPA it stays at $30, while the platform collects $12 less per 1,000 impressions at the same media cost. A lower CVR raises the studio’s cost per purchase to $60 under oCPM, oCPC and CPC. Under CPA the studio still pays $30 per purchase and the platform collects $12 less. In this example oCPC and oCPM use the same ranking score. The billing event determines how fewer clicks affect the invoice (chapter 3).

    When the platform absorbs the forecast error, it collects $12 per 1,000 impressions instead of the $24 it forecast. Under CPC a lower CTR cuts both the advertiser’s bill and its expected purchase count proportionally. A lower purchase rate per click leaves the CPC bill unchanged and increases the advertiser’s cost per purchase.

    (d) The studio still bears campaign performance risk under every payment model: whether purchases turn into D7 revenue, and the gap between attributed and incremental purchases (chapter 1).

    (e) The DSP converts; the exchange only ranks prices. A full-marks answer contains:

    • The DSP converts the target and forecast into an implied impression value of 1000×0.02×0.04×$30=$241000\times0.02\times0.04\times\$30=\$241000×0.02×0.04×$30=$24 CPM before any fees or bid shading. For illustration, applying a 20% haircut to the estimated value and then halving the result under Chapter 4’s uniform first-price model gives $24×0.8/2=$9.60\$24\times0.8/2=\$9.60$24×0.8/2=$9.60 CPM. The exercise does not specify either adjustment.
    • The exchange compares that CPM with other CPM bids and the floor. In this setup it receives a CPM bid and bills the DSP for impressions. The DSP’s forecasts are inputs to the DSP’s bid.
    • The CTR error lands on whoever the studio's contract with the DSP bills per impression: the studio if it pays a fixed amount per impression or reimburses media costs, the DSP if it pays for media and charges the studio a fixed amount per click or install.

    Scoring: (a) 2 points (four definitions and payment mode); (b) 3 points; (c) 2 points; (d) 1 point; (e) 2 points.

    Question 3: Incremental and marginal profit. An eligible population is randomly split into a treatment group (the campaign may deliver) and a holdout control group (it may not), 100,000 users each (chapter 6). Over the same matured window, treatment has 1,350 purchases and control 1,000. The attribution system credits 700 of the treatment purchases to the ad. Ad spend is $5,000. Net revenue per purchase is $50 (after refunds, before goods, fulfillment and other costs), and the pre-advertising contribution rate is 40% of net revenue. Assume correct randomization and event definitions, no interference between the groups, and that each user buys at most once, independently. Use a normal approximation to compute the confidence interval. For the spend comparison, assume both tests target the same population under comparable conditions, and use their lift estimates as point estimates. Compute attributed ROAS (attributed revenue ÷ ad spend), incremental ROAS (iROAS: incremental revenue ÷ ad spend), incremental contribution profit (incremental contribution − ad spend) and a 95% interval for that profit. Is the campaign profitable? Next, the team proposes doubling spend to $10,000 because an iROAS of 3.5 is well above break-even; a second holdout test of the same design at $10,000 measures 520 incremental purchases. Compute iROAS at $10,000, the marginal iROAS of the extra $5,000 and the change in profit, decide, and give two reasons the extra dollars return less (chapter 3). Finally, explain why you cannot just compare the treatment users who actually saw the ad with the control group.
    Reference answers and scoring points
    Worked solution

    Attributed versus incremental returns

    Given: 100,000 users per group; purchases 1,350 (treatment) and 1,000 (control); 700 attributed purchases; ad spend $5,000; net revenue $50 per purchase; contribution rate 40%.

    1. Incremental purchases (equal groups, so compare counts directly): 1,350−1,000=3501{,}350-1{,}000=3501,350−1,000=350.
    2. Attributed ROAS: 700×$50$5,000=$35,000$5,000=7.0\frac{700\times\$50}{\$5{,}000}=\frac{\$35{,}000}{\$5{,}000}=7.0$5,000700×$50​=$5,000$35,000​=7.0
    3. iROAS: 350×$50$5,000=$17,500$5,000=3.5\frac{350\times\$50}{\$5{,}000}=\frac{\$17{,}500}{\$5{,}000}=3.5$5,000350×$50​=$5,000$17,500​=3.5
    4. Incremental contribution profit: contribution per purchase $50×0.4=$20\$50\times0.4=\$20$50×0.4=$20, so 350×$20−$5,000=$7,000−$5,000=+$2,000.\begin{aligned}&350\times\$20-\$5{,}000\\ &=\$7{,}000-\$5{,}000\\ &=+\$2{,}000.\end{aligned}​350×$20−$5,000=$7,000−$5,000=+$2,000.​
    5. Break-even: iROAS 1/0.4=2.51/0.4=2.51/0.4=2.5, i.e. $5,000/$20=250\$5{,}000/\$20=250$5,000/$20=250 incremental purchases.
    6. Standard error of the lift: each group's count is binomial with variance np(1−p)np(1-p)np(1−p), and independent variances add. SE2=1350(1−0.0135)+1000(1−0.010)=1331.775+990=2321.775,SE=2321.775≈48.18.\begin{aligned}\text{SE}^2&=1350(1-0.0135)\\ &\quad+1000(1-0.010)\\ &=1331.775+990=2321.775,\\ \text{SE}&=\sqrt{2321.775}\approx 48.18.\end{aligned}SE2SE​=1350(1−0.0135)+1000(1−0.010)=1331.775+990=2321.775,=2321.775​≈48.18.​
    7. 95% interval for the lift: 350±1.96×48.18=350±94.4350\pm1.96\times48.18=350\pm94.4350±1.96×48.18=350±94.4, i.e. [255.6, 444.4][255.6,\ 444.4][255.6, 444.4] purchases. Profit is $20×lift−$5,000\$20\times\text{lift}-\$5{,}000$20×lift−$5,000, giving an approximate 95% confidence interval of [+$111, +$3,889][+\$111,\ +\$3{,}889][+$111, +$3,889].

    Result: attributed ROAS 7.0, iROAS 3.5, incremental contribution profit +$2,000, 95% interval about +$111 to +$3,889. The lower end of the lift interval, 255.6, clears the break-even 250, so the interval narrowly excludes zero profit under the stated assumptions.

    Check: attributed ROAS ÷ iROAS = 7.0/3.5 = 2 = 700/350 ✓: the attributed count is twice the estimated incremental count. Under the assumption that the ad never suppresses a purchase, the point estimate implies at least 350 attributed purchases would have happened anyway. The experiment estimates a group total. Profit also equals $5,000×(0.4×3.5−1)=$2,000\$5{,}000\times(0.4\times3.5-1)=\$2{,}000$5,000×(0.4×3.5−1)=$2,000 ✓.

    Worked solution

    The average still clears break-even; the increment does not

    Given: 350 incremental purchases at $5,000 and 520 at $10,000; $50 net revenue and $20 contribution per purchase; break-even iROAS 2.5. Use the two lift estimates for this point-estimate comparison.

    1. iROAS at $10,000: 520×$50$10,000=2.6,\frac{520\times\$50}{\$10{,}000}=2.6,$10,000520×$50​=2.6, still above 2.5; profit 520×$20−$10,000=+$400520\times\$20-\$10{,}000=+\$400520×$20−$10,000=+$400.
    2. The increment: 520−350=170520-350=170520−350=170 extra purchases for an extra $5,000, so marginal iROAS is 170×$50$5,000=1.7<2.5.\frac{170\times\$50}{\$5{,}000}=1.7<2.5.$5,000170×$50​=1.7<2.5.
    3. Change in profit: 170×$20−$5,000=−$1,600170\times\$20-\$5{,}000=-\$1{,}600170×$20−$5,000=−$1,600, which matches $400−$2,000\$400-\$2{,}000$400−$2,000.

    Result: At the point estimates, doubling reduces profit from $2,000 to $400. The extra $5,000 has an estimated iROAS of 1.7, below break-even.

    Check: the average 2.6 is a spend-weighted mix of 3.5 on the first $5,000 and 1.7 on the second, (3.5+1.7)/2=2.6(3.5+1.7)/2=2.6(3.5+1.7)/2=2.6 ✓. Reasons the extra dollars return less (any two): higher first-price bids can raise the cost of impressions the campaign would already have won, the extra impressions reach users with lower incremental purchase probability, the same users see the ad more often, and more of the people reached would have bought anyway. In practice the 170 is the difference of two noisy lifts, so for independent tests its standard error is the square root of the sum of their variances (about 1.4 times either standard error when they are similar); the second test’s lift alone does not determine its variance. To calculate a confidence interval for the change, we would need the second test’s purchase counts by arm and, if the tests overlap, the covariance between the two lift estimates.

    Why not compare exposed treatment users with control. Full-marks points (chapter 6):

    • Exposure is decided after randomization, by targeting, auction wins and how active each user is, all of which correlate with the propensity to buy.
    • Exposed treatment users and the whole control group are therefore not comparable: the comparison can be biased in either direction.
    • Analyze the ITT (intent to treat: the effect by original random assignment) first.
    • For the effect per exposed user, divide the ITT by the treatment group's exposure rate (the Wald ratio under one-sided exposure, random assignment, a nonzero exposure rate, and the assumption that assignment affects outcomes only through exposure), or use a ghost-ad design that identifies comparable would-be exposures in the control group.

    Scoring: first-test numbers and interval 4 points; doubling decision with marginal iROAS and two reasons 3 points; exposed-versus-control caveats 3 points.

    Question 4: Evidence for a moat. MAX is AppLovin's mediation product, which runs publishers' auctions across demand sources; Adjust is an MMP (mobile measurement partner) that AppLovin describes in its 2025 10-K as operated by a wholly owned subsidiary, which attributes conversions on behalf of advertisers; Axon is its prediction and bidding engine (AppLovin and Axon). Someone claims: “MAX sees all bids and Adjust has all the attribution data, so Axon necessarily trains on all of it, and a competitor that can replicate the technology only needs to subsidize data purchases to catch up.” Identify at least four missing links in this argument, and propose one validation metric better than total conversion volume.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Missing links (any four, each stated as the specific step that fails):

    1. Seeing is not permission. MAX receives bids to run auctions; contracts and privacy rules govern any other use. MAX also sees only the auctions it mediates, not all bids.
    2. Permission is not use. Data allowed for training does not necessarily enter the training pipeline. AppLovin's Axon page states that the models do not ingest other bidders' bid information; that is the company's claim, not independently verified (chapter 8).
    3. Processing is not ownership. Adjust processes attribution data on advertisers' behalf; AppLovin’s 2025 10-K says Adjust's data is not shared with AppLovin or used to optimize its recommendation engine unless a customer directs it.
    4. More data is not unbiased or transferable data. Samples collected under one delivery policy and supply mix are selection-biased for other policies.
    5. Same model, different access. Replicating the technology does not replicate supply access and execution conditions.
    6. Prediction is not incrementality. Predicting short-term responses well is not delivering incremental profit to advertisers.
    7. Subsidies prove nothing about retention. They cannot show that advertisers stay once full pricing starts; and access to equivalent data may be limited by contracts or privacy rules.

    Better metrics (any one, with why it beats volume): advertiser retention and spend after subsidies end; matured incremental contribution from holdout tests under the same budget constraint; or the marginal-return curve of additional budget. Each measures value delivered to the advertiser rather than activity. Scoring: four gaps 8 points; a suitable metric 2 points.

    Depth set: six questions, 60 points, about 90 minutes

    These six questions test the derivations behind the gist and need chapters 4–7 read in full. Questions 7 and 9 use the shared parameters at the start of the gist set.

    Question 5: Advertiser bidding under a budget.     Question 6: The winner's curse. Two ads compete for one slot. Both have the same true conversion probability, q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 per impression, and both advertisers bid $30 per conversion on an oCPM product: the platform uses a noisy score as a proxy for conversion probability and bids that score × $30 per impression, and the winner pays that bid (first price). Each ad’s score is q(1+0.2 ε)q(1+0.2\,\varepsilon)q(1+0.2ε), with an independent standard normal ε\varepsilonε per ad. The Gaussian model is an approximation. Use the unbounded scores as written in the algebra. A real auction would reject negative bids. The higher score wins (chapter 5). (a) Is each score unbiased for its ad’s true conversion probability? (b) Compute the winning ad's expected prediction relative to qqq. Hint: max⁡(x,y)=x+y2+∣x−y∣2\max(x,y)=\tfrac{x+y}{2}+\tfrac{|x-y|}{2}max(x,y)=2x+y​+2∣x−y∣​. (c) What does the winning advertiser pay per conversion on average? (d) Why can an aggregate check on randomized traffic miss this effect, and how would you detect and reduce it? (e) Without calculating, what changes with ten competing ads?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    (a) Yes. Each prediction has mean qqq, so the average prediction equals the average outcome across all scored ads. This is calibration in the mean. At any fixed score, the true conversion probability remains qqq. The bias comes from which prediction gets acted on: the auction selects the larger one.

For X∼N(0,σ2)X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)X∼N(0,σ2), by symmetry and the substitution u=x2/(2σ2)u=x^2/(2\sigma^2)u=x2/(2σ2): E∣X∣=2∫0∞x e−x2/(2σ2)σ2π dx=2σ2π∫0∞e−u du=σ2/π.\begin{aligned}\mathbb E|X|&=2\int_0^\infty x\,\frac{e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dx\\ &=\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}.\end{aligned}E∣X∣​=2∫0∞​xσ2π​e−x2/(2σ2)​dx=2π​2σ​∫0∞​e−udu=σ2/π​.​ With σ=2\sigma=\sqrt2σ=2​, E∣ε1−ε2∣=2/π\mathbb E|\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2|=2/\sqrt\piE∣ε1​−ε2​∣=2/π​.
    3. So E[M]=12⋅2π=1/π≈0.5642\mathbb E[M]=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt\pi}=1/\sqrt\pi\approx0.5642E[M]=21​⋅π​2​=1/π​≈0.5642, and the winner's expected prediction is q (1+0.2×0.5642)=1.1128 q.q\,(1+0.2\times0.5642)=1.1128\,q.q(1+0.2×0.5642)=1.1128q.
    4. (c) Payment: the winner pays $30 × its prediction per impression, on average $30×1.1128×0.0005=$0.016693\$30\times1.1128\times0.0005=\$0.016693$30×1.1128×0.0005=$0.016693 ($16.69 CPM), against a true value of $30×0.0005=$0.015\$30\times0.0005=\$0.015$30×0.0005=$0.015. Its true conversion probability is still qqq (both ads are equally good), so its cost per conversion is 0.016693/0.0005=$33.390.016693/0.0005=\$33.390.016693/0.0005=$33.39.

    Result: the winning prediction averages 11.3% above the truth, and the advertiser pays about $33.39 per conversion against its $30 target.

    Check: numerical integration of ∫m⋅2φ(m)Φ(m) dm\int m\cdot2\varphi(m)\Phi(m)\,dm∫m⋅2φ(m)Φ(m)dm (the density of the larger of two standard normals is 2φΦ2\varphi\Phi2φΦ) gives 0.5642, matching 1/π1/\sqrt\pi1/π​; and $33.3851/$30≈1.1128\$33.3851/\$30\approx1.1128$33.3851/$30≈1.1128, the same 11.3%.

    (d) On randomized traffic, positive and negative errors cancel in the aggregate. Calibration by score can still detect the error in this toy model, since the true rate is constant. Compare predictions with matured outcomes on impressions won by the current model to measure the selection effect. To reduce it, shrink noisy scores toward a well-estimated baseline and evaluate the resulting bids.

    (e) The bias grows with the number of competitors: the expected maximum of ten standard normals is about 1.5388, so the winner is overpredicted by about 31% (chapter 5). Under oCPM the advertiser absorbs the overrun; under fixed CPA billing the platform bears the conversion shortfall relative to media cost. A cost guarantee shifts risk according to its terms (chapter 3).

    Scoring: (a) 1 point; (b) 4 points; (c) 2 points; (d) 2 points; (e) 1 point.

    Question 7: Calibration and sampling. A conversion model is trained on downsampled data: every positive example is kept, and each negative is kept independently with probability 10%, regardless of its features (Prediction and the data it learns from). Training applies no weight correction, and the model gives the sampled-data conversion probability conditional on the features. For one feature vector it outputs 0.5. What is the conversion probability before sampling for that same feature vector? Separately: a new model has a higher AUC than the current one, but its predicted probabilities are about twice the observed conversion rates across the board. Can it go live as is?
    Reference answers and scoring points
    Worked solution

    Undoing negative downsampling

    Given: negative retention rate s=0.1s=0.1s=0.1, positives all kept, sampled-data prediction ps=0.5p_s=0.5ps​=0.5 (calibrated on the sampled data). Want: true probability ppp for the same feature vector.

    1. For a fixed feature vector, sampling keeps a fraction 1 of positives and sss of negatives, so it multiplies the odds by 1/s1/s1/s: ps1−ps=p(1−p) s.\frac{p_s}{1-p_s}=\frac{p}{(1-p)\,s}.1−ps​ps​​=(1−p)sp​.
    2. True odds: s⋅ps1−ps=0.1×0.50.5=0.1s\cdot\frac{p_s}{1-p_s}=0.1\times\frac{0.5}{0.5}=0.1s⋅1−ps​ps​​=0.1×0.50.5​=0.1.
    3. Back to a probability: p=0.11+0.1=111≈0.0909.p=\frac{0.1}{1+0.1}=\frac{1}{11}\approx 0.0909.p=1+0.10.1​=111​≈0.0909.

    Result: p = 1/11 ≈ 0.0909 (9.09%).

    Check: the closed form p=s ps1−ps+s ps=0.050.5+0.05=0.0909p=\frac{s\,p_s}{1-p_s+s\,p_s}=\frac{0.05}{0.5+0.05}=0.0909p=1−ps​+sps​sps​​=0.5+0.050.05​=0.0909 ✓; at s=1s=1s=1 it returns p=psp=p_sp=ps​, as it must. Using the raw 0.5 would overstate value 5.5-fold here, and about 1/s1/s1/s-fold when ppp is small.

    Recalibrate the higher-AUC model before using its probabilities directly to price bids. A full-marks answer contains:

    • ROC AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) measures ranking. It depends only on ranking and is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of the scores.
    • Bids use absolute probabilities. The network's expected receipts per impression are v=30qv=30qv=30q, so doubling qqq doubles the value the bidder thinks it buys. In the shared example without a budget, the first-price bid rises from v/2v/2v/2 = $7.50 CPM to (2v)/2=$0.015(2v)/2=\$0.015(2v)/2=$0.015 per impression = $15 CPM, where the true spread (0.015−b) b/L(0.015-b)\,b/L(0.015−b)b/L is zero: the whole $2,812.50 of spread per million requests (chapter 4's appendix) is lost.
    • Launch checklist. Confirm the sampling correction was applied exactly once; recalibrate on matured labels; check calibration by segment (a uniform factor of 2 rarely holds everywhere); evaluate monetary loss, not ranking metrics; then run a limited online experiment.

    Second-order point: under a binding budget a pacing multiplier would absorb a perfectly uniform factor for one campaign (the appendix's $6.3246 CPM network bid is set by its binding $2,000 media budget, not by vvv), but across campaigns and segments with different errors it misallocates spend. Scoring: number 4 points; calibration and launch logic 6 points.

    Question 8: Price feedback. In a first-price auction you bid $8 CPM, win, and pay $8 CPM. Can you use $8 as a supervised label for that auction's competitive threshold ZZZ (Learning competing prices from censored auction feedback)? In a second-price auction with no additional floor or fees, suppose you hold the bid fixed and the winner pays ZZZ, what bias results if you fit a model of ZZZ only on the prices you paid in auctions you won, and how do you fix it?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    First price: no. You pay your own bid, so the price carries no information about ZZZ beyond the win itself. Full-marks points:

    • A win says only Z≤8Z\le 8Z≤8 (CPM): a censored observation bounding ZZZ from above, not a label. A loss says only Z>bZ>bZ>b.
    • Win/loss records are still informative: their likelihood pins down the win probability at the bids actually placed, so learning the whole curve needs varied bids (or a parametric form).
    • You learn more only if the exchange returns an extra signal, such as the minimum bid that would have won.

    Second price: downward bias. Full-marks points:

    • A win reveals ZZZ exactly, but only when Z≤bZ\le bZ≤b; training on wins alone drops every auction with Z>bZ>bZ>b, truncating the sample from above.
    • The fitted ZZZ is biased low: the empirical win-price distribution gives the conditional CDF given a win. It overstates the win probability wherever the unconditional CDF is positive and below one, provided some auctions are lost. With varying bids, condition on features that make bids and thresholds independent before treating losses as ordinary censoring.
    • Fix: keep losses as censored observations at bbb and maximize the censored likelihood, in which each win contributes the density f(Z)f(Z)f(Z) and each loss 1−F(b)1-F(b)1−F(b).
    Illustration

    Wins-only versus censored estimate

    Given (for illustration, not stated in the question): Z∼Uniform(0,$20 CPM)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,\$20\ \text{CPM})Z∼Uniform(0,$20 CPM), the shared example's LLL, and you always bid $8 CPM in a second-price auction.

    1. Win rate: F(8)=8/20=40%F(8)=8/20=40\%F(8)=8/20=40%. The other 60% of auctions produce no price.
    2. Prices seen on wins: Z∣Z≤8∼Uniform(0,8)Z\mid Z\le 8\sim\text{Uniform}(0,8)Z∣Z≤8∼Uniform(0,8), mean $4 CPM. A model fitted to them puts all its mass below $8 and predicts a 100% win rate at an $8 bid; the truth is 40%.
    3. Censored estimate: for a uniform threshold the censored likelihood is maximized at L^=b/win rate=$8/0.40=$20\hat L=b/\text{win rate}=\$8/0.40=\$20L^=b/win rate=$8/0.40=$20 CPM, so the estimated mean is L^/2=$10\hat L/2=\$10L^/2=$10 CPM. Here 40% is the population win rate. A finite sample yields an estimate that can differ from $10.

    Result: At the population rates, wins alone average $4 CPM. Using wins and losses recovers the model’s $10 CPM mean.

    Check: for this uniform model and a bid below the upper endpoint, the wins-only mean is b/2b/2b/2, which reaches the true L/2L/2L/2 only at b=Lb=Lb=L, when you win everything and nothing is censored ✓. The censored estimate uses only the win and loss counts, as chapter 5 derives.

    Scoring: 5 points per part.

    Question 9: Offline versus online. A new conversion model beats the current one on offline log loss, but in an online A/B test the network's advertiser payments less media cost (collections minus media cost; chapter 4's appendix) falls. Give four distinct diagnostic hypotheses, and for two of them name the logs or metrics that would confirm or rule them out.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Any four distinct mechanisms from this list, each explaining how it could reduce collections minus media cost:

    HypothesisMechanismEvidence
    Miscalibration where it mattersAverage log loss improves while calibration on high-bid traffic worsens. The auction buys where the model overestimates (the winner's curse), so overbidding concentrates on won traffic.Predicted vs matured realized conversion rate on won impressions, by arm, publisher and predicted-score bucket.
    Traffic or price mix shiftOffline data were selected by the old model's wins; the new model bids differently and wins traffic and prices the evaluation set never covered.Per-arm bids, win rate, clearing price, traffic composition, cost and collections per impression.
    Label problemsLabel delay (immature conversions offline) or leakage (features carrying post-impression information) inflates the offline score (chapter 5).Re-score offline on fully matured labels; feature timestamps vs impression time.
    Training–serving skewFeature or model versions differ online, features are missing, or higher latency causes timeouts.Logged online features vs offline recomputation; missing-feature and timeout rates by arm.
    Downstream interactionsBid shading, pacing or budget control tuned to the old score distribution; pacing oscillation.Pacing multiplier and spend-rate traces by arm; bid-shading factor distributions.
    Measurement differencesFees, attribution definitions or label windows differ between arms, or the arms share budgets and interfere (chapter 6).Arm configuration diff; A/A comparison; shared-budget audit.

    A full-marks answer gives four mechanisms that are actually distinct (not four flavors of “the model is worse”) and, for two of them, evidence that would localize the problem rather than merely restate it. Scoring: four mechanisms 6 points in total; two pieces of evidence 4 points in total.

    Question 10: Ledger states. A bid is placed under display-based billing, where only a confirmed display incurs a charge (Real-time advertising systems): the publisher is paid only after a successful impression, and the contract names the OpenRTB billing notice burl as the signal that confirms billing. Before the bid was sent, the budget system reserved the bid's maximum possible cost. After the bid, a win notice (nurl) arrives but no billing notice; then a duplicate of the same win notice arrives. Can the system book this as confirmed media spend? Can it release the whole reservation? How should it handle the billing notice when it later arrives twice?
    Reference answers and scoring points
    • Confirm spend? No. Under this contract a win creates no payment obligation; only a successful impression does, and burl is what confirms it. The duplicate nurl is suppressed by the deduplication key (exchange, request, impression and bid IDs, plus the event type) and changes nothing.
    • Release the whole reservation? No. The impression may still render and burl may arrive late, so the external obligation is still open. Releasing the reservation would let the same budget be spent twice. Release it only on authoritative evidence that the obligation is gone: a confirmed loss or cancellation, a reconciliation result, or a binding contractual cutoff. A local timeout is not such evidence.
    • Billing notice twice. The first valid burl finds the bid open and, in one atomic step, moves the actual billed amount from reserved to confirmed spend, releases the difference between the reservation cap and that amount, and closes the bid. An exact duplicate finds the bid closed and is a no-op, logged for reconciliation. The closed state, checked and changed in the same step as the posting, is what guarantees the money moves at most once; the deduplication key alone only suppresses repeats of the same event (chapter 7). Missing notices and notices that conflict with the recorded state or amount go to reconciliation and are settled against the exchange's settlement reports. An amount above the cap means the cost-cap premise has broken: send it to exception handling.

    The ledger, with cap ccc (the reservation) and actual billed amount 0≤p≤c0\le p\le c0≤p≤c, starting from confirmed spend CCC and open reservations RRR:

    EventLedger actionConfirmed spendReserved
    Bid admittedReserve cap cccCCCR+cR+cR+c
    nurlMark “won, not billed”; no money movesCCCR+cR+cR+c
    nurl againDeduplicate on business key: no-opCCCR+cR+cR+c
    burlBid open: book ppp, release c−pc-pc−p, close the bid (one atomic step)C+pC+pC+pRRR
    burl againBid closed: no-op; log for reconciliationC+pC+pC+pRRR
    Instead: authoritative “not billable”Bid open: release ccc, close the bidCCCRRR

    Only admission raises confirmed + reserved, and admission checks it against the budget; every later step keeps it flat or lowers it. That is what makes the hard budget safe. Scoring: distinguishing the states 4 points; managing the open obligation 3 points; idempotency and reconciliation 3 points.

    Sources, errata, and glossary

    In this chapter

    • Erratum. The RTB monograph's budget-constrained second-price bid counts the win rate twice. The correct coefficient is 6LB/N\sqrt{6LB/N}6LB/N​; the published one overspends the budget by at least 18% wherever the correct one applies (43.6% in the running example).
    • Where to read next. A staged list: one textbook and one newsletter for the broad map, then the papers behind each chapter's mechanism.
    • Glossary. The reader's canonical definitions of ad-tech terms, alphabetical, each linked to where the reader defines or uses it.
    • Review record. What was checked in each editorial pass, and what was not.

    The gist. This chapter is for lookup, not for reading straight through. The erratum warns about one wrong formula in the most-cited free reference on real-time bidding. The reading list says what to read first for the broad picture and which paper to open for each mechanism the reader uses. The glossary defines every ad term in one place and links to the chapter that explains it. The review record says what was checked and what was taken on trust.

    An erratum in the RTB monograph's second-price example

    The RTB monograph's budget-constrained second-price bid (its Section 5.3.4) counts the win probability twice, so the published bid coefficient is too high and overspends the budget. Expected cost per bid request already includes zero on losses; multiplying it by the win probability again undercounts spend. For example, a 30% win rate and a $3 average payment per win imply $0.90 per request; a second multiplication gives $0.27. The correct coefficient is 6LB/N\sqrt{6LB/N}6LB/N​, valid for B/N≤L/6B/N\le L/6B/N≤L/6. The published one overspends by at least 18% wherever the correct one applies, and by 43.6% at the running example's numbers. The rest of the monograph is a sound reference; the proof below is for readers checking the book.

    Optional: proof and numerical impact of the monograph erratum

    The monograph is “Display Advertising with Real-Time Bidding (RTB) and Behavioural Targeting” by Jun Wang, Weinan Zhang and Shuai Yuan (arXiv:1610.03013v2, 122 pages; arXiv date July 15, 2017, title page July 18). Equation and page numbers below refer to v2 and were checked against the PDF. arXiv metadata

    Symbols

    Notation follows Auctions and bidding. The monograph's symbol, where different, is in brackets.

    • ZZZ: the competitive threshold, the highest competing bid on one bid request. We win if our bid is at least ZZZ [market price zzz].

    • b≥0b\ge 0b≥0: our bid on one request. ZZZ, LLL and bbb are dollars per impression (×1,000 for CPM).

    • b(r)b(r)b(r): the bidding function, mapping pCTR to a bid.
    • NNN: bid requests over the campaign's life [TTT]. BBB: total media budget in dollars. B/NB/NB/N is the budget per request.

The monograph's cost function cˉ(b)\bar c(b)cˉ(b) (Eq. 5.5) is the expected payment given a win, cˉ(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b]\bar c(b)=E[Z\mid Z\le b]cˉ(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b], so C(b)=cˉ(b) F(b)C(b)=\bar c(b)\,F(b)C(b)=cˉ(b)F(b).

    Model and correct solution

    The monograph's special case: an ideal second-price auction (the winner pays ZZZ; no floor, fees or bid increments); every win is one billable impression; r∼Uniform(0,1)r\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)r∼Uniform(0,1), independent of ZZZ; a risk-neutral buyer that maximizes expected clicks subject to expected spend at most BBB. Nothing assumes the bid is linear in rrr; linearity falls out of the first-order condition.

    Pitfall: conditional vs per-request cost

    “Expected cost” has two meanings: given a win, E[Z∣Z≤b]E[Z\mid Z\le b]E[Z∣Z≤b], and per request, E[Z 1{Z≤b}]E[Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z\le b\}]E[Z1{Z≤b}]. They differ by a factor F(b)F(b)F(b). A budget constraint needs the per-request one: the win rate enters exactly once. Units will not catch a second factor of FFF, which is dimensionless; scaling will. Under a uniform threshold, per-request second-price spend must grow as b2b^2b2; a formula that grows as b3b^3b3 has counted the win rate twice.

    Size of the error

    Bidding with cpaperc_{\mathrm{paper}}cpaper​, the true expected spend per request is cpaper2/(6L)c_{\mathrm{paper}}^2/(6L)cpaper2​/(6L) as long as cpaper≤Lc_{\mathrm{paper}}\le Lcpaper​≤L. Divided by the budget per request:

    cpaper2/(6L)B/N=4 (L2B/N)2/36L B/N=23(LNB)1/3.\begin{aligned} \frac{c_{\mathrm{paper}}^2/(6L)}{B/N}&=\frac{4\,(L^2B/N)^{2/3}}{6L\,B/N}\\ &=\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{LN}{B}\right)^{1/3}. \end{aligned}B/Ncpaper2​/(6L)​​=6LB/N4(L2B/N)2/3​=32​(BLN​)1/3.​

    The published coefficient keeps every bid at or below LLL exactly when 8L2B/N≤L38L^2B/N\le L^38L2B/N≤L3, i.e. B/N≤L/8B/N\le L/8B/N≤L/8. The factor decreases in B/NB/NB/N, so on that range it is at least 23⋅81/3=43\tfrac23\cdot 8^{1/3}=\tfrac4332​⋅81/3=34​. On L/8<B/N≤L/6L/8<B/N\le L/6L/8<B/N≤L/6 some published bids exceed LLL; true spend is then L/2−L2/(3cpaper)L/2-L^2/(3c_{\mathrm{paper}})L/2−L2/(3cpaper​) per request, and the factor keeps falling to 3−61/3≈1.1833-6^{1/3}\approx1.1833−61/3≈1.183 at B/N=L/6B/N=L/6B/N=L/6. Wherever the correct closed form applies, the published one overspends by at least 18%, and by more as the budget tightens. This is not a boundary effect.

A request with pCTR rrr gets a bid of r×$15.49r\times\$15.49r×$15.49 CPM.

Published coefficient: cpaper=2(L2B/N)1/3=2 (0.0004×0.002)1/3=2×(8×10−7)1/3=2×0.0092832=$0.018566\begin{aligned} c_{\mathrm{paper}}&=2(L^2B/N)^{1/3}\\ &=2\,(0.0004\times0.002)^{1/3}\\ &=2\times(8\times10^{-7})^{1/3}\\ &=2\times0.0092832=\$0.018566 \end{aligned}cpaper​​=2(L2B/N)1/3=2(0.0004×0.002)1/3=2×(8×10−7)1/3=2×0.0092832=$0.018566​ per click: a bid of r×$18.57r\times\$18.57r×$18.57 CPM, 19.8% higher.
    4. True expected spend at the published coefficient: N cpaper26L=106×4×(8×10−7)2/30.12=106×3.44710×10−40.12=$2,872.58.\begin{aligned} N\,\frac{c_{\mathrm{paper}}^2}{6L}&=10^6\times\frac{4\times(8\times10^{-7})^{2/3}}{0.12}\\ &=10^6\times\frac{3.44710\times10^{-4}}{0.12}\\ &=\$2{,}872.58. \end{aligned}N6Lcpaper2​​​=106×0.124×(8×10−7)2/3​=106×0.123.44710×10−4​=$2,872.58.​
    5. Clicks. Expected clicks are Nc/(3L)Nc/(3L)Nc/(3L): 258,199 at c∗c^*c∗ and 309,439 at cpaperc_{\mathrm{paper}}cpaper​. The extra 51,240 clicks cost $872.58, or $0.0170 each, above the optimum's marginal cost of 1/λ∗=$0.01551/\lambda^*=\$0.01551/λ∗=$0.0155 per click.
    6. In a fluid approximation with $2,000 available and expected spend accruing at a constant rate, the published bidder runs out after 2000/2872.58=69.6%2000/2872.58=69.6\%2000/2872.58=69.6% of the flight, so the approximation gives 69.6% of 309,439 clicks, or 2B/cpaper=215,4432B/c_{\mathrm{paper}}=215{,}4432B/cpaper​=215,443, against the optimum's 2B/c∗=258,1992B/c^*=258{,}1992B/c∗=258,199: 16.6% fewer clicks for the same money.

    Result: the published coefficient spends $2,872.58 in expectation against a $2,000 budget (1.436×); the fluid approximation gives 16.6% fewer clicks at the same spend. Actual hard-cap delivery also depends on the order and size of realized payments.

    Check: the overspend formula gives 23(LN/B)1/3=23×101/3=23×2.15443=1.436290\tfrac23(LN/B)^{1/3}=\tfrac23\times10^{1/3}=\tfrac23\times2.15443=1.43629032​(LN/B)1/3=32​×101/3=32​×2.15443=1.436290, and 1.436290×$2,000=$2,872.581.436290\times\$2{,}000=\$2{,}872.581.436290×$2,000=$2,872.58, matching step 4. The click shortfall is 1−c∗/cpaper=1−0.015492/0.018566=16.6%1-c^*/c_{\mathrm{paper}}=1-0.015492/0.018566=16.6\%1−c∗/cpaper​=1−0.015492/0.018566=16.6%. Unitless case L=1L=1L=1, B/N=0.01B/N=0.01B/N=0.01 (below L/8L/8L/8): coefficients 0.244949 and 0.430887, overspend factor 23×1001/3=3.094\tfrac23\times100^{1/3}=3.09432​×1001/3=3.094.

    The main text derives its budget results independently and does not reuse this example.

    Where to read next

    Read in two stages: first a textbook and a newsletter for the map of the field, then, chapter by chapter, the paper behind each mechanism this reader uses. In every paper, write down the explicit assumptions first; they matter more than the model names. Bibliographic details below were checked against publisher, DBLP, RePEc or arXiv records in November 2026.
