    Glossary

    This is the reader's canonical glossary, in alphabetical order. Definitions give the sense used in this reader; individual contracts and platforms may define a term differently, and the contract wins. A link after a definition goes to where the reader defines or uses the term.

    Term Definition
    A/B testA randomized experiment that assigns users (or requests) to treatment or control so that the difference in outcomes estimates a causal effect. Ch. 6
    Ad exchangeThe marketplace that runs the auction between buyers' DSPs and sellers' SSPs and sets the clearing price; today an exchange and an SSP are usually one product. Ch. 2
    Ad groupThe level below a campaign that carries finer targeting, bids or creative combinations; the hierarchy differs across platforms.
    Ad loadHow many ads are shown per session or per unit of content; raising it trades user retention for short-term revenue.
    Ad networkAn intermediary that aggregates publishers' inventory and sells it to advertisers, often buying in one pricing unit (e.g. CPM) and selling in another (e.g. CPA) and keeping the spread. Ch. 1
    Ad spendThe amount charged to the advertiser for advertising. Under the example’s CPA contract it equals the number of billable conversions times the agreed price per conversion.
    Ad opportunityOne chance to show one ad to one user in one slot at one moment; also called an impression opportunity. Ch. 1
    Ad Rank / Quality ScoreGoogle's search-ad ranking score combines the bid with a quality estimate built from expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; the Quality Score is the advertiser-facing summary of that estimate. Ch. 2
    Ad requestAn app's or page's request for an ad to fill one slot; mediation or an SSP may fan one ad request out into many bid requests.
    Ad serverThe system that selects which ad to show for a request, delivers it and logs the result.
    AdAttributionKitApple's privacy-preserving attribution framework (iOS 17.4 and later), successor to SKAdNetwork; it reports conversions in delayed, crowd-anonymized postbacks without user-level identifiers. Ch. 2
    ads.txt / app-ads.txtA file the publisher hosts on its own domain listing the ad systems authorized to sell its inventory (app-ads.txt is the app variant). Ch. 6
    AdvertiserThe buyer: the business that pays for impressions, clicks or actions in order to reach users.
    ATTApp Tracking Transparency: Apple's iOS permission prompt (from iOS 14.5), required before an app tracks a user across other companies' apps and websites or reads the IDFA. Ch. 2
    AttributionRule-based assignment of credit for a conversion to earlier ad interactions (commonly last-touch); it is an accounting rule, not a causal estimate. Ch. 6
    Attributed conversionA conversion assigned to an ad or campaign under the reporting system’s attribution rules.
    Attribution windowThe maximum delay between an ad interaction and a conversion for the conversion to be credited; click-through and view-through windows are set separately. Also called a lookback window. Ch. 6
    AxonAppLovin's ad prediction and bidding engine. Ch. 8
    BidThe price a buyer offers for one opportunity; most interfaces quote it in CPM.
    Bid requestThe message, usually in OpenRTB format, by which a seller invites buyers to bid on one ad opportunity before a response deadline.
    Bid shadingBidding below one's value in a first-price auction, trading win probability for a lower payment; at an interior optimum b=w−F(b)/f(b)b=w-F(b)/f(b)b=w−F(b)/f(b). Ch. 4
    Billable eventThe event that triggers payment under a given contract: a win, a rendered impression, a click, an install or a qualifying action. Ch. 3
    Billed, credited and caused valueThe running campaign's three values per impression: billed qa=$0.015qa=\$0.015qa=$0.015 (the advertiser's expected bill), credited qg=$0.020qg=\$0.020qg=$0.020 (contribution the attribution report assigns to the ad) and caused w=Δq g=$0.008w=\Delta q\,g=\$0.008w=Δqg=$0.008 (contribution the ad actually adds). Ch. 1
    Budget multiplier (μ_A)Under a binding budget the advertiser bids as if each impression were worth w/(1+μA)w/(1+\mu_A)w/(1+μA​); μA=0\mu_A=0μA​=0 when the budget is slack. It equals the contribution after spend gained per extra budget dollar (about 0.26 at chapter 4's $500 first-price cap). Pacing adjusts it from observed spend. Ch. 4
    burlOpenRTB billing notice URL: the exchange calls it when the impression becomes billable under the exchange's policy. Ch. 7
    CalibrationThe property that predicted probabilities match observed frequencies (among requests with pCTR 2%, about 2% are clicked); bidding needs it because bids multiply value by probability. Ch. 5
    CampaignAn advertiser's unit of budget, objective, schedule and targeting.
    Censoring (winning prices)Partial observation of the competitive threshold: on a win in a second-price auction it is observed (in first price, a win shows only that it was at most our bid); on a loss we know only that it exceeded our bid. Regression on wins alone is therefore biased. Ch. 5
    Clearing priceThe price the auction winner actually pays.
    Competitive thresholdThe highest competing bid for an opportunity (or the floor, if higher): the bid needed to win, written ZZZ. The RTB monograph calls it the market price. Ch. 4
    ContributionIn this reader, pre-advertising contribution per order: sales revenue minus cost of goods, fulfillment and other variable non-advertising costs. Ch. 1
    ConversionThe advertiser's target action after an ad, such as an install, purchase or registration.
    Cost guaranteeA promise by some platforms offering optimized bidding to compensate the advertiser when realized cost per conversion exceeds the target by more than a stated tolerance. Ch. 3
    CPACost per action: the price paid per agreed conversion; as a metric, spend divided by conversions. Ch. 3
    CPCCost per click: the price paid per click; as a metric, spend divided by clicks. Ch. 3
    CPICost per install: the price paid per attributed app install. Ch. 3
    CPMCost per mille: the price per 1,000 impressions. A $6 CPM bid is $0.006 for one impression; auctions still sell one impression at a time. Ch. 3
    CTR / pCTRClick-through rate: clicks divided by impressions. pCTR is a model's predicted probability that one impression is clicked.
    CTVConnected TV: streaming video watched on a television set; high-attention, high-CPM inventory with few clicks, so linking it to sales needs statistical matching. Ch. 2
    CVR / pCVRConversion rate; the denominator (per click, per impression or per install) must be stated. pCVR is the model's predicted value.
    D7 ROASA cohort's attributed revenue in the first 168 hours after acquisition (for apps, the install), divided by its ad spend; valid only once the window has closed for every user. Ch. 3
    Deal typesDirect deal (negotiated by hand, fixed price and volume); programmatic guaranteed (fixed price, reserved volume, automated execution); private auction (invitation-only; the same thing as a PMP, see that entry); open auction (any qualified buyer). Ch. 2
    Delayed feedbackConversions arriving hours to days after the impression, so recent training examples carry incomplete labels: a negative may still convert. Ch. 5
    Demand sourceAny buyer that can fill an ad request: an ad network, a DSP or a direct campaign.
    DSPDemand-side platform: the buyer's software, which receives bid requests across exchanges, predicts what each impression is worth to its advertisers and bids within their budgets. Ch. 2
    Dual bidTwo prices, one for a frequent shallow event (e.g. install) and one for a rare deep event (e.g. purchase); the platform buys only if both targets look met, capping the variance of a young deep-event model at some cost in volume. Ch. 3
    eCPMEffective CPM: expected revenue or value per 1,000 impressions, whatever the pricing unit. The auction ranks bids made on different events by it, e.g. 1000×pCTR×pCVR×CPA bid1000\times\text{pCTR}\times\text{pCVR}\times\text{CPA bid}1000×pCTR×pCVR×CPA bid. Ch. 2
    Fill rateThe share of ad requests that receive an ad.
    First-price auctionAn auction in which the winner pays its own bid. Ch. 4
    Floor priceThe seller's minimum acceptable price for an opportunity; bids below it lose. Also called a reserve price.
    Ghost adsAn experiment design that logs, for control users, the impressions the campaign would have won, so the effect on users who would actually be exposed can be estimated without placebo ads. Ch. 6
    Gross vs net revenueRevenue recognition: a platform that controls the service before it reaches the customer (a principal under IFRS 15 and ASC 606) books the full advertiser spend as revenue (gross); an agent books only what it keeps (net). Ch. 3
    GSPGeneralized second-price auction for several ranked slots, as in search ads: each winner pays the minimum bid needed to keep its position, i.e. the next-ranked bid (quality-weighted where quality scores apply). Bidding one's value is not a dominant strategy and in general not an equilibrium. Ch. 2
    Guaranteed dealA contract that fixes price and volume in advance and commits the publisher to deliver the qualifying impressions, with a remedy for shortfall; executed by software it is called programmatic guaranteed. Ch. 2
    Hard capA spend limit that must hold on every realized path, not just in expectation; enforced by reserving each bid's maximum possible cost before the bid is sent. Pacing and expected-budget constraints do not guarantee it. Ch. 7
    HoldoutA randomly selected group withheld from a campaign to serve as the control when measuring what the campaign caused. Ch. 6
    IABInteractive Advertising Bureau, the industry body whose Tech Lab publishes OpenRTB, ads.txt and sellers.json.
    IDFAIdentifier for Advertisers: Apple's per-device advertising identifier, readable only after ATT consent. Ch. 2
    ImpressionOne rendered display of an ad. A “successful impression” here means the display event the contract counts actually completed; a won auction can still fail to render.
    Incremental conversionsThe additional conversions caused by a campaign, estimated by comparing outcomes with a baseline, such as a randomized holdout group.
    Incremental impression value (w)Advertiser contribution before advertising cost caused by one successful impression, w=Δq g=$0.008w=\Delta q\,g=\$0.008w=Δqg=$0.008 in the running example: causal purchase-probability lift times contribution per added order. The value the advertiser bids on in chapter 4; distinct from a network's CPA receipts v=qav=qav=qa. Ch. 4
    IncrementalityThe change in an outcome caused by showing ads, measured against a randomized counterfactual; also called lift. Contrast with attribution. Ch. 6
    InterstitialA full-screen ad shown at a natural break, such as between game levels.
    IPSInverse propensity scoring: an off-policy estimator that reweights each logged reward by π(a∣x)/μ(a∣x)\pi(a\mid x)/\mu(a\mid x)π(a∣x)/μ(a∣x), the ratio of the new policy's to the logging policy's action probability. Ch. 5
    iROASIncremental ROAS: revenue caused by the ads (treatment minus control) divided by ad spend; break-even is one over the contribution margin. Ch. 3
    ITTIntent-to-treat effect: the average effect of being assigned to treatment, whether or not the user was actually exposed. Ch. 6
    LTVLifetime value: the value a user generates over a stated horizon. State whether it is revenue or contribution, the horizon, the discounting and whether acquisition cost is already subtracted. Ch. 3
    lurlOpenRTB loss notice URL: the exchange calls it when the bid loses, optionally with a loss-reason code. Ch. 7
    MAXAppLovin's mediation platform for app publishers. Ch. 8
    MediationSoftware in a publisher's app that decides which of several demand sources fills each ad request, by in-app bidding, a waterfall or both. Ch. 2
    MMPMobile measurement partner (e.g. Adjust, AppsFlyer): a third party whose SDK records installs and in-app events and attributes them to ad networks. Ch. 3
    Mobile advertising IDA per-device identifier any app could read for advertising: Apple's IDFA and Google's advertising ID on Android. Since ATT, the IDFA reads as zeros without the user's permission. Ch. 2
    Modelled conversionsConversions a platform estimates, from similar users it can observe, where it cannot link a conversion to an ad, and reports together with observed ones. Training labels built on them are partly model output. Ch. 2
    nurlOpenRTB win notice URL: the exchange calls it when the bid wins. On its own it does not mean the ad rendered or is billable. Ch. 7
    oCPM / oCPCOptimized CPM or CPC: the advertiser states a target price per conversion, the platform turns it into a per-impression bid with its own pCTR and pCVR, and billing stays per impression or per click. oCPX names both. The advertiser bears the platform's estimation error. Ch. 3
    OpenRTBThe IAB Tech Lab protocol for bid requests, bid responses and notices; this reader cites version 2.6.
    Optimized biddingProducts in which the advertiser states a target per action (or a return target) and the platform bids per impression on its behalf: oCPX, Google's Smart Bidding (tCPA, tROAS), and campaign types that also automate audience and placement, such as Performance Max and Advantage+. Ch. 2
    PacingOnline control of the spend rate over the budget period, e.g. by adjusting the budget multiplier toward a target spend trajectory; it works alongside, and does not replace, a hard budget cap. Ch. 4
    Performance Max / Advantage+Google's and Meta's goal-based campaign types, in which the platform's models choose audience, placement and creative as well as the bid; Performance Max buys across all Google inventory. Ch. 2
    PMPPrivate marketplace: an auction open only to invited buyers, often with a floor price; between open auctions and guaranteed deals. Ch. 2
    PostbackA server-to-server message that reports a conversion, and possibly its value, to the ad network or MMP.
    ProgrammaticBuying and selling ad opportunities through automated systems, one opportunity at a time; RTB is its auction form. Ch. 2
    PSAPublic-service ad: a placebo ad shown to control users in older experiment designs; biased when an optimizer chooses who sees ads. Ch. 6
    PublisherThe owner of the app or website whose ad slots (its inventory) are sold.
    Reach and frequencyBrand-campaign planning units: reach is the number of distinct people who see the ad at least once; frequency is the average number of times each of them sees it. Ch. 2
    Retail mediaAds sold by a retailer on its own site or app, such as Amazon's Sponsored Products; the retailer observes the sale itself, so its conversion labels are complete and timely. Also called commerce media. Ch. 2
    Retrieval and rankingThe stages of ad selection: retrieval picks a small candidate set worth scoring; ranking then estimates response probabilities and value for each candidate. Ch. 5
    Rewarded videoA video ad the user opts into in exchange for an in-app reward. Ch. 2
    ROASReturn on ad spend: attributed revenue divided by ad spend. It ignores cost of goods and does not measure incrementality. Ch. 3
    RPMRevenue per 1,000 ad requests (also called request eCPM); if each filled request yields one impression, RPM = fill rate × impression eCPM.
    RTBReal-time bidding: an auction run separately for each ad opportunity while the user's page or app waits, within a deadline the exchange sets per request (OpenRTB tmax, commonly on the order of 100 ms). Ch. 2
    SDKSoftware development kit: a library embedded in an app, e.g. by an ad network, mediation platform or MMP.
    Second-price auctionAn auction in which the winner pays the highest competing bid, or the floor if higher. “Ideal second-price” in this reader ignores floors, bid increments and fees. Ch. 4
    sellers.json / SupplyChain objectsellers.json is a file each SSP or exchange publishes listing the sellers it pays; the OpenRTB SupplyChain object lists every intermediary a bid request passed through. Ch. 6
    SettlementThe final, contractually checked computation of who owes whom. Ch. 7
    Shadow priceThe increase in the optimal objective per extra unit of a constrained resource, given by the constraint's Lagrange multiplier; for a budget, extra value (or clicks) per extra budget dollar. Written μA\mu_AμA​ for the advertiser's budget and λ\lambdaλ or μ\muμ in the appendix and the erratum. Ch. 4
    SKAdNetworkApple's earlier privacy-preserving install-attribution API (SKAN), succeeded by AdAttributionKit. Ch. 6
    SSPSupply-side platform: the seller's software, which offers each impression to many buyers, applies the publisher's floor prices and rules, and collects payment. Ch. 2
    Statistical arbitrageHere, buying impressions on CPM while selling outcomes on CPA: profitable in expectation, but exposed to conversion, attribution and payment risk. Ch. 4 appendix
    Take rateThe amount the platform keeps after paying publishers, divided by the total advertiser spend that flows through it. Ch. 3
    tCPATarget CPA: the average cost per action an advertiser asks the bidder to aim for; a bidding goal, not a billing price. Ch. 2
    Third-party cookieA browser identifier stored by a domain other than the site being visited, typically an ad-tech company embedded on many sites, so one browser can be recognized across them. Safari blocks them by default and Firefox blocks known trackers' cookies; Chrome still allows them unless the user blocks them. Ch. 2
    tmaxOpenRTB bid-request field: the maximum time, in milliseconds, the exchange allows for bids to arrive, including network latency. Ch. 7
    TOT / CACETreatment effect on the treated / complier average causal effect: the effect on users actually exposed. If control users cannot be exposed and assignment acts only through exposure (the exclusion restriction), it equals the ITT divided by the treatment group's exposure rate (the Wald ratio). Ch. 6
    tROASTarget ROAS: the return on ad spend an advertiser asks the bidder to aim for; a bidding goal, not a billing contract. Ch. 2
    View-through conversionA conversion credited to an impression that was not clicked; a click-through conversion follows a click. Ch. 6
    Walled gardenA company that owns the users, the ad slots, the auction and the measurement, such as Google, Meta, Amazon or ByteDance; outsiders cannot see user-level data. Ch. 2
    WaterfallA mediation method that calls demand sources one at a time in a configured priority order until one fills the request. Ch. 2
    Win rateThe probability of winning at bid bbb, F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b); as a metric, wins divided by bids. Ch. 4
    Winner's curseThe auction's winner is the ad with the highest prediction, and the highest of several noisy unbiased predictions is biased upward: with ten equal ads and 20% noise, about 31%. Calibrate on won impressions and shrink noisy predictions. Ch. 5

    Review record

    Every chapter has been recomputed by script and reviewed section by section; what was taken on trust is listed at the end of the latest entry.

    November 12, 2026 (ten-chapter restructure and section review).

    • Structure. The reader was reorganized into ten chapters for a reader who wants the gist first: a new “Start here” chapter with a three-hour gist path; a new landscape chapter (formats, how ads are sold, the supply chain, pricing products, the privacy era, where the money is); prediction and training data merged into one chapter; measurement separated from data; real-time systems marked optional for non-engineers.
    • New mechanisms. Billable events and bidding strategies (chapter 3): who bears each funnel segment's estimation error under CPM, CPC, CPA, oCPC and oCPM. The winner's curse (chapter 5): why auction winners are overpredicted by an unbiased model. The exercises gained one question on each and lost the two weakest (a tCPA-versus-billing question subsumed by the four-points question, and a budget-free bidding question folded into the budget question).
    • Three-question section review. Every section and optional block was checked against the owner's three questions: is it needed to understand the system, is it the best example or formula, is its math complete without extensive background. Sections that failed the first question moved into Optional blocks or were cut; chapters over 4,000 words lost at least a quarter of their main-line words. Each chapter has a verification script that recomputes every number. The per-section tables are in reviews/sections/ in the repository.
    • Not verified from a primary source. Cost guarantees in Chinese advertising platforms (practitioner sources only; described without a tolerance figure); Firefox's default blocking of known trackers' cookies (supported by a Google help page, not a Mozilla page); the wording of Meta's “total value” auction score (Meta's help page could not be fetched); GoTo/Overture's late-1990s pay-per-click ranking and the 2002 date of Google's GSP auction (from Edelman, Ostrovsky and Schwarz as remembered, not re-fetched). Performance Max's launch to all advertisers was confirmed from Google's own announcement of November 2, 2021.
    • Independent audit. Four reviewers who wrote none of the chapters recomputed every number and checked every factual claim against primary sources (company filings, the IAB/PwC report, Apple, Google and IAB Tech Lab documentation, the monograph PDF). They found no arithmetic errors. Fixed as a result: SKAdNetwork/AdAttributionKit postbacks are per install, not aggregated, and their windows start at first launch, not install (chapters 2 and 6); Chrome dropped cookie removal in 2024; Firefox partitions rather than blocks most third-party cookies; the bid-shading rule's corner case when the first-order condition stays positive; the existence of the budget multiplier, now proved by the intermediate value theorem, and its general marginal-value interpretation (chapter 4); the hard-budget proof's at-most-once guarantee, which needs per-bid state, not only a deduplication key (chapter 7); what loss notices can and cannot reveal about auction neutrality, and that AppLovin owns Adjust (chapter 8); plus clarity fixes and full citations.
    Optional: earlier review passes

    These entries use the chapter numbers of their time (eight chapters: roadmap, products, prediction and bidding, attribution and data, real-time systems, AppLovin, exercises, sources).

    November 11, 2026 (Chinese edition). An independent Claude Opus 5.5 review covered all eight chapters, formulas, tables, exercises and calculator code. It found no arithmetic or derivation errors but flagged gaps: incremental-ROAS labelling, the successful-impression condition, symbol scope, and definitions used before they were given. The editor revised accordingly and, from the source monograph, corrected one misreading in the review: there rrr is the predicted click-through rate, not a monetary value. Derivations were also checked by numerical integration, grid search over the budget-feasible region, and recomputation of every worked example.

    November 12, 2026 (English edition, first pass). Corrections to translation at inline boundaries, the pacing multiplier, the derivative variable, Axon data qualifiers, chapter references and billing units.

    November 12, 2026 (English edition, close-reading revision). Each chapter was re-derived and rewritten by a separate reviewer and cross-checked by the editor. Main outcomes: the validity range of the corrected budget-bid coefficient; KKT derivation of the calculator bid with shadow prices; pacing as projected dual subgradient descent; censored likelihoods; an uncertainty analysis of the holdout experiment; definitions before first use; the AppLovin chapter's facts checked against AppLovin's 2025 10-K and its MAX and Axon documentation; US dollars and one notation across chapters.

    November 12, 2026 (worked examples, charts and independent audit).

    • Verification scripts. For every chapter, a script recomputes every number on the page (over 1,000 checks in total) and checks that each chart's plotted function and marked points agree with the text. Charts are drawn from their formulas at build time, so a curve cannot drift from the equation it illustrates.
    • Independent audit. Four auditors who had not written the chapters recomputed everything from the page alone. They found no arithmetic errors. They did find imprecise claims, all fixed at the time, including: an open-reservations estimate that ignored winning bids; a ledger example that silently used ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1; a sum of two one-way P99 latencies; the budget-free bid quoted where the budget binds; NNN used for impressions won rather than bid requests; a pacing stability bound that holds only near μ∗\mu^*μ∗; AUC invariance stated for "monotone" rather than strictly increasing transformations; the cost bias of a wins-only threshold model; and symbol clashes across chapters (mmm, FFF, nnn).
    • Corrections found while adding detail. A $230.93 shortfall in the old real-time chapter's display-billing example was attributed to (1−ρ)B(1-\rho)B(1−ρ)B; it was lost collections, vNB/L (ρ−ρ)v\sqrt{NB/L}\,(\sqrt\rho-\rho)vNB/L​(ρ​−ρ) (that example was later cut; display-based billing is now treated only in chapter 4's appendix). The old attribution chapter's claim that treatment-on-the-treated estimation adds precision was false (the Wald ratio rescales the estimate and its standard error alike). The description of ESMM was corrected. In the errata, the overspend bound now covers the whole validity range (at least 18%), and the formula for L/6<B/N<L/2L/6<B/N<L/2L/6<B/N<L/2 was added.
    • Sources. The RTB monograph's equation and page numbers were checked against the arXiv v2 PDF. The AppLovin chapter's facts were re-checked against the 2025 10-K, the Q3 2026 10-Q and AppLovin's MAX, Axon and OpenRTB documentation, including product naming, fee wording, revenue, the Tripledot transaction and pending litigation.

    Objective revision, November 12, 2026. The bidding chapter (now chapter 4) leads with the advertiser's incremental contribution after its complete advertising bill. It explicitly separates the original unprofitable CPA contract from a no-fee direct-buying contract. The original network-spread derivation, charts, pacing example and calculator remain inside a closed optional appendix; they do not describe Axon's internal objective. Claude Opus 5.5 reviewed this revision in two passes; the second returned PASS for the supplied math, contract definitions, teaching flow, exercises and calculator code. The editor ran the build, feasible-bid grid checks, UI tests and appendix-link checks independently. This review does not establish real-platform objectives or validate the causal-value assumptions in actual markets.

    The review covers the text, code and charts under their stated assumptions. It does not establish that those assumptions hold in any real market. Not verified: whether MAX sends the final price to bidders rejected below the floor, and Apple's framework details beyond secondary summaries of Apple's documentation.
